chapters.name: The First Map
chapters.content:
“The first map,” Ilyra repeated, “and the day I learned the North Barrage had been sealed against the water and against the truth.”

Pell let the silence lengthen. It was one of his methods. Silence made an answer feel like an intrusion, a stone dropped into a clean basin. Above them, the lenses held their patient gleam.

“Maps,” he said at last. “You expect the city to believe that a drawing made you act.”

“A map does not make anyone act.”

“Then what did?”

“The conditions the map recorded.”

He opened the red folder to a page she could not see. “You have described yourself as a careful engineer. Careful engineers verify their information before making accusations.”

“Careful engineers examine the old information when the new information refuses to balance.”

“And if the old information is obsolete?”

“Then one marks it obsolete. One does not remove it.”

Pell’s eyes narrowed. “Tell the record when you first became dissatisfied with the North Barrage.”

“I did not become dissatisfied with it. I became afraid of it.”

She closed her eyes.

The chamber fell away, though not entirely. The present remained in the scrape of a clerk’s stylus, in the ache around her wrists, in Senn’s breathing behind her. Memory did not open like a door. It opened like a sluice whose hinges had rusted: reluctantly, then all at once.

It had been late autumn, nine years before the flood. Rain had fallen for six days over the western hills, and Veyr’s gutters had turned brown with silt. Ilyra was twenty-three and still believed that if a calculation was precise enough, it could force a truth into the hands of someone willing to read it.

She had been sent to the North Barrage because a pressure gauge in the lower service gallery had begun to tremble.

The assignment bore Deputy Venn’s seal. *Inspect, recalibrate, report.* Nothing urgent. Nothing that required a senior engineer to leave the warmth of the Crown offices.

The road north passed beneath the city’s walls and then along the embankment. From there, Veyr looked arranged rather than inhabited. Crown towers rose clean and pale above their terraces. Merchant warehouses crowded the middle slopes. Far below, beyond the old freight canal, the Low Quarter lay in a red-brown sprawl of roofs and chimneys. The city’s defenses followed the same order. The higher districts had stone retaining walls, overflow gardens, and three separate pumping stations. The Low Quarter had the North Barrage, the eastern embankment, and the faith that both had been built for everyone.

Ilyra entered the service gate with a ring of borrowed keys and a lantern that smoked whenever the wind changed. The barrage workers nodded to her but did not salute. They knew her from the lower channels. She was the engineer who came in person, who knelt in sewage, who measured a leak twice when the first measurement offended her.

“Gauge is making a bird of itself,” said Harl, the night keeper.

“What kind of bird?”

“Angry one.”

The needle shuddered at the edge of its brass face. Ilyra placed her fingers against the pipe. A vibration moved through the metal, too regular to be ordinary turbulence. The western channels were carrying more water than the rainfall justified.

“Where is the overflow coming from?” she asked.

Harl shrugged. “Crown line.”

“The Crown reservoirs are closed.”

“Closed to us.”

He said it without bitterness. That was what frightened her first: the sentence had become ordinary.

She followed the pipe into the inspection gallery. The North Barrage was older than the Council admitted, its original stones buried beneath layers of repair. Maps in the current service manuals showed a simple system: three intake channels, two pressure chambers, and a series of gates distributing water toward the agricultural flats east of the city. The manuals did not show the abandoned galleries beneath the eastern embankment. They did not show the emergency basins that had been filled with rubble and leased as storage yards. They did not show the narrow Crown line, which drew water uphill toward private reservoirs.

Ilyra knew these absences because she had spent two years being sent to places the official maps considered unimportant.

The pressure gauge trembled again.

She took out her notebook and copied the readings. Then she climbed a ladder into the old archive room, where obsolete plans were stacked in cabinets with swollen wooden doors. Dust lay over everything except the handles. Someone had been searching them recently.

She found the first map behind a shelf of drainage revisions.

It was a linen-backed sheet, folded into quarters and stained at the creases. The original engineer had drawn the barrage in blue and black ink, with red marks added later in a different hand. Ilyra spread it across the floor and weighted the corners with bolts.

The eastern embankment was not a single wall. It was a sequence of terraces, each one designed to take pressure from the next. If the upper chamber exceeded its reserve threshold, water should have been diverted into the storage fields east of the city. From there, it could spread shallowly, lose force, and return through the agricultural drains.

But the diversion gate was marked in red.

*Sealed pending land-use conversion.*

The date was seven years old.

Ilyra checked the current maps. The diversion gate did not exist on them. Neither did the storage fields. In their place, the service plans showed an unbroken embankment and a notation that read: *eastern protection reinforced to Crown standard.*

She looked back at the old map.

The words did not mean the embankment had been strengthened. They meant the standard had been changed. The old design assumed the eastern terraces would absorb pressure. The new design assumed pressure would never reach them because the Crown line would remain open and the upper reservoirs would take the excess.

Yet the Crown line was closed to the city’s flood system. It was drawing water away from the lower channels only when the Council required it, and returning it through the western intake whenever the private reservoirs neared capacity.

The arrangement protected the Crown District first. It also placed the Low Quarter beneath the final failure point.

Ilyra sat on the archive floor until the lantern burned low. She calculated the pressure twice, using the rainfall estimates from the service ledger and then the older figures written in the map’s margin. On the current numbers, the eastern embankment would hold for three days of sustained rain. On the older, more accurate measurements, it would hold for less than two.

At the bottom of the map, the original engineer had written a warning:

*No gate is neutral. When the upper district is sealed, the lower district becomes the basin.*

She traced the sentence with one finger.

In the interrogation chamber, Pell said, “You see how neatly the story has arranged itself. A young engineer discovers a document that confirms what she already believes about the city.”

“I discovered a pressure design.”

“You discovered an insult.”

“I discovered a failure.”

“Did you not feel humiliated by the way your superiors treated you?”

“Of course I did.”

Senn gave a short, contemptuous laugh. “There it is.”

Ilyra turned her head as far as the chair allowed. “Humiliation is not a flood forecast.”

“It can be the reason someone ignores procedure,” Pell said.

“It can. So can greed. So can indifference. So can the belief that certain people are expendable.”

“The Council was not on trial when you opened the barrage.”

“The Council was the reason the barrage had been left in that configuration.”

Pell lifted a hand. “The record will show that the accused admits professional resentment.”

“The record will show that I admitted humiliation, not that it caused the failure.”

He looked toward the screen. “The distinction is noted.”

Ilyra heard the clerk’s stylus move. She could almost see the words being selected: *resentment toward superiors; escalating grievance.* A sequence shortened until it became a motive.

Memory pulled her back.

The next morning she carried the map to the Civic Engineering Service. Rain had begun again. It struck the Hall windows in slanting threads, and the gutters outside were already overflowing. She found Halvek in the drafting room, standing over a model of the Crown fountains. Tiny brass jets rose and fell under his hand.

“I need you to look at this,” she said.

He did not look up. “If it concerns the lower channels, file it with the lower channels.”

“It concerns the North Barrage.”

“Then file it with Venn.”

“I have.”

“Did he return it?”

“He has not read it.”

Halvek sighed as though she had brought him a personal inconvenience. “Ilyra, the service has procedures.”

“Your procedures removed the eastern storage fields from the map.”

“Land-use administration did that.”

“And sealed the diversion gate.”

“Land-use administration.”

“And routed Crown reservoir discharge into the western intake.”

“That is reservoir management.”

“Water does not recognize your departments.”

At that, he finally looked at her. His face had the tired patience of a man speaking to a child who had discovered a dangerous word.

“Water recognizes gravity,” he said. “The city recognizes authority.”

She laid the old map on his desk.

For a moment his gaze fixed on the warning at the bottom. Then he folded the map before she could stop him.

“This is restricted archive material.”

“It is a safety document.”

“It is obsolete.”

“Then why was it searched?”

His fingers paused on the fold.

“Do you know what happens when junior staff mistake every inconsistency for conspiracy?” he asked.

“They submit a report.”

“They frighten workers. They disrupt maintenance. They create public panic.”

“The eastern embankment will fail if the pressure rises past reserve.”

“Then make a proper calculation.”

“I have.”

“Make one that does not begin with an accusation.”

She left his office with the map confiscated and the numbers still in her head.

By noon she had redrawn the barrage from memory. By evening she had gone to Deputy Venn. By the following week she had submitted three reports, each narrower than the last, because Pell was not the first person to teach her that a fact could be refused if it arrived carrying too much meaning.

Venn told her the Crown line was a protected asset. Sorell told her the eastern embankment had passed inspection. Halvek told her that the rain would turn.

The rain did not turn.

In the present, Ilyra felt the old certainty rise in her like pressure behind stone. She had been right. The phrase had become both her defense and her trap.

Pell leaned toward her. “You were ignored, then. Denied recognition. Passed over by men who considered you inferior. Is it not obvious that your later act was an answer to that humiliation?”

“No.”

“You wanted them to see you.”

“I wanted them to open the eastern gates.”

“You wanted the Council to fear your competence.”

“I wanted the Council to fear the water.”

“You wanted power.”

Ilyra looked at the red folder, at the missing blue notation, at the lens that kept her face centered no matter how she moved.

“Yes,” she said. “I wanted power over a system that was already deciding who would drown.”

Pell smiled. “And that is the same as wanting power.”

“No. It is the difference between holding a lever and being held beneath it.”

“An elegant distinction.”

“A necessary one.”

“Necessary,” Pell repeated, tasting the word. “You use it often.”

“Because the city uses it to excuse everything.”

“Your superiors were necessary to the city. The Crown reservoirs were necessary. The sealed gates were necessary. Then you decided your judgment outranked theirs.”

“My judgment was supported by the map.”

“Your map.”

“The city’s map.”

“Your interpretation.”

“The pressure readings.”

“Your grievance.”

“The eastern embankment.”

Their voices crossed like instruments in a confined pipe. Ilyra could feel herself reaching for control—not only of the facts, but of the order, the emphasis, the shape of the conclusion. She wanted to force Pell to admit that the catastrophe had begun long before her hand touched a gate. She wanted the lenses to carry that admission into every district.

But the first map had not saved anyone. Knowing the design had not given her authority to change it. The knowledge had made the city’s silence unbearable, and that was not the same thing as innocence.

Maret shifted at the door. Her keys struck once against her belt.

Pell noticed. “You see? Even the guard understands. A professional slight became a private war.”

Maret did not answer.

Ilyra watched her. “Ask Maret whether Lessa’s death was caused by my resentment, or by the flood line being placed beneath the laundry.”

The room tightened.

Senn stepped forward. “Do not use her name.”

“I am not using it. I am remembering it.”

“You think memory makes you honest?”

“No. I think forgetting makes the city comfortable.”

Pell closed the folder with deliberate care. “We will return to motive.”

“We have not finished with the map.”

“We have finished with the map for today.”

“No. You have finished with the portion you can fit into your theory.”

His expression hardened. “The record will show that Ilyra Voss was warned, opposed, and still chose escalation.”

“The record should show that I brought evidence to the Council.”

“Later.”

“Before the barrage.”

“Later.”

He pressed the copper stud. The lenses angled toward her, and the chamber lights brightened until the table’s surface shone like wet stone.

Ilyra held herself still. Beneath the table, her abraded wrists trembled once, then stopped. The first map had taught her that hidden structures could govern visible disaster. The interrogation was teaching her the same lesson in another form.

A city could seal a gate and call it protection. A magistrate could seal a fact and call it order.

She looked directly into the nearest lens.

“The eastern embankment was not built to protect the Low Quarter,” she said. “It was built to fail after the Crown District had been saved. I told the Council. They called me alarmist. That is the next thing that happened.”

chapters.name: The Price of Water
chapters.content:
The first thing Ilyra learned about water was that it could be made to look innocent.

It came down the pipes at the appointed bell. It gathered in the public cisterns beneath blue-painted signs. It appeared on the tables of the Crown District in glass pitchers clouded with beads of cold, and in the Low Quarter it arrived brown at the edges, measured by ladle and watched by a clerk.

When people went thirsty, the notices called it a failure of weather.

When children fainted in the ration lines, the notices called it an unfortunate seasonal condition.

When the grain stores closed their shutters and families began boiling leather, the notices blamed theft.

Ilyra had been eight when she first understood that a lie could have pipes beneath it.

“Again,” Pell said.

His voice brought the chamber back around her. Bronze lenses hung above the circular table, each one reflecting a pale, warped version of her face. The clerk’s stylus waited over the record.

“You were speaking of your family,” Pell said. “Your brother Tomas. Tell the record why he was arrested.”

Ilyra looked at the red folder beside his hand. It was closed now, but she could feel the pages inside it, the missing things pressing against the cover. She had spent years believing that if a sequence was exact, no one could make it mean something else. Pell was teaching her otherwise. A fact could remain in the record and still be buried beneath the shape of the question.

“Tomas was arrested for taking a ration ledger,” she said.

“For stealing?”

“He took it.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“It is what happened.”

Senn shifted behind her chair. His glove creaked. Ilyra imagined his sister in the south laundry, red scarf damp against her throat, and felt the old reflex rise in her: sort the loss, compare the causes, assign the weight. The reflex had once made her good at engineering. It had become a way of avoiding the dead.

Pell leaned forward. “Was Tomas angry with the city?”

“Tomas was sixteen.”

“That was not an answer.”

“It was the answer you wanted to exclude.”

Maret glanced toward the lenses. The chamber was too warm. Heat gathered under Ilyra’s collar and ran down her back, though the stone beneath her chair remained cold. Somewhere beyond the wall, the Hall’s public galleries murmured. Veyr liked to hear a prisoner remember. It gave the city the pleasure of believing that pain could be made orderly after the fact.

Ilyra closed her eyes.

In the Low Quarter, every morning began with the water bell.

Their room stood above a cooper’s shed on Gutter Street, where the air smelled of wet wood, yeast, and the black river beyond the retaining wall. There were four of them then: her mother, Tomas, Ilyra, and their father, who had vanished into a dredging crew and returned only in rumors. Her mother kept a strip of blue cloth tied around the handle of the water pot. She said it made the pot easier to find in the dark. Ilyra knew she tied it there because blue was the color stamped on Low Quarter water permits, and because she wanted one thing in their room to look official.

At the first bell, Tomas would take the pot and join the line.

At the second, Ilyra followed with a smaller tin cup.

At the third, the clerk measured each household’s allotment according to the number written on its brass tag. The number could be reduced for unpaid district fees, increased for a registered birth, suspended for a disputed address. The city called this distribution. In the Low Quarter they called it the hand.

The hand gave. The hand withheld. No one ever saw the arm attached to it.

One summer the ration fell by a quarter. The Council’s notice said the upper reservoirs had suffered an algae bloom. Ilyra was old enough to read the notice and young enough to believe the reason might be true. Then Tomas took her through the service alley behind the Crown market. He showed her carts of clear water rolling uphill under guard, their barrels marked for the conservatories.

“Algae doesn’t climb,” he said.

The next day the water clerk told their mother that Tomas had been pushing ahead in line. He had not. The clerk had seen him looking at the cart.

After that, Tomas began collecting papers.

He gathered discarded permits, spoiled delivery tickets, torn notices, anything that showed a household’s allotment beside the amount actually received. He copied figures onto the backs of old flour wrappings. He discovered that three streets in the Low Quarter had lost water while a new bathhouse opened in the Merchant District. He discovered that grain deliveries were delayed whenever the dock unions threatened a strike, then released at higher prices through private sellers.

“Numbers make people nervous,” their mother told him.

“Good,” Tomas said. “People should be nervous.”

Ilyra admired him for saying it. She admired the way he could make a fact stand upright and glare.

She was the one who taught him to draw columns.

Together they made a table on the floorboards: street, date, ration, household count, missing measure. Ilyra used a burnt stick for a pencil. Tomas supplied the anger. When their mother coughed, they stopped and listened until the coughing passed.

The ledger belonged to the district ration office on Lantern Row. It was not a grand book. Its leather cover had swollen from damp, and one brass corner was missing. But it contained the official household numbers and the adjustments made by clerks. Tomas believed it would prove that the shortages were not accidents.

Ilyra told him not to take it.

“Copying is slower,” he said.

“Copying is safer.”

“Safe for whom?”

She hated him a little for the question because she had no answer that did not sound like surrender.

The night he took the ledger, rain hammered the roof. The water bell had been silent for two days because the canal gates were closed, though the official announcement claimed repairs were underway. Their mother lay beneath three blankets, shivering despite the heat. Her breath made a wet clicking in her chest.

Tomas tied his boots.

“If you go,” Ilyra said, “they’ll see you.”

“They already see us.”

He kissed their mother’s forehead. Then he looked at Ilyra with an expression she would spend years misremembering as certainty.

“Keep the table,” he said.

He came back before dawn with the ledger under his coat.

The guards came after him.

There were four of them, though the ration office was less than a street away. They carried hooked staves and wore the gray sashes of civic custody. One asked Tomas where he had obtained the book. Another struck him in the ribs when he did not answer quickly enough. Their mother rose from the mattress and tried to put herself between them. She was already weak; one guard pushed her down.

Ilyra remembered the sound of her head against the floor more clearly than Tomas’s face.

“Wait,” Tomas said.

The guard holding him laughed. “You should have waited for your allotment.”

He was taken to the district lockhouse. The ledger vanished with him.

For three days their mother and Ilyra went from office to office. The first clerk said the arrest was procedural. The second said Tomas had endangered public order. The third said no one named Tomas Voss was being held. At the fourth office, a woman with silver ink on her fingers advised Ilyra to stop asking questions if she wanted her family’s water permit renewed.

On the fifth day, they were told Tomas had contracted fever.

On the sixth, that he had refused food.

On the seventh, a guard left a parcel outside their door. Inside were Tomas’s boots, his belt, and a folded scrap of paper with no writing on it.

The city recorded his death as an illness occurring during temporary detention.

Ilyra found the phrase months later in a copied register. Illness occurring. As if sickness had entered the lockhouse by choice. As if the walls had not been shut against air, and as if the bruise beneath Tomas’s eye had not been the color of a spoiled plum.

In the chamber, Ilyra opened her eyes.

“He died under custody,” she said.

Pell’s stylus moved. “From fever.”

“After being beaten.”

“Was that established?”

“It was visible.”

“To whom?”

“To me.”

Pell gave a small, almost sorrowful sigh. “Your grief is understandable, Ilyra. But private impressions cannot replace evidence.”

She laughed once. It hurt her throat.

“The city’s evidence was a sentence written after his body was gone.”

“Your brother stole a civic document.”

“He stole the city’s explanation of hunger.”

Senn’s hand touched the back of her chair. Not striking. A warning, or perhaps a reminder that he was there. Maret looked down at the floor.

The winter after Tomas died, the water froze in the upper pipes. Not in the Crown District. There, the fountains continued to run beneath heated grates, and the Crown notices praised the engineers for preserving civic dignity during an exceptional cold season.

In the Low Quarter, the ration lines formed before dawn. People wrapped their hands in rags and stood on the ice. Grain was mixed with ground husk. The flour scratched the mouth. A child on Gutter Street ate paste made from wallpaper and died before spring.

Their mother stopped leaving the room.

At first she said the cold had settled in her joints. Then she forgot whether Tomas had gone to work or to the lockhouse. She called for him at night. Sometimes she accused Ilyra of hiding him. Sometimes she pressed her fingers to Ilyra’s lips and whispered that the walls were listening.

The walls were listening. Ilyra knew that much.

She began taking measurements. Temperature near the window. Hours between her mother’s coughing fits. Weight of the water pot before and after boiling. She made columns because columns did not moan. They did not ask when Tomas was coming home. They did not look at her with the dull accusation of someone who had survived.

One morning their mother could not stand. Ilyra ran to the district clinic, but the nurse asked for a heating allotment token. Ilyra had none. She offered Tomas’s blue permit. The nurse read the name, lowered her eyes, and said the token had been suspended pending review.

“Who reviews it?” Ilyra asked.

The nurse did not answer.

Their mother lived until the thaw. She died while Ilyra was counting breaths.

The last number she wrote was forty-three.

For years afterward, she would tell herself that Tomas and her mother had not died separately. The ration system had killed Tomas, and the cold had finished what the lockhouse began. The city had made a chain of causes and then named each link an accident. This interpretation gave her something solid to hold. It gave shape to the anger. It gave her a reason to study channels, reservoirs, gates, and the habits of people who called themselves custodians while deciding which streets could drown.

But there was another truth beneath it, less useful and harder to carry.

She had wanted the city to be guilty because she was guilty of wanting the city to suffer.

Not as a child. Not at first. As a child she had wanted Tomas returned. She had wanted her mother warm. Later, when she learned the scale of Veyr’s design, she began imagining the officials standing in their bright districts with water rising around their shoes. She imagined them reading the notices they had written while the words blurred in the flood.

In the interrogation chamber, Pell watched her carefully.

“Is that when you began to hate the Council?” he asked.

“I began to understand it.”

“Those are not the same.”

“No.” Ilyra’s wrists throbbed where the restraints had abraded them. “They are not.”

“And yet you chose the North Barrage.”

“I chose to act after every lawful warning failed.”

“You chose to punish a city.”

“I chose a gate.”

Pell’s expression sharpened, pleased to find the old distinction. “You see how easily you turn people into mechanisms?”

For an instant she saw the barrage map on the table between them instead of the red folder. Eastern basin. Crown line. Pressure differential. Open. Close. Sacrifice.

She had spent half her life resisting the city’s habit of treating people as quantities. Then she had learned to speak in its language so fluently that she could no longer tell whether she was using the numbers or hiding inside them.

Maret’s voice came softly from the door. “Her mother died after the permit was suspended?”

Pell did not look at her. “That is not relevant to the charge.”

“It is relevant to why she—”

“Guard Maret.”

The word ended the sentence, but not the question. It remained in the chamber with the heat, the lenses, and the careful movement of the clerk’s stylus.

Ilyra thought of Tomas telling her to keep the table. She had kept it. She had kept the figures, the copied notices, the dead household numbers. She had carried them into the service, into the Council offices, into the barrage tunnels. She had believed that preserving the pattern was a form of loyalty.

Now she understood that a pattern could become a weapon in the hands of the person who drew it.

“Write this,” she said.

The clerk looked up.

Pell’s mouth tightened. “You do not dictate the record.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “But you cannot say I did not tell you.”

She faced the nearest lens.

“Tomas Voss died in civic custody after taking a ration ledger. My mother died the following winter after the city suspended our heating and water permits. Those deaths taught me that Veyr makes its choices look accidental. They also taught me to mistake understanding a cause for having the right to decide the consequence.”

No one moved.

“Write both,” she said. “If you leave out either one, you will be telling another convenient lie.”

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: seated at the central table in the circular interrogation chamber of Veyr's Hall of Civic Judgment. Goal: preserve the complete sequence and structural causes of the flood in the official record, resisting Pell's effort to isolate blame and reduce motive to vengeance. Relationships: distrusts and openly challenges Magistrate Oren Pell; opposed by Senn, whose sister Lessa died in the Low Quarter; wary of Maret, who remains conflicted and attentive; understands the city and its surveillance machinery as an audience shaped by official selection; carries enduring grief for her brother Tomas and mother, whose deaths she connects to Veyr's engineered scarcity. Knowledge: knows Veyr's hereditary districts determine occupation, education, housing, and legal standing; knows her appointment was treated as a public exception and that she was assigned lower-channel work; knows Senior Engineer Halvek, Deputy Venn, and Director Sorell dismissed her objections; knows the North Barrage's old design made the eastern storage fields a pressure basin, that the diversion gate was sealed after a land-use conversion, and that current plans erased this danger while the Crown line remained protected; knows she submitted three increasingly narrow reports that were dismissed; knows the red folder omits the reserve-capacity notation and that a service-archive refusal letter is being softened in the record; remembers that water and grain were deliberately managed by district, that Tomas died in civic custody after taking a ration ledger, and that her mother died after their permits were suspended. Possessions: prison clothing, no visible tools, and memory of the Hall's relay geometry, missing documents, old barrage map, dismissed reports, ration records, and family losses. Condition: physically weakened with abraded wrists, intellectually controlled and combative, grieving and increasingly honest about how anger shaped her loyalties; aware that her desire to control the sequence and consequences resembles the authority she opposes.

set.name: Oren Pell
set.description: Location: presiding at the central table of the circular interrogation chamber beneath Veyr's surveillance lenses. Goal: obtain a confession of personal vengeance, control which facts enter the record, and keep responsibility for the flood focused on Ilyra rather than the Council. Relationships: adversarial toward Ilyra; commands Senn, Maret, clerks, lens attendants, and screened Council witnesses; politically aligned with the Council. Knowledge: knows Ilyra's appointment history and technical testimony could expose hereditary district policy; possesses the red barrage-report folder, which omits the reserve-capacity notation; recognizes Ilyra has identified a missing service-archive refusal letter and is challenging the clerk's record; knows her family history of scarcity and custody death can be framed as the emotional source of vengeance; is framing her professional humiliation, grief, and anger as motives for terrorism. Possessions: white judicial robes, bronze chain of office, red report folder, procedural authority, and access to the surveillance relay. Condition: composed and calculating, angered and cautious as Ilyra exposes how the record is shaped, but pleased when her grief can be used to narrow the public narrative toward personal vengeance.

set.name: Maret
set.description: Location: guarding the interrogation chamber door near Ilyra, Senn, Pell, and the screened witnesses. Goal: enforce custody and protect the procedure while deciding what Ilyra's responsibility means in relation to her sister Lessa's death and the systemic evidence emerging in the interrogation. Relationships: civic guard; conflicted toward Ilyra, neither forgiving nor simply hostile; works with Senn but restrains his rough handling; subordinate to Pell's procedure; increasingly willing to question what counts as relevant to justice. Knowledge: knows Lessa was twenty-two, worked at the south laundry, hated the water ration, wore a red scarf with a brass pin, and was killed in the flood; has heard Ilyra expose the hereditary district system, the erased North Barrage design, the clerk's altered wording, and the history of engineered scarcity that preceded Ilyra's choices; recognizes that the interrogation's procedure itself is being used to limit truth and that Ilyra's warnings were dismissed before the disaster. Possessions: civic uniform and keys. Condition: tired, guarded, emotionally shaken but increasingly attentive to the distinction between procedure and justice; tense when Ilyra invokes Lessa and quietly questions Pell's exclusion of family and district history.

set.name: Senn
set.description: Location: standing behind Ilyra's chair in the circular interrogation chamber, guarding her under Pell's orders. Goal: enforce custody and make Ilyra answer for the flood that killed his sister, whom he believes she murdered through deliberate action. Relationships: openly hostile to Ilyra; works alongside Maret but resents her interventions; subordinate to Pell while driven by grief. Knowledge: has heard Ilyra admit opening the gate and explain the city's district hierarchy, the North Barrage's erased storage fields, the technical warnings dismissed by her superiors, and the family history that shaped her anger; suspects her insistence on sequence is an evasion of responsibility, while also sensing that civic custody and ration policy contributed to the losses; knows the interrogation is broadcast and that the record is being controlled. Possessions: civic uniform, keys, authority over Ilyra's movement. Condition: angry, grieving, physically forceful, and unsettled by the possibility that the city's institutions contributed to the disaster; reacts sharply when Ilyra invokes Lessa as evidence of the city's design and remains suspicious that structural explanation is being used to escape personal guilt.
As a child in the Low Quarter, Ilyra and Tomas documented ration shortfalls and discovered water and grain were diverted or delayed according to district and political pressure.
Tomas Voss was arrested after taking the district ration ledger, died in civic custody after reported mistreatment, and was officially recorded as having died from illness during temporary detention.
After Tomas's death, Ilyra's mother deteriorated through the following winter and died after the family's heating and water permits were suspended or denied.
Ilyra recognized in the interrogation that her grief and anger led her to treat understanding a system's causes as if it granted her the right to decide its consequences.

Ilyra's childhood experience of engineered scarcity and Tomas's death in civic custody will continue shaping her belief that Veyr disguises deliberate sacrifice as accident, while her admission that she confused understanding causes with authority over consequences will complicate her later choices.

chapters.name: The Feast Approaches
chapters.content:
Three days before the Feast of Renewal, the North Barrage began to speak.

It spoke through the iron under Ilyra’s boots, through the tremor in the handrail and the thin ringing of bolts that had held for ninety years. It spoke in the pressure gauges, whose needles climbed by fractions too small for a frightened man to notice and too steady for an engineer to dismiss.

The city was preparing to celebrate the river’s obedience.

Flags had already been strung between the towers. White cloth for renewal, bronze thread for the Crown, blue ribbons for the water guilds. At night, workers fitted lamps to the ceremonial platforms above the river. The governor’s barge had been polished until its prow shone like a blade.

In the barrage control room, Ilyra watched the eastern gauge tremble past the red mark.

“Read it again,” Halvek said.

She looked at him. “You heard me.”

“Read it again.”

“The upper reservoir is exceeding the seasonal load. The eastern embankment has lost margin. If the diversion gate remains sealed and the Crown line stays at full draw, the storage fields will take the pressure.”

Halvek folded his hands over his belly. He had been a senior engineer before Ilyra was born and had acquired, with age, the confidence of a wall. Behind him, Deputy Venn stood beside the map cabinet, tapping a finger against the brass lock.

“Storage fields,” Venn said. “That term is obsolete.”

“The fields are still there.”

“Not in the current plan.”

“Water does not consult the current plan.”

The room went quiet except for the gauges.

Ilyra had brought three reports to the Council offices by then. The first contained the old maps and the complete pressure sequence. Halvek had taken it from her desk and called the archival markings unverified. The second reduced the argument to measurements. Venn had returned it with a note requesting that she avoid inflammatory language, though the only words she had used were basin, overflow, and probable casualties. The third contained one page, six figures, and a diagram any apprentice could have followed.

Director Sorell had read it while standing beside a window overlooking the Crown gardens.

“You are asking us to frighten the city over a possibility,” he had said.

“I am asking you to open a diversion gate before the possibility becomes water in someone’s bedroom.”

“The Feast is in three days.”

“That is why the load is rising.”

Sorell glanced at the diagram and then at her face. “You have a gift for making maintenance sound like insurrection.”

She had wanted to ask whether it was insurrection only because she was the one saying it. Instead, she pointed to the Crown line.

“Why is this still drawing at full capacity?”

“Because the Crown District cannot be deprived during the festival.”

“And the Merchant District?”

“Food stores and guest houses require protection.”

“The Low Quarter is downstream.”

Sorell’s expression did not change. “The Low Quarter is downstream of everything.”

In the interrogation chamber, Pell lifted his eyes from the page.

“Did he say that?”

“Yes.”

“Exactly?”

“Near enough to the truth.”

The clerk hesitated. Pell gave him a look, and the stylus resumed its scratching.

Ilyra could feel the old room returning around her: the smell of lamp oil, wet stone, and hot metal; the bronze faces of the pressure gauges; the distant clatter of crews working behind sealed doors. Memory did not arrive as a picture. It arrived as a system. Every sound belonged to a mechanism. Every person occupied a position within it.

Three days before the Feast, she had gone back to the barrage after midnight.

The official work crews were on the upper terraces, reinforcing the Crown retaining wall with new stone and iron braces. She saw their lamps from the eastern service walk. Below, the lower spill channels remained choked with silt. Two maintenance pumps had been stripped for parts. The diversion gate had been painted with a red mark: SEALED PENDING LAND-USE CONVERSION.

The city had not forgotten the gate.

It had remembered it and chosen not to use it.

Ilyra descended to the service office. A young clerk named Pellis was asleep over a stack of work orders. He woke when she struck the desk.

“Where are the crews assigned to Channel Six?”

He squinted at her badge. “Crown reinforcement.”

“Channel Six is below the eastern fields.”

“Yes.”

“Why are they reinforcing the Crown wall?”

“Written order.”

“From whom?”

He reached for the top sheet. “Governor’s infrastructure committee.”

“Let me see it.”

Pellis pulled the order back against his chest. “Engineer Voss, I can’t release committee documents.”

“I am asking to inspect a work assignment.”

“It has a seal.”

“So do I.”

He looked at the bronze badge pinned to her coat, then at the red stamp on the order. His fear was not of her. It was of the possibility that he might answer correctly and still be punished.

“The crews are under emergency priority,” he said. “Crown District first. Merchant District second. Lower channels if capacity permits.”

“Capacity permits what?”

He lowered his voice. “Evacuation.”

The word struck harder than any accusation.

“Evacuation of whom?”

Pellis looked toward the dark windows. “I don’t know.”

But he did know enough to be afraid.

Ilyra took the work order when he reached for another page. The paper bore three seals: the infrastructure committee, the water guild, and Governor Arven Dault’s private office. Beneath the assignments, in a smaller hand, someone had written: Preserve primary districts. Accept lower-basin discharge if required.

Lower-basin discharge.

Not flood. Not deaths. Not homes.

The language had been washed clean of human beings.

She carried the order to the civic announcement network before dawn.

Veyr’s announcement towers stood at the intersections of the main districts, their copper throats pointed toward every street. The network had been built for emergency warnings and used mostly for market notices, festival songs, and the governor’s speeches. Ilyra still possessed an engineer’s access to the relay room. Her badge opened the outer door.

Inside, the air smelled of dust and hot wire. Rows of crystal switches glowed beneath glass covers. A relay attendant rose from his stool.

“Engineer Voss.”

“Connect me to the public band.”

He stared at the work order in her hand. “For what purpose?”

“Flood warning.”

“Has one been authorized?”

“No.”

“Then I cannot open the band.”

“You can. You are choosing not to.”

His eyes went to the ceiling lens.

Ilyra softened her voice. “Listen to me. The barrage is above safe load. The Council has begun reinforcing the upper districts and has left the lower channels without crews. If the pressure rises another two points, the eastern embankment will fail.”

“Then report it.”

“I have.”

“Through the proper office.”

“The proper office signed this.”

She put Dault’s order on the console.

The attendant did not touch it. “I have a family in the Merchant District.”

“So do the people downstream.”

“I didn’t say they mattered more.”

“You don’t need to say it. The order says it for you.”

For a moment she thought he might reach for the switch. His hand lifted, hovered, and fell.

Then every crystal on the console went dark.

Her badge gave a small mechanical click as the network revoked her access.

The attendant flinched. “I’m sorry.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “You are frightened.”

“Yes.”

“That is not the same thing.”

She left before the guards arrived.

At the Council’s emergency session that afternoon, Governor Dault sat beneath a mural of the river in spring. The painter had given the water a color it had never possessed: clear blue, without silt, reflection, or bodies. Around him were Sorell, Venn, two water-guild masters, and the deputy commander of civic defense. A map of Veyr covered the wall.

The Crown District was marked in white chalk. The Merchant District was marked in gold. The Low Quarter was unmarked.

Ilyra stood before the map with her report in her hand.

“Remove the seal from the diversion gate,” she said. “Open it by one-quarter turn. Reinforce the eastern embankment and reduce the Crown draw until the pressure falls.”

Dault examined her as though she were an interesting tool with a crack in it.

“And what becomes of the festival?”

“The festival becomes a day when the city does not flood.”

“The ceremonial platform is built over the river.”

“Then move it.”

“You make that sound simple.”

“It is simpler than rebuilding ten thousand homes.”

One of the guild masters laughed under his breath. He wore a ring shaped like a wave, its silver crest polished bright.

“Engineer Voss,” Dault said, “your projections assume the old basin remains structurally sound.”

“It does.”

“You have not inspected it.”

“I inspected it yesterday.”

“Without authorization.”

“Because the authorized inspection was canceled.”

Dault turned to Sorell. “Was it?”

Sorell spread his hands. “We redirected personnel to the primary districts.”

“Primary,” Ilyra said. “Meaning Crown and Merchant.”

“Meaning the districts whose failure would endanger the whole city,” Sorell replied.

“The lower districts are part of the city.”

“Civic language is not improved by sentiment.”

Ilyra looked again at the map. The unmarked quarter seemed larger than the others, not because of its size but because the Council had refused to draw a boundary around what it was willing to lose.

Dault touched the white chalk with one finger.

“If the embankment fails,” he said, “what is the probable discharge?”

“Enough to overrun the eastern fields and enter the Low Quarter.”

“How many casualties?”

“I cannot calculate that without knowing how many evacuation orders will be honored.”

A silence followed. It had the shape of an answer.

The deputy commander leaned toward the map. “If the lower basin takes the first surge, it will reduce pressure on the Crown wall.”

“It will destroy the lower basin.”

“Temporarily.”

“There are tenements there.”

“Some.”

“Workshops. Schools. The south laundry.”

Dault sighed. “No one is proposing destruction, Engineer. We are discussing contingencies.”

“Contingencies with preassigned victims.”

His face hardened. “You are relieved from barrage duty until after the Feast.”

“Governor—”

“Your access to the announcement network has been revoked. Your reports will be reviewed by Director Sorell. You will surrender all unauthorized copies of the old maps.”

He said it gently, almost kindly. That was what made it obscene.

Ilyra placed the work order on the table.

“Who wrote this?”

Dault glanced at it. “A committee clerk.”

“Who told him to accept lower-basin discharge?”

“Engineer, you are confusing administrative language with intent.”

“No. I am translating it.”

Sorell moved first. He took the order from the table and folded it once, then again, until the words disappeared inside the paper.

“Leave,” Dault said.

She did.

Outside the chamber, bells began ringing for the Feast rehearsals. Their notes passed through the Hall’s stone and entered her body as vibration. Somewhere, decorators were hanging bronze ribbons. Somewhere, crews were driving braces into the Crown wall. Somewhere below, children were sleeping in rooms whose floors had begun, imperceptibly, to tilt.

In the present, Pell’s stylus stopped.

“You disobeyed a direct order,” he said.

“I was removed from duty.”

“That was not my question.”

“No. It was your conclusion.”

He closed the red folder. “After the Council rejected your recommendation, you decided to act outside the law.”

“After the Council refused to warn the people it governed, I continued looking for a way to warn them.”

“By force?”

“By any means available.”

Senn gave a bitter sound behind her. “There it is.”

Ilyra turned as far as the restraints allowed. “What?”

“The part where you make yourself the only person willing to do what had to be done.”

She wanted to deny it. The denial rose quickly, cleanly, supported by facts. She had gone to the network. She had shown them the order. She had asked for a quarter turn, not a revolution.

But beneath those facts was the memory of the white-and-gold map, the Low Quarter left blank. Beneath that was another image she had not offered Pell: Governor Dault standing on the ceremonial platform while the river climbed toward him, his polished shoes filling with brown water.

She had seen it before she ever opened the gate.

“I was trying to correct an engineering failure,” she said.

Pell leaned back. “And the government?”

“The government had made the failure worse.”

“That is not what I asked.”

Ilyra looked into the nearest lens. Her face appeared there in fragments, one eye stretched across bronze, her mouth cut by reflected light.

“I did not think I was challenging the government,” she said.

It was almost true.

At the time, she had called it a correction. A diversion. A necessary release of pressure. The language had steadied her hands as she copied seals and studied lock schedules. It had kept the human shape of the decision at a distance.

But the city had taught her that names mattered. Flood became discharge. Hunger became shortage. Sacrifice became contingency.

She had learned those substitutions from the people she despised.

“Write this,” she told the clerk. “Three days before the Feast, the Council knew the barrage was failing. It reinforced the Crown and Merchant districts and left the Low Quarter downstream. I tried to use the announcement network. They disconnected me.”

Pell’s eyes narrowed. “And then?”

Ilyra felt the old machinery begin to turn: reports, seals, gates, pressure, the seductive narrowing of a problem until only her hand remained on the lever.

“Then,” she said, “I began to consider what an unauthorized intervention would require.”

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: seated at the central table in the circular interrogation chamber of Veyr's Hall of Civic Judgment after recounting events three days before the Feast. Goal: preserve the sequence showing that the Council knew of the impending flood, prioritized the Crown and Merchant districts, and blocked her public warning, while resisting Pell's effort to make her unauthorized intervention appear purely personal vengeance. Relationships: distrusts and openly challenges Magistrate Oren Pell; opposed by Senn, whose sister Lessa died in the Low Quarter; wary of Maret, who is increasingly disturbed by the Council's treatment of the Low Quarter; understands that Governor Arven Dault, Halvek, Venn, and Sorell chose protected districts over downstream residents; recognizes that her own language of engineering correction concealed an emerging desire to make powerful officials afraid. Knowledge: knows the North Barrage was above safe load three days before the Feast; knows the Council's work order assigned Crown reinforcement first, Merchant reinforcement second, and lower-channel work only if capacity permitted; knows the order used the phrase accept lower-basin discharge; knows Dault removed her from barrage duty, revoked her announcement access, and ordered her old maps surrendered; knows she tried to warn the public through the civic announcement network but the warning was disconnected; has begun considering an unauthorized intervention and knows that the distinction between correcting a failure and challenging the government is becoming morally unstable. Possessions: prison clothing, no visible tools, and memory of Dault's sealed work order, the Council map, the announcement relay geometry, revoked engineer access, old barrage maps, dismissed reports, ration records, and family losses. Condition: physically weakened with abraded wrists, intellectually controlled and combative, newly confirmed in her belief that lawful channels were closed, but unsettled by the private image of Dault and the governors trapped by rising water; aware that her desire to control the sequence and consequences resembles the authority she opposes.

set.name: Oren Pell
set.description: Location: presiding at the central table of the circular interrogation chamber beneath Veyr's surveillance lenses. Goal: obtain a confession of personal vengeance and unauthorized intent, control which facts enter the record, and keep responsibility for the flood focused on Ilyra rather than the Council. Relationships: adversarial toward Ilyra; commands Senn, Maret, clerks, lens attendants, and screened Council witnesses; politically aligned with Governor Arven Dault and the Council. Knowledge: knows Ilyra's technical warnings were rejected, that crews were directed to reinforce the Crown and Merchant districts, that Dault removed her from barrage duty, and that she attempted to use the civic announcement network; possesses the red barrage-report folder and understands these facts can either expose Council priorities or be reframed as the setting for her illegal escalation; knows her admission that she began considering unauthorized intervention can support the prosecution's narrative of deliberate vengeance. Possessions: white judicial robes, bronze chain of office, red report folder, procedural authority, and access to the surveillance relay. Condition: composed and calculating, pleased to have Ilyra admit unauthorized intent, but cautious because her account places official decisions immediately before it.

Knowledge: knows Lessa was twenty-two, worked at the south laundry, hated the water ration, wore a red scarf with a brass pin, and was killed in the flood; has heard Ilyra establish that the Council knew of the danger, reinforced Crown and Merchant districts, accepted lower-basin discharge, revoked Ilyra's warning access, and removed her from duty; recognizes that Ilyra's unauthorized choice followed institutional refusal but remains uncertain whether that reduces her guilt. Relationships: openly hostile to Ilyra; works alongside Maret but resents her interventions; subordinate to Pell while driven by grief; increasingly unsettled by evidence that the Council knowingly left the Low Quarter downstream. Knowledge: has heard Ilyra admit opening the gate, explain the city's district hierarchy, identify dismissed warnings, and establish that Dault's Council reinforced the protected districts while blocking a public warning; suspects her claim of correcting an engineering failure is an evasion of responsibility, but now knows the city treated the Low Quarter as a pressure sink before she acted; knows the interrogation is broadcast and that Pell is controlling the record. Possessions: civic uniform, keys, authority over Ilyra's movement. Three days before the Feast of Renewal, Ilyra confirms through a governor's work order and an emergency Council session that crews are reinforcing the Crown and Merchant districts while officials accept lower-basin discharge as a contingency for protecting them.
Ilyra attempts to broadcast a flood warning through Veyr's civic announcement network, but her engineer access is revoked and the public warning is never transmitted.
Governor Arven Dault removes Ilyra from barrage duty, orders her unauthorized maps surrendered, and leaves the Low Quarter exposed to the predicted flood.
Ilyra will forge an authorization order and steal a civic seal to enter the North Barrage during the Feast, using the Council's own procedures to begin her unauthorized intervention.

chapters.name: The Shape of a Warning
chapters.content:
Pell did not ask what the intervention required.

He smiled as if the omission were an answer.

The clerk’s stylus moved across the page. Ilyra watched the black lines gather beneath his hand, neat and obedient. The words she had spoken entered the record stripped of their weather: no hot wire, no sealed doors, no low quarter left blank on the Council map. Only intention remained. She had considered an unauthorized intervention. She had sought means. She had persisted after lawful authority withdrew its permission.

Pell opened the red folder again.

“Let us examine the warnings,” he said.

“I have already given them.”

“You have given us a sequence of allegations.”

“Measurements.”

“Political language disguised as measurements.”

He drew out a sheet and placed it between them. The paper was familiar. The crease down its center was hers, made when she had folded it in the barrage stairwell to keep rain from blurring the figures.

At the top, in her hand, stood: NORTH BARRAGE—LOAD INSTABILITY.

Below it, in a darker ink, someone had added: The writer alleges deliberate district abandonment and demands immediate redistribution of Crown water privileges.

Ilyra stared at the sentence.

“I did not write that.”

“No one said you did.”

“Then why is it attached to my report?”

“Because it summarizes your purpose.”

“My purpose was to prevent a breach.”

“Your purpose,” Pell said, “was to force the Council to surrender control of the water allocation.”

“Reducing a draw during an emergency is not surrendering control.”

“To you, perhaps. To the people responsible for the city, it was an attempt to seize it.”

He produced another sheet. This one contained six figures, the same six she had put on the one-page report. Beside them, a clerk had written: Arithmetic incomplete. Casualty projection unsupported. Tone inflammatory.

The figures were not incomplete. They were the minimum needed to show the eastern embankment’s remaining margin. The casualty projection was unsupported only because the Council had refused to disclose the occupancy rolls for the lower terraces.

“What happened to the second page?” she asked.

Pell’s expression remained smooth. “There was no second page.”

“There were four pages.”

“You are mistaken.”

“I drew the cross-section on the reverse.”

“The reverse is blank.”

She looked at the paper. The reverse was blank now. A faint graphite smear remained near the lower edge, like a bruise beneath skin.

In the screened gallery, someone shifted. The lenses clicked as they adjusted focus.

Pell leaned toward her. “You see how difficult this is? You insist that every omission proves conspiracy. A missing page becomes suppression. A redirection of crews becomes a plan to murder. A warning becomes a demand for political reform.”

“A warning can be both a warning and a demand.”

“Not in a technical report.”

“That is why the report was changed.”

His eyes sharpened. “Changed by whom?”

Ilyra glanced at the clerk. The young man’s stylus had stopped. Beyond him, the lens attendants sat behind their bronze screens, faces hidden. She remembered the archive refusal letter from her earlier testimony, the missing reserve-capacity notation, the way facts were not denied so much as made to vanish between one copy and the next.

“By the people who need the record to begin after they made their decision,” she said.

Pell tapped the altered summary. “The trial is not interested in your theories about clerks.”

“The trial is interested in proving that I had no reason to act except resentment.”

“The trial is interested in why four thousand eight hundred twelve people died.”

He said the number carefully, allowing it to settle in the chamber. Senn’s shoulders tightened. Maret looked toward the floor.

Ilyra had heard the number before. It was printed on the execution broadsheets, beneath her face and above the promise of purification. Four thousand eight hundred twelve: precise enough to appear honest, small enough to be managed.

“And the people who prepared the lower basin?” she asked.

“Not on trial.”

“The people who knew the flood was coming?”

“Not on trial.”

“The people who cut the announcement network?”

Pell folded his hands. “We are discussing your conduct.”

There it was. Not a question but a wall. The trial had already been built around its desired conclusion, and every fact brought against it would be forced to serve as decoration. Her warnings would prove agitation. Her knowledge would prove planning. Her anger would prove motive. The Council did not need to show that she was wrong. It only needed to make her rightness look like the weapon of a dangerous woman.

For one breath, she imagined overturning the table. The thought arrived with an almost comforting clarity: the angle of her shoulder, the distance to Pell, the guard’s reaction time, the weight of the bronze chain at his throat.

Then the memory beneath the thought opened.

Three nights before the Feast, after Dault removed her from the barrage, Ilyra returned to the service quarter by a route that no longer appeared on official maps.

The old drainage passage began behind a disused lime kiln below the eastern wall. Its iron door had been painted over so many times that the hinges looked embedded in the stone. Ilyra carried a lamp, a pry bar, and no authorization at all. She had copied the passage’s location from a map she was not supposed to know existed.

The map lay in the abandoned survey archive beneath the municipal library, inside a drawer labeled RIVER IMPROVEMENTS—DISCONTINUED. She had found it by remembering a notation from her first year of service: a reference to pre-Crown hydraulic works, marked with the initials of an engineer who had been dismissed for refusing to certify the upper wall.

The archive keeper, old Beren, had seen her read the drawer label.

“Those plans are not current,” he said.

“That is why they may be useful.”

“They were rejected.”

“By whom?”

“By everyone who had the authority to reject them.”

He had watched her lift the map from its sleeve. The cloth smelled of mildew and dust. Across its surface, in faded blue and brown, the river had been drawn before Veyr’s districts were divided into hereditary jurisdictions.

There were channels beneath the channels. Overflow fields. Maintenance stairs. Three gates omitted from the new survey.

And beneath the North Barrage, a broad storage basin marked COMMON RELEASE, its lettering crossed out in red.

“Why was this sealed?” she asked.

Beren gave a tired shrug. “The Crown wanted gardens where the water went.”

“Gardens cannot replace a basin.”

“Neither can a warning, apparently.”

She copied the map by lamplight until her fingers cramped. Then she folded the original inside her coat.

Beren caught her wrist.

“Engineer Voss.”

She looked at his hand.

“If they discover you took it, they will say you stole state property.”

“It is state property.”

“No. It belongs to whoever is willing to use it against you.”

The drainage passage led beneath the workers’ terraces and emerged near the old survey house. Two people were waiting there beside a stack of tool crates.

Nera Vale stood first.

She was seventeen, perhaps eighteen, narrow-shouldered and quick-eyed, with copper dust on her sleeves and a braid tied back using a strip of blue gasket cloth. She had been assigned to the lower-channel crews before they were redirected to the Crown wall. Beside her stood Hobb, a pump mechanic whose left thumb had been crushed in a winch, and Pellis, the frightened clerk from the service office.

Nera’s gaze went immediately to the map beneath Ilyra’s arm.

“You found it,” she said.

“You knew it was there?”

“I knew the old survey house had a basement. I did not know the basement had a river in it.”

Hobb grunted. “Everything has a river in it if you dig far enough.”

Pellis glanced back toward the passage. “We should not be here.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “We should be at the barrage.”

Nera smiled, and the expression held no fear yet. That frightened Ilyra more than Pellis’s trembling.

“Tell us what you need,” Nera said.

Ilyra spread the copied plan across a crate. The lamp flame bent in the draft, making the blue channels ripple.

“The eastern storage fields are still connected to the old release system,” she said. “The current survey erased the connection, but the masonry will remain. If the central sluice is opened by a quarter turn and the western pressure is reduced, the surge can be drawn away from the lower terraces.”

“Can,” Hobb said. “Not will.”

“Can, if the emergency valves hold.”

“Do they?”

“I have not inspected them.”

Nera traced a finger along the old line. “And if they do not?”

“Then we close the sluice and use the secondary channels.”

“Which ones?”

Ilyra pointed to three narrow marks near the western wall. “These.”

Nera frowned. “Those are under the storage fields.”

“Most of the fields are empty.”

“Most?”

Ilyra felt the answer catch behind her teeth. The Council had not issued occupancy rolls. The old maps showed farm plots, not tenements. She had seen lamps below the eastern terraces, but she had not counted them. Displaced workers lived wherever the city left a dry floor, and the city left few.

“People can be moved,” she said.

“Who will move them?”

“We will warn them.”

“How?”

Ilyra looked at the map instead of Nera. “Through the service bells. Through the crews.”

It was not an answer. Nera knew it.

“You said the public network was cut.”

“It was.”

“Then people need to know before anything opens.”

“I am working on that.”

Nera’s eyes lifted. She admired Ilyra; it was visible in the way she leaned toward every uncertainty, trusting that Ilyra had already built a bridge across it. Trust was a form of pressure. Ilyra understood that better than anyone, and still she let the girl keep it.

“We need tools,” Ilyra said. “A lock key for the old service gates. Two relay bypasses. Grease for the western spindle. And a current crew schedule.”

Pellis swallowed. “The schedule is restricted.”

“You can access it.”

“I can lose my position.”

“You can lose more than that if the barrage fails.”

He looked at Nera, as though hoping youth might contain a gentler order. Nera only said, “Get the schedule.”

Hobb gave a low laugh. “There. The apprentice has spoken.”

Nera flushed, but she did not look away from Ilyra.

For the next hour, they divided tasks. Hobb would find the bypasses. Pellis would copy the crew assignments. Nera would acquire the old gate key from the survey workshop. Ilyra would inspect the access route and calculate how long the pressure could be held.

She did not tell them about the governors’ platform.

She did not tell them that the Feast had gathered every official who had ignored her beneath one roof of painted wood and bronze.

She did not tell them how often she had imagined the water rising around their ceremonial shoes.

The omission felt, at first, like protection. They needed the mechanics, not the anger. They needed a plan narrow enough to carry without breaking. If Nera knew that the chosen date had a second purpose, she might mistake vengeance for strategy—or worse, she might understand it.

So Ilyra gave her only the clean shape of the warning.

The barrage was overloaded. The Council had blocked lawful remedies. The old channels could reduce the pressure. They would act because no one else would.

Nera listened as if each sentence were a fastening being tightened.

When the others left, she remained beside the map.

“Do you think we can save everyone?” she asked.

Ilyra almost said yes. The word would have been easy, warm, and false.

“No,” she said.

Nera’s face changed.

“We can reduce the damage,” Ilyra continued. “We can keep the eastern wall from taking the full load.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “It is what I can calculate.”

Nera studied her for a long moment. “My mother says engineers always answer the question they prefer.”

“Your mother is observant.”

“She says that is why governors like engineers. We make terrible things sound arranged.”

The lamp popped. A bead of oil rolled down the glass.

Ilyra folded the map.

“Your mother is wrong about one thing,” she said. “Governors do not like engineers. They like obedient engineers.”

Nera’s smile returned, smaller now. “Then you are brave.”

Ilyra felt, unexpectedly, the beginning of shame.

“Bravery is not the same as being right.”

“But you are right.”

Ilyra looked toward the passage, where black water ticked somewhere behind the wall.

“I am right about the pressure,” she said.

She did not say: I may be wrong about what follows.

In the interrogation chamber, Pell placed the altered reports in a careful row.

“Your own associates,” he said. “Pellis, Hobb, Nera Vale. All confirm that you spoke of unauthorized access and interference with civic controls.”

“Nera was an apprentice.”

“She was old enough to understand you.”

“She was young enough to trust me.”

The sentence escaped before Ilyra could stop it.

Pell noticed. Of course he noticed.

“Trust,” he said. “That is an interesting word.”

“No. It is an inconvenient one.”

“Did you tell her the full extent of the danger?”

Ilyra heard Nera’s voice beneath the chamber’s silence: Do you think we can save everyone?

“No,” she said.

Senn shifted behind her. Maret’s keys gave a small metallic chime.

Pell’s smile faded, pleased by the admission. “Why not?”

“Because I did not know the full extent.”

“Or because you feared she would refuse?”

Ilyra looked at the blank reverse of her report. The erased cross-section waited there like a buried door.

“I decided what she was allowed to know,” she said. “That was my choice.”

Pell leaned back, sensing a confession.

But she would not give him the shape he wanted.

“I did not invent the flood,” Ilyra said. “I did not invent the Council’s order. I did not invent the city’s decision to leave people downstream. But I chose what to conceal from someone who trusted me. That belongs to me.”

The lenses clicked and held her face.

For the first time since the questioning began, Pell seemed uncertain whether the admission helped him. He wanted a single line from warning to murder, a clean descent with no other hands on the rope. Ilyra had given him a knot instead.

The clerk resumed writing.

Outside, somewhere above the Hall, the city rehearsed its Feast songs. The melody passed through stone, bright and hollow, while beneath it the old water moved toward the gates.

chapters.name: The Stolen Seal
chapters.content:
The seal had belonged to a dead man for six years.

Ilyra remembered that first because it was the sort of detail Pell would call irrelevant. The magistrate liked facts that arrived already sorted: a hand on a lever, a gate opening, a district drowning. He disliked the small continuities that made an act possible—the clerk who left a cabinet unlocked, the widow who sold a uniform, the dead official whose authority remained useful because no one had bothered to cancel it.

In the interrogation chamber, Pell turned a page in his red folder.

“You obtained a civic authorization,” he said. “Is that correct?”

“I obtained paper bearing the appearance of authorization.”

“By fraud.”

“By necessity.”

Senn’s hand tightened on the back of her chair. The wood pressed into the bruises beneath her shoulders. Maret stood beside the door, watching Pell instead of Ilyra.

Pell smiled with no warmth. “You see how easily she changes the word. Fraud becomes necessity. Theft becomes intervention. Murder becomes—what did you call it?”

“I have called nothing murder for you.”

“Not yet.”

Above them, one of the surveillance lenses clicked and adjusted. Ilyra could feel the city leaning closer through the glass.

She had stolen the seal on the thirty-ninth day before the flood, though at the time she had not thought of it as stealing. She had thought of it as returning a voice to an order that had been silenced.

That was the first lie she told herself.

The second was that the date had been chosen only for practical reasons.

The Feast of Renewal gathered every governor, deputy, investor, and ceremonial engineer onto the river platform beneath the Crown terraces. It was the one night when the Council made a public display of its command over water. Bronze boats carried lanterns in formation. Children in white masks threw paper flowers into the current. The governors drank from silver cups while the floodgates opened and closed in a sequence designed to resemble obedience.

If the barrage had to be entered without permission, the Feast provided the thinnest guard rotation and the deepest distraction. If she needed to redirect water through the old storage fields, crews would be watching the platform. If the Council tried to deny what she had done, half the city would have seen the first movement of the river.

Strategic leverage, she had written in her notebook.

She had not written: Let them see the water turn toward them.

The authorization order began in the records room beneath the east service stairs. Ilyra had no access to the civic archive anymore, but access was a habit as much as a credential. She knew which doors were inspected, which locks were decorative, and which clerks left their work gloves on the radiator when the room grew warm.

Pellis had found the blank forms in a drawer marked RETIRED BRIDGES. Hobb had supplied a strip of old pressure paper thin enough to lift an impression from a discarded order. Nera had stood lookout in the corridor, her blue gasket-cloth tie dark against her braid.

“Tell me again,” Nera whispered.

Ilyra sat beneath the green-shaded lamp, ruling lines with a steel edge. “The order authorizes emergency inspection and manual release at North Barrage Four. It names me as acting field engineer under Director Sorell’s delegated authority.”

“Nobody believes Sorell would delegate to you.”

“Nobody will read it if the seal is right.”

“That is not the same as believing it.”

“It only needs to survive long enough to get us through the first door.”

Nera glanced toward the corridor. “And after that?”

“After that, the machinery will decide.”

Ilyra kept her eyes on the paper. She could hear what Nera wanted to ask. What happens if the machinery does not decide as you expect? What happens if the old channel is blocked? What happens if the storage fields are not empty?

She had answered those questions for herself in columns.

The old hydraulic map showed three possible releases beneath the North Barrage. The eastern storage fields could take a sudden discharge if the feeder channels remained open. The industrial terraces could absorb a second wave, though the foundries would lose power for at least two days. The common-release basin, if the old retaining wall had not been filled during the Crown expansion, might divide the pressure before it reached the Low Quarter.

Might.

She had calculated the word six different ways and it remained the same size.

Nera touched the edge of the form. “You said the storage fields were abandoned.”

“They are marked inactive.”

“That is not what I asked.”

Ilyra looked up. Nera’s face was young enough that fear had not yet learned to disguise itself as irritation. Her trust was not a soft thing. It had weight. Ilyra felt it each time Nera followed an instruction without demanding the whole map.

“The fields are the safest release,” Ilyra said.

“For whom?”

“For the city.”

Nera held her gaze a moment longer, then nodded. It was a small movement, but Ilyra recognized the surrender in it. Nera had allowed the answer to stand because Ilyra was the senior engineer, because the reports had been blocked, because someone had to choose.

Ilyra bent back over the order.

The handwriting had to imitate Sorell’s without flattering it. Sorell pressed too hard on downstrokes, as if every letter owed him obedience. Ilyra copied the pressure, the cramped signature, the unnecessary phrase pursuant to civic continuity. She left one blot near the margin, because clean documents looked newly made. Then she held the page above the steam kettle until its fibers softened and acquired the faint waviness of something carried through a damp service tunnel.

Pellis watched from the corridor.

“If they catch you,” the clerk said, “they will say I forged it.”

“They will say you were coerced.”

“That is meant to comfort me?”

“No. It is meant to be accurate.”

He gave a thin laugh. Pellis had the narrow shoulders of a man built for fitting between shelves. He knew where the records slept and which ones had been removed. He had brought her the crew schedules, but his hands shook when he handed them over.

Ilyra understood the shaking. Courage was not a substance that filled a person. It was a debt a person incurred and kept paying.

The seal waited in the office of Deputy Venn, inside a locked case beside the ceremonial keys. Civic seals were not supposed to be portable. They authenticated the city’s will, and the city’s will was meant to remain in rooms where ordinary hands could not reach it.

But Venn had a habit of carrying the case between offices during festival preparations. He liked to show visitors the silver disk engraved with the three towers and the river beneath them. He called it the city’s promise.

Hobb had watched him place it in a desk drawer at dusk.

The office smelled of dust, hot metal, and Venn’s clove oil. Ilyra entered wearing a maintenance coat borrowed from a dead pump supervisor. Hobb waited outside with a tool bag and a story about a leaking pressure line. Nera had the forged order folded beneath her shirt.

“Three minutes,” Hobb murmured.

“Two,” Ilyra said.

“You always say two.”

“And you always take three.”

The drawer lock was old. She opened it with a flattened hairpin, then lifted the seal case. For one breath she saw herself reflected in the silver: a narrow face, dark hair pinned badly, eyes too bright from sleeplessness.

Not a criminal, she thought.

Then: Not yet.

The case held the seal in black wool. It was heavier than she expected. The disk had a deep central groove where generations of officials had pressed it into wax. She imagined all those orders—ration diversions, eviction notices, emergency closures, district transfers—leaving the same round authority behind.

The seal had never distinguished between a command that saved and a command that sacrificed. It only made obedience look official.

She wrapped it in cloth and put it inside her coat.

At the door, footsteps sounded in the outer hall.

Hobb began his story loudly. “If the west line ruptures, Deputy, you’ll have steam in the archive vault.”

A guard answered him. “You have a work order?”

“Of course I have a work order. Everyone has a work order. The question is whether your office has filed it.”

Ilyra slipped through the side passage and found Nera waiting under the stairwell. The apprentice’s face had gone pale.

“Was it there?”

Ilyra nodded.

Nera exhaled. “Then we can enter.”

“We can pass the first gate.”

“And the second?”

“If the relay bypass works.”

“And the manual chamber?”

“If the old key fits.”

Nera stared at her. “You have an answer for everything except whether we come back.”

Ilyra wanted to say that coming back was not the measure of a sound operation. She wanted to say that if they stabilized the pressure, the city would continue, and continuation was a kind of return.

Instead she said, “We will follow the sequence.”

The sequence was what she trusted. Numbers did not praise her or pity her. They did not call her dockside resentment. They did not tell her that the Low Quarter could absorb one more failure. A pressure curve rose or fell. A gate was open or shut. A consequence could be estimated if one had enough information and the discipline not to flinch from it.

But she had not given Nera enough information.

In the chamber, Pell leaned back. “You selected the Feast deliberately.”

“Yes.”

“For the reduced patrols?”

“And the public visibility.”

“Public visibility,” Pell repeated. “You wanted witnesses.”

“I wanted the Council unable to deny the danger.”

“Or unable to escape it.”

The lens clicked again. Senn shifted behind her.

Ilyra could have denied it. She could have said that the governors’ presence was incidental, that no engineer considered the people standing on a platform when calculating a discharge. The denial rose easily. It had the smoothness of a practiced defense.

She let it die.

“The platform was part of my calculation,” she said.

Pell’s pen paused. “Explain.”

“The governors controlled the water because they believed distance made them safe. They gathered above the river to celebrate that belief. If the first release occurred beneath them, they would see the pressure they had assigned to other districts.”

“That is not engineering.”

“No. It is politics.”

“You intended to frighten them.”

“I intended to make them act.”

“You intended to make them helpless.”

For an instant, the chamber vanished.

She saw the ceremonial platform lit in white and bronze. Governor Dault stood at its center with one hand raised toward the lantern boats. Sorell laughed beside him. Venn wore a red sash. Their shoes were dry. Their glasses were full. Below them, the river held the reflected towers in a trembling line.

Then the line broke.

Water climbed the steps. The governors turned toward one another, searching for the person who could command it. Dault’s mouth opened. Sorell reached for a guard. Venn dropped his glass.
