Goal: stabilize the feeder and prevent a larger surge into the lower districts, while resisting the impulse to open the door and abandon the machinery. Relationships: Nera now openly condemns her refusal to help the trapped; Hobb witnesses her continued choice; she remains opposed to Pell and the Council. Knowledge: remembers that she once consciously chose a valve key and larger hydraulic design over a child stranded on a roof; knows Lio's water is chest-high, knows the trapped workers are in danger, and recognizes that her technical justification conceals deliberate choices. Possessions: ceremonial white-and-bronze engineer's coat, forged authorization, stolen civic seal, old gate key, wax pencil, and the brass valve key in her bleeding hand; access to damaged barrage controls. Condition: soaked, bruised, exhausted, bleeding at the palm, procedurally focused, and morally shaken as she repeats the choice to preserve machinery over the nearest life.

set.name: Oren Pell
set.description: Location: in the Hall of Civic Judgment beside the surveillance lenses and civic clerks during the Feast, directing the official response to reports of surging lower channels. Goal: maintain the official narrative, suppress destabilizing evidence, and keep responsibility focused on Ilyra. Relationships: adversarial toward Ilyra and aligned with Dault and the Council; commands guards, clerks, and surveillance operators including Senn and Maret. Knowledge: knows lower channels are surging, has access to Lessa's testimony identifying Ilyra's refusal to help a child, and has ordered that testimony withheld until the Council chooses how to use it; still does not know the full extent of the barrage chamber's failures. Possessions: judicial robes, bronze chain of office, red report folder, Lessa's testimony packet, procedural authority, and surveillance access. Condition: composed, calculating, controlling, and irritated by Senn's resistance while preparing to convert evidence into a prosecutorial weapon.

set.name: Senn
set.description: Location: in the Hall of Civic Judgment beside the surveillance lenses and clerk's testimony packet during the Feast, away from North Barrage Four. Goal: enforce custody and make Ilyra answer for the flood while resisting Pell's suppression of evidence and the Council's narrative. Relationships: openly hostile to Ilyra because Lessa died, but now also distrustful of Pell and the Council; works with Maret under Pell's authority. Knowledge: has read Lessa's recorded account identifying Ilyra as the white-coated engineer who heard a child calling from a roof and turned away with a brass key; knows Pell is withholding the statement from the public record and that new lower-channel surges are being sealed. Possessions: civic uniform, keys, and access to the testimony packet and surveillance area. Condition: angry, grieving, morally unsettled, and increasingly prepared to challenge official procedure.

set.name: Nera Vale
set.description: Location: inside North Barrage Four's flooded control chamber at the sealed emergency door and maintenance tube, beside Ilyra and Hobb. Goal: save the trapped workers and child Lio rather than accept machinery or calculations as sufficient justification. Relationships: has lost trust in Ilyra and challenges her directly; remains allied with Hobb and the trapped lower crew. Knowledge: knows Ilyra deliberately keeps the emergency door shut, hears that Lio's water is chest-high, and understands that Ilyra is again choosing control over immediate rescue. Possessions: apprentice tools, copied hydraulic map, wax pencil, copper-dusted work clothes, and blue gasket-cloth tie. Condition: soaked, frightened, furious, physically strained, and poised to act against Ilyra's order.

set.name: Hobb
set.description: Location: inside North Barrage Four's flooded control chamber near the damaged control frame and sealed emergency door. Goal: keep the failing machinery from causing a larger surge while trying to prevent the trapped workers and child from being abandoned. Relationships: allied with Nera and still physically assisting Ilyra, but now quietly accusatory after seeing her repeat the choice to preserve controls over people. Knowledge: knows the western feeder is backing up, the pressure is unstable, Lio is trapped below, and opening the door would destroy the controls and alter the flood path. Possessions: tool case, bypass wires, damaged lantern, maintenance instruments, and burns from hot spray. Condition: injured, soaked, exhausted, frightened, and increasingly doubtful that Ilyra's command is courage.

Ilyra remembers a prior flood in which she consciously abandoned a child stranded on a roof because she chose to carry the valve key to the pump station, then allowed the official success of the drainage repair to obscure the child's fate.

Lessa's recorded testimony states that she saw Ilyra hear a child calling from a roof and turn away while carrying a brass key; Senn reads the statement and understands Ilyra's refusal as a conscious choice rather than an unknowable accident.
In the present barrage chamber, child Lio reports that floodwater has reached her chest while Ilyra chooses to continue stabilizing the feeder controls instead of opening the emergency door.
Lessa's account that Ilyra heard a child calling from a roof and chose the brass valve key must be entered during the later trial testimony, where its incompleteness will be treated as total truth.

The child Lio and the workers trapped below North Barrage Four remain in immediate danger while Ilyra continues operating the feeder controls, requiring the next chapter to resolve or sharply escalate their fate.

chapters.name: The Drowned Quarter
chapters.content:
The key entered the feeder lock.

For half a second, nothing happened. Then the mechanism caught. Deep below the chamber, a series of iron teeth began to turn, each one striking the next with a blunt, deliberate clack.

Nera watched Ilyra’s hand. “What did you open?”

“The lower release.”

“You said it would hold.”

“It will.”

“That is not what I asked.”

The emergency door groaned behind them. Water threaded beneath its lower seam, black and quick. From the maintenance tube came a burst of voices—Hobb shouting, someone praying, Lio crying out that she could no longer feel the floor.

Ilyra leaned over the gauge board. The needle dropped three marks.

“There,” she said.

Nera stared at her. “You’re pleased.”

“No.”

“You sounded pleased.”

The feeder shuddered. A pressure line split somewhere in the wall, spraying a white jet across the chamber. Hobb threw himself against the handwheel and caught it before it spun loose. Steam rolled over his shoulders.

“Lower release is taking,” he called. “But the east channel is full.”

“Open the spill gate.”

“It’s chained.”

“Cut it.”

“With what?”

Ilyra looked at the tool case floating near the steps. Hobb followed her gaze, swore, and lunged through the water. Nera seized the speaking lever.

“Lio,” she said into the tube. “Stay against the wall. Hold the rail.”

“There is no rail.”

“Then hold a worker’s hand.”

“They’re slipping.”

“I know.”

Ilyra heard the child’s breath, thin and fast. A memory opened beneath the sound—not the roof this time, but the city after the roof, when the flood had ceased to be a single advancing body and become a thousand separate violences.

The first tenement fell at the corner of Ash and Tallow.

It did not collapse like a tower. It sagged. The lower storey filled, its windows turning into dark mouths. The upper floors leaned toward the street, carrying beds, cooking pots, sleeping families, and the painted wooden saint from the stairwell. For a moment the whole building remained upright in a posture of astonishment.

Then the walls folded.

A woman on the third floor waved a white shirt through a window. Ilyra saw the shirt vanish. She saw three people fall with the outer wall. She saw a boy catch a drainpipe and hang there until the pipe tore free.

The water carried the sound away before it carried the bodies.

At the pump station, Ilyra had been told to clear the intake grates. She waded through a street filled with furniture and broken shutters. A workshop roof had come down across the channel. Brass fittings, wool, splintered barrels, and human hands turned in the current around her legs.

“Don’t stop!” someone shouted.

She did not know who had spoken. Everyone sounded like the voice of the city.

She found the first grate beneath a table. She found the second beneath a dead horse. The third was blocked by a door with two children clinging to its upper edge. Their father was on the other side, beating against the wood, unable to reach them.

Ilyra took the pry bar from her belt.

The pump wheel was turning. Every moment mattered. The eastern wall was holding because the drainage channel had opened, but the station would clog if she did not clear the grate.

She looked at the door. She looked at the wheel.

Someone else pulled the children away. Or the current did. She had never learned which.

The memory shifted. She was inside a cooper’s workshop, waist-deep in water, trying to lift a roof beam from a trapped apprentice. The boy’s name was Perren. She remembered that because he kept saying it, as if a name could be tied to a person and keep him from floating away.

“Perren,” Ilyra repeated, though he could not hear her through the hammering water.

The pump station bell rang twice. The second ring broke in the middle. The wall behind her cracked, and the beam rolled toward the boy. Ilyra had a choice of reaching for him or keeping the intake gate clear. She reached for the gate. The beam struck the water with a force that lifted her from her feet.

When she came up, Perren was gone.

She had not put his name on the wax board. There had been no line for workers whose records belonged to another district.

The memory broke into flashes.

A loom workshop filling to the rafters, women climbing onto the beams while dyed water spread blue and red across the floor.

A bell tower ringing under the flood, its warning swallowed one note at a time.

A mother tying her infant to her chest with a curtain cord, then losing the cord when a roof beam struck her.

Two brothers separated in a stairwell, one carried upward in a barrel and the other downward through a doorway.

A dog swimming beside a floating mattress until the mattress turned over.

The river entering houses through fireplaces.

The river leaving houses through windows.

The city’s lowest streets becoming black corridors in which every shout came from nowhere.

At the station, the engineers had made lists on wax boards. Street. Building. Occupants. Rescued. Missing. The wax softened in the heat of the pump room, and names ran into one another. By dawn, no one could tell whether a mark meant a person found alive or a person last seen.

Ilyra had wiped a sleeve across the board and erased half a family.

She had done it without noticing.

In the barrage chamber, Hobb returned with the cutter. He struck the spill chain once, twice. The metal gave with a sound like a gunshot.

The gauge dropped.

Behind the door, the pounding stopped.

Nera turned toward the maintenance tube. “Hobb.”

“I heard it.”

“Open the door.”

Ilyra looked at the needle. It had fallen below the red band, but the eastern channel still trembled. The pressure had not dispersed. It had moved.

“If we open now, the surge enters the control chamber.”

“They may already be under water.”

“I know.”

Nera’s face went utterly still. “You keep saying that as if knowing is a kind of rescue.”

Ilyra reached for the next lever.

The water rose through the Low Quarter.

It climbed the market steps and entered the ration offices first. It soaked ledgers, dissolved seals, and lifted the Council’s carefully numbered scarcity into a brown slurry. Grain stores burst. Casks rolled through alleys. People who had been denied a second bucket broke into warehouses and found the floors already submerged.

The flood took the signs from the streets. It took the paint from doors. It took the chalk marks rescuers used to show which rooms had been searched.

At the western terraces, displaced families crowded onto roofs that the maps had labeled empty. They had come from the demolished river camps, from villages purchased by the Crown reservoir, from districts whose names did not appear on the city plans. They had built lean-tos between old retaining walls and believed the stone made them safe.

Ilyra had believed it too.

A wave struck the terraces just before dusk. Lanterns scattered across the water. Some floated upward. Some winked out. The people who had been waiting for rescue became points of light moving in opposite directions, each one briefly visible before the dark closed over it.

A boy on a chimney waved a strip of blue cloth. Ilyra saw him from the station window and marked the location on her sleeve with wax. Before she could send a boat, the roof turned. The cloth remained caught on the chimney after the water took him. For days afterward she would find herself looking for that blue scrap among the wreckage, as if the cloth were an unfinished instruction.

The ceremonial river platform stood above the eastern quay, bright with Feast banners and polished bronze. Musicians had been playing when the first channel burst. The crowd turned toward the sound, expecting fireworks.

Then the platform tilted.

Officials fell against one another. Guards formed a ring around Governor Dault. A section of railing tore loose and swept three magistrates into the river. The governor’s white cloak snagged on a chair. He cut himself free with a ceremonial knife, crawled across the slick boards, and reached the private stair beneath the platform.

The stair led to a barge no map admitted existed.

Ilyra saw it only once, through the pump station’s broken upper window. Dault was carried aboard by two guards while people behind the platform called for help. His face was pale. Not repentant. Not surprised. Merely offended that the city had become dangerous without asking permission.

The barge pushed into the flood.

It passed a woman clinging to a lamp bracket. It passed a boy trapped in a tree. It passed a whole roof turning slowly beneath the Feast lanterns.

Dault did not look toward them.

At the control chamber, Nera seized the speaking lever from Ilyra.

“Lio,” she said. “Can you hear me?”

Static answered.

“Lio?”

The tube hissed. A distant impact traveled through it, followed by a low rush.

Ilyra’s hand froze over the controls.

“Open the door,” Nera said.

“The pressure—”

“Open it.”

“We have not cleared the feeder.”

“Open it.”

Ilyra saw the gauge, the lines, the narrowing window. She saw the flooded streets below. She saw the platform struck and Dault escaping. She saw the child on the roof and the child in the corridor become one shape in her mind, a small hand extended toward the person holding the key.

She turned the wheel.

The emergency door moved one inch.

Water exploded through the gap.

Hobb shouted and threw his weight against the control frame. Nera was knocked sideways. Ilyra caught the wheel with both hands as the door slammed back into its housing.

“Not yet,” she gasped.

Nera struck her across the face.

“You don’t get to say that anymore.”

The chamber lights went out.

In the dark, Ilyra heard the lower districts collapsing.

Not one sound. Thousands. Brick breaking. Glass breaking. People calling names. Timber rolling through streets. The long iron moan of a bridge giving way. A bell drowning beneath the water.

She worked by touch.

One lever. Then another. The spill gate opened. The feeder bucked. The pressure tore through the eastern channel and spread into the old storage fields, where it found no empty earth but rows of houses, workshops, and tents.

The pump station received the surge at midnight.

By then, Ilyra’s coat was torn from collar to hem. Blood had dried across her palm. She climbed over the collapsed intake wall and reached the main drainage wheel. Around her, the station had become a ruin of iron, mud, and broken lantern glass.

A dead engineer lay beneath the stairs with his hand closed around a wrench.

Ilyra pulled the wrench free.

The wheel resisted. She braced one foot against the masonry and turned. The mechanism moved a fraction. Water poured through the lower culvert, carrying beams and roof tiles into the dark.

“Again,” she told herself.

She turned it again.

A survivor crawled from the pump room. His hair was white with plaster, though he could not have been old. “Stop,” he said.

“If I stop, the western basin backs up.”

“It’s already gone.”

“The lower channel can still take pressure.”

“Who told you?”

Ilyra looked at the wheel. “The calculations.”

The man laughed once. It was not amusement. “The calculations didn’t have a house.”

She turned the wheel.

At dawn, the rain stopped. Water remained in every street.

Rescue crews began counting the dead. They found bodies in tenements, workshops, cellars, courtyards, and trees. They found them in boats that had overturned and in rooms whose doors had swollen shut. They found children whose families were alive and families whose children were not. They found no complete account of the people from the western terraces.

The Council’s first notice listed 3,906 deaths.

By the second day, the number was 4,812.

The figure settled because the clerks needed it to settle. Survivors said it was higher. They named neighbors omitted from the registers, lodgers never entered on household rolls, workers sleeping in workshops, children whose births had not been recorded, and those carried away before anyone could say their names.

At the ruined pump station, Ilyra kept turning the wheel.

She told herself she was preventing another surge.

She told herself the eastern wall had held because of her.

She told herself that if the calculations were right now, then the deaths had not made them meaningless.

A woman arrived carrying a soaked ledger against her chest. She had lost one shoe and wore a child’s red scarf around her wrist. “Write them,” she said.

Ilyra looked at the ledger. “Who?”

“All of them.”

“There is no room.”

The woman shoved the book into her hands. Brown water ran between its pages. “Then make room.”

Ilyra opened it. The names had blurred into dark threads. She could not tell where one ended and another began. She held the ledger above the pump’s heat, waiting for the ink to separate, while the woman watched her with an expression more terrible than hatred: expectation.

Beyond the broken window, Veyr lay under a skin of brown water. A red scarf hung from a chimney. A brass pin glinted in the mud below it.

Ilyra stopped turning.

For the first time since the gate opened, there was no lever in her hand, no pressure gauge demanding an answer, no mechanism that could make the past obey.

She looked toward the drowned quarter and could not decide whether she had stayed at the pump station to repair the damage or to prove that she had been right about the water.

The distinction frightened her more than the flood.

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: at the ruined pump station in the drowned Low Quarter after the flood, beside a damaged drainage wheel and a soaked ledger of blurred names. Goal: restart drainage and prevent further surges, while confronting whether her labor is repair or an attempt to prove her calculations right. Relationships: Nera and Hobb have witnessed her repeated choice of machinery over immediate rescue; she remains opposed to Pell, Dault, and the Council, while survivors increasingly see her as responsible for the devastation. Knowledge: knows the flood destroyed much of the Low Quarter, that the ceremonial platform was struck but Dault escaped by private barge, and that the official death toll of 4,812 excludes people survivors remember; does not know the final fate of Lio and the trapped workers below North Barrage Four. Possessions: torn ceremonial white-and-bronze engineer's coat, forged authorization, stolen civic seal, old gate key, wax pencil, brass valve key, wrench, and the soaked ledger handed to her by a survivor. Condition: soaked, bruised, exhausted, bleeding at the palm, emotionally stunned, and unable to distinguish technical responsibility from moral accounting.

set.name: Oren Pell
set.description: Location: in the Hall of Civic Judgment during and after the Feast, directing clerks, surveillance operators, and sealed reports about the flood. Goal: preserve the Council's authority and prepare a solitary-terrorist narrative that excludes its evacuation decisions and protected routes. Relationships: aligned with Dault and the Council, adversarial toward Ilyra, and increasingly suspicious of Senn's resistance. Knowledge: knows lower channels surged and that the Council has reasons to suppress reports; will receive news that the Low Quarter was devastated and Dault escaped, but does not yet know the full fate of the barrage workers. Possessions: judicial robes, bronze chain of office, red report folder, Lessa's testimony packet, procedural authority, and surveillance access. Condition: composed, calculating, controlling, and preparing to turn mass devastation into prosecutorial evidence.

set.name: Maret
set.description: Location: on civic guard duty in Veyr's Hall and escort routes after the flood, awaiting orders about the devastated lower districts. Goal: enforce custody and protect procedure while learning whether her sister Lessa's death is being used to conceal the Council's responsibility. Relationships: works under Pell with Senn; conflicted toward Ilyra because Lessa died, and increasingly distrustful of official claims that district history is irrelevant. Knowledge: knows Ilyra entered the barrage and that protected districts were reinforced; now knows the Low Quarter has been devastated, but does not know the full fate of the workers or child below North Barrage Four. Possessions: civic uniform and keys. Condition: tired, guarded, and emotionally vulnerable as grief collides with orders.

set.name: Senn
set.description: Location: in the Hall of Civic Judgment near the surveillance lenses and sealed testimony packet after reports of the flood's devastation arrive. Goal: make Ilyra answer for the deaths while resisting Pell's suppression of evidence and the Council's attempt to hide its own abandonment. Relationships: grieving over Lessa and hostile toward Ilyra, but increasingly distrustful of Pell and the Council; works with Maret under civic authority. Knowledge: knows Lessa's account identified Ilyra's conscious refusal to help a child, and now knows the lower districts have been devastated and the official response is being controlled. Possessions: civic uniform, keys, and access to the testimony packet and surveillance area. Condition: angry, grieving, morally unsettled, and increasingly ready to challenge official procedure.

set.name: Nera Vale
set.description: Location: last known inside North Barrage Four's flooded control chamber near the emergency door and maintenance tube, after forcing Ilyra to crack the door open. Goal: reach and save Lio and the trapped workers, rejecting further sacrifice of people for machinery. Relationships: openly condemns Ilyra and has lost trust in her judgment, while remaining allied with Hobb and the lower crew. Knowledge: knows the flood has become a mass disaster, that Ilyra repeatedly chose the controls over immediate rescue, and that the emergency door briefly opened before pressure slammed it shut; does not know whether Lio and the workers survived. Possessions: apprentice tools, copied hydraulic map, wax pencil, copper-dusted work clothes, and blue gasket-cloth tie. Condition: soaked, frightened, furious, physically strained, and at immediate risk in the damaged chamber.

set.name: Hobb
set.description: Location: last known inside North Barrage Four's flooded control chamber beside the damaged control frame and emergency door, where he cut the spill chain and helped manage the failing feeder. Goal: keep the machinery from producing another surge while trying to reach the trapped workers and child. Relationships: allied with Nera and the lower crew but deeply distrustful of Ilyra's priorities; continues assisting because he understands the controls. Knowledge: knows the feeder pressure was redirected through the eastern channel, the emergency door briefly opened and failed, and the lower crew's condition is unknown. Possessions: tool case, bypass wires, damaged lantern, maintenance instruments, cutter, and burns from hot spray. Condition: injured, soaked, exhausted, frightened, and trapped amid failing machinery.

set.name: Governor Arven Dault
set.description: Location: escaping Veyr aboard a concealed private barge after the ceremonial river platform was struck by the flood. Goal: survive, preserve his authority, and protect the private reservoir and evacuation decisions that exposed the Low Quarter. Relationships: aligned with Pell and the Council, while abandoning citizens and officials trapped at the platform. Knowledge: knows the flood struck the districts the Council treated as a sacrifice zone and that his private evacuation route existed outside public maps. Possessions: ceremonial knife, torn white cloak, and access to the private barge and protected reservoirs. Condition: shaken, wet, politically endangered, and focused on survival rather than rescue.
The flood devastates Veyr's Low Quarter: tenements, workshops, bridges, streets, and families are destroyed or separated as bells and rescue marks disappear beneath the water.
The governors' ceremonial river platform is struck during the flood, while Governor Arven Dault escapes aboard a private barge through a concealed stair and reservoir route.
The Council settles the official death toll at 4,812, while survivors insist the number is higher because unregistered residents, workers, children, and people swept away are omitted.
Ilyra works alone at a ruined pump station after the flood, restarting drainage while unable to tell whether she is repairing the damage or trying to prove her calculations right.
Civic forces will arrest Ilyra at the ruined pump station two days after the flood, while the Council confiscates her maps and suppresses evidence of its evacuation plans.
The disputed death toll and the soaked ledger of blurred names will remain evidence that the official count excludes unregistered residents, workers, and missing families.

chapters.name: The Arrest
chapters.content:
Two days after the flood, the pump station still breathed.

It breathed through cracked pipes and split masonry, through the slow cough of the drainage wheel and the wet collapse of walls that had not yet decided whether to stand. Each time the wheel turned, brown water withdrew from the lower street by the width of a finger. Each time it stopped, the water returned with the patience of an animal that had learned the shape of the door.

Ilyra had not slept.

She sat beside the wheel with the soaked ledger open across her knees. The pages had dried into warped curls. Names had become stains. Here and there a letter survived—a hooked R, the upright stroke of an L, a child’s name reduced to one black loop. She had tried copying what she could onto the wall in wax pencil. The wall was already covered.

Nera. Hobb. Perren. Lio.

She had written Lio three times, though she did not know whether the child was alive.

At the bottom of the wall she had written: 4,812.

Then she had crossed it out.

The pump wheel gave a heavy click.

Ilyra pushed herself upright and gripped the handle. The skin of her palm had opened again. Blood ran into the rust-colored water beneath the machinery.

“Turn,” she told it.

The wheel turned a fraction.

Behind her, someone coughed.

Ilyra reached for the wrench before she remembered that the dead engineer had left it in her hand and that no one had come to take it back. She rose, staggering, and faced the doorway.

Three civic guards stood in the street.

Their uniforms were clean.

That was the first thing she noticed. The flood had left a film of gray silt over every surviving surface, but the guards’ boots shone black and their bronze shoulder plates had been polished. Behind them waited a narrow transport carriage with sealed windows. Its wheels rested on planks laid over the mud.

The guard in front carried a red folder beneath his cloak.

“Engineer Ilyra Voss?”

She looked past him at the drowned street. “Who is asking?”

“Civic custody.”

“Under whose order?”

The guard opened the red folder. The top page bore Sorell’s seal, though Sorell had not been at the station when the water came. “By authority of the Hall of Civic Judgment.”

Ilyra laughed, and the sound scraped her throat. “The Hall survived?”

“The Hall is functioning.”

“Of course it is.”

A second guard stepped into the pump room. He saw the wall of names, the ledger, the broken controls. His expression changed when he saw the brass valve key beside the wheel. Not pity. Recognition. Someone had told him what detail mattered.

“Put down the wrench,” the first guard said.

“I need it.”

“For what?”

“To keep the station from backing into the lower streets.”

“The rescue crews will take over.”

“There are no rescue crews.”

“There will be.”

Ilyra looked again at their clean boots. “When?”

The guard’s jaw tightened. “Put it down.”

She could have refused. The wrench was heavy, and the room offered angles: the broken intake wall, the hanging chain, the rusted lever that still controlled the secondary drain. She measured the three guards, the carriage, the distance to the street. Her mind made a map without asking permission.

One guard could be disarmed. Two could be delayed. The carriage horse was frightened and might bolt if the chain were cut. The pump wheel would stop within six minutes without someone at the handle. The lower street would rise. Perhaps not enough to drown anyone. Perhaps enough to trap those still searching the cellars.

There was always a pressure window.

There was always a cost hidden behind it.

Ilyra set the wrench on the floor.

The third guard bound her wrists. He used a wire restraint, not rope, and tightened it until the metal bit the bruises left by the barrage controls.

“Where are Nera and Hobb?” she asked.

No one answered.

“Where is the lower crew?”

The guard with the folder closed it. “You will be questioned at the Hall.”

“Are they alive?”

“Engineer Voss.”

“Are they alive?”

The wire pulled tighter. “You are under arrest for the deliberate destruction of civic infrastructure, mass casualty homicide, unlawful seizure of water controls, and acts against the public peace.”

The words seemed to come from far away. The pump station groaned. Water slid through the culvert. On the wall, Lio’s name trembled in the damp.

“Acts against the public peace,” Ilyra repeated.

The guard did not look at the dead engineer beneath the stairs. “You will have an opportunity to respond.”

She turned toward the wheel.

“Wait.”

The guard seized her shoulder. Ilyra twisted against him. “The station is not stable.”

“The rescue crews will manage it.”

“You don’t know how.”

“Neither did you.”

His voice held no uncertainty. That frightened her more than the wire.

Ilyra looked at the wheel one last time. It was still moving, though no hand held it. The mechanism had learned momentum, or perhaps the water had found a temporary balance. She tried to decide whether this was a sign of success or merely another condition she had failed to account for.

They led her outside.

The Low Quarter had become a city of thresholds. People stood on roofs, staircases, broken balconies, and the upper floors of buildings whose lower rooms were filled with water. They watched the guards escort her through the mud. Some shouted. Some did not have the strength.

A woman hurled a brick. It struck the carriage and broke into pale pieces.

“Barrage Butcher!” someone cried.

Another voice shouted, “Murderer!”

A man on a roof raised both hands. “She warned you!”

The guards turned toward him.

The man lowered his hands.

Ilyra saw a child wrapped in a gray blanket beside him. The child had a blue cloth tied around one wrist.

Her breath stopped.

The carriage door opened. She climbed in without being pushed. Before the guards shut it, she looked back at the pump station. The wheel continued its slow rotation. The broken window admitted a strip of white morning light. Beneath the stairs, the dead engineer remained where he had fallen, as if custody had arrived for everyone except him.

The carriage crossed the river by the old stone bridge. Water streamed between the stones below. The bridge had held, though three of its lamps were gone and a section of railing leaned outward over the current.

At the Crown approach, the streets were dry.

Workers had piled sandbags along the gardens. Shopkeepers washed mud from their thresholds. A bakery had opened beneath a striped awning, and people stood in line for sweetcakes stamped with the image of a broken sluice.

Ilyra saw her own face on the paper wrappers.

The artist had made her narrower, sharper, more feral than she was. Her hair streamed behind her like smoke. In one hand she held a gate key. In the other, a flame.

A boy bought a cake and bit into the printed eye.

The carriage continued.

By noon, the Hall of Civic Judgment had issued its first notice.

The notice appeared on every surviving announcement tower, on the walls of the dry districts, and in the hands of clerks sent through the flooded streets. It said that a lone radical engineer had exploited the Feast of Renewal to sabotage the North Barrage. It said her actions had been calculated to maximize civilian deaths. It said she had selected the festival because the city’s leaders were gathered, intending to murder the Council and overthrow the lawful order.

It did not mention the eastern storage fields.

It did not mention Dault’s private barge.

It did not mention the removed pressure valves, the evacuation lists, or the order to reinforce the Crown and Merchant districts first.

It did not mention that Ilyra had spent two days turning a pump wheel while rescue crews waited for instructions that never came.

By evening, the city had accepted the story.

Not everyone believed it. Belief was unnecessary. The notice supplied a shape, and grief rushed into it.

At the Hall, Magistrate Oren Pell stood beneath the central surveillance lens while clerks moved around him carrying sealed boxes. His judicial robes were immaculate. He had changed the bronze chain at his throat; the old one had been scratched during the platform evacuation. On the table before him lay Ilyra’s maps, her reports, the forged order, and a list of confiscated tools.

A clerk held up the forbidden hydraulic map.

“Seal this with the restricted archive records,” Pell said.

“It shows the lower basin.”

“Then it will show nothing.”

The clerk hesitated. “Should it be entered as evidence?”

Pell looked toward the lens. Somewhere beyond it, the city was watching the Hall’s response. “It is evidence that the accused possessed materials associated with sabotage.”

“That is not what the map says.”

Pell’s gaze settled on him.

The clerk lowered his eyes. “Yes, Magistrate.”

“Also seal the governor’s evacuation orders.”

“The orders concern district reinforcement.”

“They concern protected routes.”

“Will they be needed for the inquiry?”

Pell closed the red folder. “The inquiry will determine what is needed.”

The clerk carried the maps away.

Only then did Pell enter the interrogation room.

Ilyra sat in a metal chair bolted to the floor. Her wrists were still bound. Dried mud marked the hem of her torn white-and-bronze coat. Someone had washed the blood from her face but not from beneath her fingernails.

Pell took the chair opposite her.

“You were arrested at the pump station,” he said.

“I noticed.”

“You resisted custody.”

“I put down the wrench.”

“After considering whether to attack the guards.”

“Did you bring a witness who can read minds?”

Pell placed a sheet of paper on the table. “The city needs clarity.”

“The city needs names.”

“The city needs an account of why 4,812 people are dead.”

“Then ask why the Council knew the lower basin would flood.”

Pell did not blink. “You are already attempting to distribute responsibility.”

“I am describing a system.”

“You are describing an excuse.”

He slid another sheet toward her. It was the public notice, printed in black ink. Her name appeared three times. The words terrorist and butcher appeared six times. The Council appeared once, in the phrase lawful Council.

Ilyra read it without touching the page.

“You have not disproved my reports,” she said.

“We have not yet examined them.”

“You altered them before the flood.”

“You claim they were altered.”

“I saw the clerk change the record.”

“Then you will testify to that.”

“And the original pages?”

Pell folded his hands. “What original pages?”

For a moment she felt the old impulse rise in her: to seize the sequence, establish the pressure, force each fact into the place where it could not be denied. She imagined the map spread between them. She imagined her finger tracing the erased channel, the lower basin, the line marked sealed. She imagined Pell following the calculation until the conclusion became unavoidable.

But the map was already sealed.

The records were already somewhere beyond his reach—or hers.

The notice had done what the water could not. It had made one figure large enough to cover the whole horizon.

Pell leaned toward her. “The city will understand that you entered the barrage without authorization, disabled the surveillance relays, and opened the central sluice by hand.”

“I did.”

“It will understand that you selected a day on which the governors were gathered.”

“I did.”

“It will understand that you withheld information from your assistants and continued operating the controls after workers called for rescue.”

Ilyra looked at the table. “I did.”

Pell waited.

She heard the maintenance tube hiss. Heard Nera saying, You keep saying knowing is a kind of rescue. Heard the pump wheel turning after she had left it. Heard the woman with the ledger say, Then make room.

“What it will not understand,” Pell said, “is that there was no larger conspiracy. There was only your resentment, your training, and your decision.”

“There was a Council order.”

“Orders are made by many people. Crimes are committed by one.”

The sentence entered the room like a lock sliding shut.

Ilyra looked at him. “You don’t need to disprove the warnings.”

Pell’s expression softened, almost kindly. “No.”

“You only need to make me more memorable than the records.”

He did not deny it.

Outside the interrogation room, the announcement towers began repeating the notice. A woman’s civic voice, calm and resonant, described the Barrage Butcher’s calculated hatred. The words traveled through the Hall’s ducts and trembled in the metal chair beneath Ilyra.

Pell gathered the papers.

“Where are Nera and Hobb?” Ilyra asked again.

“The names of your accomplices will be addressed in due course.”

“Are they alive?”

Pell paused at the door. “You are concerned with the fate of people who followed you into a massacre.”

“I am concerned because I asked them to follow.”

“That distinction may prove useful.”

He left.

The lock turned.

Ilyra sat alone beneath the lens. Its black glass reflected her face, but the reflection was too small to be the woman on the wrappers, too tired to be the woman in the notice. She lifted her bound hands and counted the links between them.

Six.

She counted again.

Six.

In the pump station, the wheel had continued turning without her. In the Hall, the city continued speaking without her. Both machines had found a way to move her absence through their mechanisms.

She had believed control meant holding the lever.

Now she understood that control could also mean choosing which facts were allowed to survive.

The Council had not stopped the flood. It had not saved the Low Quarter. It had not even needed to prove that she was wrong.

It had only needed to give the dead a single face.

The announcement repeated her name.

Ilyra closed her eyes and listened until the voice became indistinguishable from the water.

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: detained in an interrogation room at the Hall of Civic Judgment after arrest at the ruined pump station. Goal: establish the Council's prior knowledge and protect the names and fate of those lost, while struggling against her old need to control the sequence of facts. Relationships: openly opposed to Pell and the Council; fears for Nera, Hobb, and Lio; viewed by the public as the Barrage Butcher, though some Low Quarter survivors insist she warned them. Knowledge: knows the Council has issued a solitary-terrorist narrative, that Pell sealed her maps and the governor's evacuation orders, and that her reports will be reframed rather than disproved; does not know whether Nera, Hobb, or Lio survived. Possessions: torn ceremonial white-and-bronze engineer's coat, bound wrists, and no longer-controlled access to her maps, tools, forged order, civic seal, or keys. Condition: exhausted, bruised, bleeding beneath her nails, emotionally lucid but shaken as she accepts both her personal responsibility and the regime's manipulation of meaning.

set.description: Location: directing clerks and sealed evidence at the Hall of Civic Judgment after Ilyra's arrest. Goal: preserve the Council's authority by making Ilyra the memorable solitary cause of the flood and suppressing records of protected routes, district reinforcement, and evacuation planning. Relationships: aligned with Dault and the Council, adversarial toward Ilyra, and reliant on clerks and civic announcers to enforce the official narrative. Knowledge: knows Ilyra entered North Barrage Four, disabled surveillance, opened the sluice, withheld information from assistants, and continued operating after workers called for help; knows the Council's records could implicate it and has ordered them sealed. Possessions: judicial robes, repaired bronze chain of office, red report folder, Ilyra's confiscated maps and reports, sealed evacuation orders, procedural authority, and surveillance access. Condition: composed, calculating, publicly confident, and actively converting evidence into a prosecutorial story.

set.name: Maret
set.description: Location: on civic guard and escort duty in Veyr after the flood, with the Hall enforcing Ilyra's arrest and public notice. Relationships: works under Pell with Senn; grieves Lessa and remains conflicted toward Ilyra, while increasingly distrustful of official claims. Knowledge: knows Ilyra has been arrested and publicly branded the sole terrorist, that protected districts remained dry while the Low Quarter drowned, and that official evidence is being controlled; does not know the fate of the barrage workers or Lio. Possessions: civic uniform and keys. Condition: tired, guarded, grieving, and morally unsettled.

set.name: Senn
set.description: Location: serving in or near the Hall of Civic Judgment after Ilyra's arrest, amid the controlled public response to the flood. Goal: make Ilyra answer for Lessa's death while resisting Pell's suppression of evidence and questioning the solitary-villain narrative. Relationships: grieving over Lessa and hostile toward Ilyra, but increasingly distrustful of Pell and the Council; works alongside Maret. Knowledge: knows Lessa's testimony identified Ilyra's conscious refusal to help a child, knows Ilyra has been arrested, and sees the Council omitting its own evacuation and reinforcement decisions from the public notice. Relationships: openly condemned Ilyra and lost trust in her judgment; allied with Hobb and the lower crew. Possessions: apprentice tools, copied hydraulic map, wax pencil, copper-dusted work clothes, and blue gasket-cloth tie. Condition: unknown, presumed endangered, soaked and physically strained if alive.

set.name: Hobb
set.description: Location: last known in the flooded lower control chamber of North Barrage Four, with his fate unknown after the feeder failed and communication stopped. Goal: keep the machinery from producing another surge while reaching the trapped workers and child if possible. Relationships: allied with Nera and the lower crew but deeply distrustful of Ilyra's priorities. Knowledge: knows the feeder pressure was redirected through the eastern channel, the emergency door failed, and the lower crew's condition is unknown. Goal: avoid discovery while preserving documentary evidence of manipulated civic authority and the Council's reservoir and evacuation decisions. Relationships: allied with Ilyra's intervention but physically separated from her; fears Pell and the Council's investigation. Knowledge: knows the order was forged in Sorell's handwriting and that records of valve removal, private reservoir routing, and evacuation plans may expose the Council; now knows the Council is sealing such evidence. Two days after the flood, civic guards arrest Ilyra at the ruined pump station, confiscating her tools and leaving the unstable drainage works to unnamed rescue crews.

The Council's sealed maps, evacuation orders, and altered records will become contested evidence in the trial, while Pell will continue presenting Ilyra as the sole cause of the flood.
The fate of Nera, Hobb, and Lio after the barrage remains uncertain and must be clarified through later testimony or discovery.

chapters.name: The Trial Begins
chapters.content:
The trial began beneath a ceiling painted with victories no living person remembered.

Above the Hall’s central chamber, bronze figures carried bowls of water toward a seated woman whose face had been worn smooth by generations of hands. The old inscription beneath them read: ORDER IS MERCY. Someone had polished the letters for the occasion. Someone else had hung white cloth over the cracks in the eastern wall.

By the time the doors opened, every seat was filled.

Officials occupied the raised galleries in their district colors. Merchants wore black ribbons tied with silver thread. Engineers from the Crown service sat together beneath the surveillance lenses, their faces arranged into professional grief. Below them crowded the survivors, pressed shoulder to shoulder in clothing still marked by the flood: stiffened sleeves, mud-dark hems, boots crusted with salt. Some had come to hear Ilyra condemned. Some had come to say what the city had done. Most had come because the Hall had promised them a broadcast.

The lenses turned toward the public benches.

A clerk announced that the proceedings of the Civic Judgment would be transmitted to every functioning tower in Veyr. The words carried through the chamber, then returned from the walls as a faint metallic echo.

Ilyra was brought in last.

Her wrists were chained before her. The torn white-and-bronze coat had been washed and mended badly at one shoulder. Her hair had been cut away from her face. The Hall had not bothered to conceal the bruises along her jaw; they made the image more convincing. The city’s most notorious criminal was permitted to look like someone who had survived something.

Senn walked at her left. Maret walked at her right.

Maret’s hand held the chain between them, but her eyes stayed lowered. Senn watched Ilyra with the blunt hatred he had carried since Lessa’s name appeared on the casualty list.

Ilyra looked toward him. “Is she listed?”

His mouth tightened.

“Lessa,” Ilyra said. “Is her name in the official count?”

“Keep walking.”

“Is it?”

Senn’s fingers closed around the chain. “You’ll hear the names they choose to read.”

That was not an answer. It was the closest thing to one the Hall had offered her.

At the front, Magistrate Oren Pell sat beneath the largest lens. His robes were dark blue, his bronze chain freshly repaired. Before him stood three desks: prosecution, civic record, and judgment. The third was empty, though the judges had already taken their places behind a carved screen. Their faces would not be transmitted. The city was to see law as a voice without a body.

Pell struck the table once with his gavel.

“Let the record show that the accused is Ilyra Voss, formerly appointed engineer of the lower civic channels, charged with unlawful seizure of North Barrage Four, destruction of civic infrastructure, conspiracy against the lawful Council, and the deaths of four thousand eight hundred and twelve citizens.”

A murmur moved through the chamber.

Ilyra turned toward the public benches. “That is not the number.”

Pell did not look at her. “The accused will remain silent unless addressed.”

“The number is not complete.”

“Engineer Voss.”

“There were unregistered families in the storage fields. Workers without district papers. Children—”

Pell lifted one hand. Two guards moved behind her.

“She has been instructed,” he said, “and chooses to disrupt the opening.”

The civic announcer repeated his words for the towers: The accused has been instructed and chooses to disrupt the opening.

Ilyra heard her own interruption transformed into evidence before it had finished leaving her mouth.

Pell read the indictment.

He read it slowly, giving each accusation a polished shape. Ilyra had forged an authorization order. She had stolen a civic seal. She had entered the barrage during the Feast of Renewal, disabled surveillance, overridden the locks, and opened the central sluice by hand. She had known the act would endanger civilians. She had chosen the festival because the governors were gathered on the ceremonial platform. She had continued operating after receiving pleas from trapped workers.

All of it was true.

The truth stood in the indictment like a row of stones, each one placed to prevent anyone seeing the river around them.

When Pell finished, he called the first witness.

A clerk named Veylan approached the testimony rail. Ilyra recognized him from the service archive: a thin man with a pale mustache, formerly responsible for copying reports into the civic register. His hands trembled as he took the oath.

“Did the accused submit warnings concerning North Barrage Four?” Pell asked.

“Yes.”

“How many?”

“Three written reports and several oral objections.”

The prosecution clerk displayed copies beneath the nearest lens. The pages enlarged across the chamber’s suspended glass: cramped figures, pressure estimates, a diagram of the eastern gate. The headings had been altered. The margins had been cut away.

“Were these reports technical safety documents?”

Veylan looked at the papers. “They contained technical material.”

“Did they also contain political demands?”

Ilyra rose as far as the chain allowed. “That is not the original—”

Pell turned toward her. “Sit.”

“The second page is missing the reserve notation.”

“Sit down.”

“The notation changed the entire pressure estimate.”

Pell faced the witness again. “Did the accused demand authority over the district water controls?”

Veylan’s eyes flicked toward Ilyra. “She said the controls needed to be opened.”

“Without Council authorization?”

“Yes.”

“Did she threaten that people would die if her instructions were not followed?”

“She said the lower basin would flood.”

“That was not my question.”

Veylan swallowed. “She said people would die.”

The civic announcer carried the phrase outward. People would die.

Pell let the silence lengthen. “No further questions.”

Ilyra stared at Veylan. He had not lied exactly. He had allowed the room to decide what his words meant.

“Cross-examination,” Pell said, though he held the authority to limit it.

Ilyra stepped to the rail. The guards did not stop her. Pell wanted her standing there, pale and chained, an engineer unable to control even the order of her questions.

“Veylan,” she said, “did you copy the reserve-capacity notation into the original record?”

“I copied what was given to me.”

“Was the notation present?”

Pell tapped his gavel. “The record has not established any notation.”

“It was present.”

“Engineer Voss.”

“Ask him who removed it.”

Pell leaned toward the microphone. “The accused is attempting to introduce unverified material that has been sealed under civic security procedure.”

“Because it proves the Council knew.”

The chamber shifted. A woman in the upper benches began to shout, but her words disappeared beneath the sudden crackle of the broadcast system.

Pell’s expression did not alter. “This is precisely the pattern described in the indictment. The accused cannot distinguish testimony from accusation, or a court from a platform for grievance.”

He nodded to the guards.

Ilyra was returned to her place.

The next witness was a senior engineer from the Crown district, a man named Halven Or who had never met her but had reviewed the authorized barrage plans. He spoke with calm certainty. The plans, he said, contained no lower-basin emergency release. The accused had therefore acted outside all recognized procedure.

“Were you aware,” Ilyra asked, “that the older plans contained a common-release basin?”

Pell interrupted before Halven could answer. “That document is not before the court.”

“It is in the sealed archive.”

“The accused is not permitted to characterize sealed material.”

“Then unseal it.”

A laugh broke from the public benches. It was a short, exhausted sound, and several people turned toward the woman who had made it. She wore a soaked dockworker’s coat and held a child against her hip.

Pell pointed. “Remove her.”

The woman stood. “My husband was in the east fields. You told us those fields were empty.”

“Remove her.”

“You knew the water would go there.”

Two guards reached for her. She twisted away and shouted toward the lenses, “They had lists! They had boats for the Crown road! They left us under the gates!”

The child began crying.

The chamber erupted. Survivors rose from their benches. Voices struck one another—Butcher, Council, liar, murderer, show us the orders. The lenses rotated rapidly, unable to hold one face.

Pell stood and raised both hands.

“This disturbance,” he said, “is not testimony. It is organized agitation.”

The guards dragged the woman toward the side door. Her child’s shoe came loose and fell onto the floor. Maret flinched. Senn looked at the shoe, then at Pell.

“Give her a receipt,” Senn said.

Pell’s gaze sharpened. “Guard Senn.”

“So the child can be returned.”

“Your role is custody, not commentary.”

Maret bent and picked up the shoe. For one instant she held it against her uniform. Then she carried it after the woman.

The broadcast resumed with a summary prepared before the disturbance. The accused’s supporters attempted to disrupt the lawful opening of the trial. Civic guards restored order. No mention was made of the child.

Ilyra watched Maret disappear through the door.

“Do you see?” Pell asked quietly.

He had returned to his seat. “Even those who claim to speak for the drowned bring disorder into the chamber.”

“They were asking why their families were abandoned.”

“They were repeating your language.”

“My language is pressure and water.”

“Your language is blame.”

Ilyra looked at the public benches. Some survivors had sat down. Others remained standing, guarded on all sides. Their faces were not a single crowd. There was rage, terror, disbelief, and the vacant patience of people who had learned that pleading made no difference. Pell’s court gathered them into one category because categories were easier to remove.

The prosecution called a final witness before the midday recess.

Senn was ordered to the rail.

He stopped beside Ilyra on his way forward. “If you use Lessa’s name to save yourself,” he said, “I’ll tell them what you did.”

“I don’t want to save myself with her.”

“What do you want?”

Ilyra looked at the lenses. “For her not to become a weapon.”

He gave a bitter smile. “You’re late.”

At the rail, Pell asked him to describe the accused’s behavior after the flood. Senn spoke of the pump station, the wrench, the wall covered in names. He said she had resisted arrest, then surrendered. He said she had asked whether the lower crew was alive.

Pell listened. “Did she express remorse?”

Senn looked at Ilyra.

“She asked for information.”

“That was not my question.”

“No.”

“Did she say she regretted opening the barrage?”

“No.”

“Did she say she would do it again?”

Senn’s jaw worked. “No.”

Pell smiled faintly. “So she offered neither remorse nor denial.”

“That isn’t what I said.”

“It is what the record will show.”

Ilyra rose. “He is being made to answer a question he did not answer.”

Pell turned to the judges’ screen. “The accused again interrupts to instruct a witness and control the record.”

“I am objecting.”

“You are not counsel.”

“Then appoint someone who can object.”

The chamber went very still.

Pell’s voice softened. “The accused rejects counsel appointed by the Hall. She rejects procedure, supervision, and every restraint placed upon her. This is not principled resistance. It is the same extremism that led her to seize the barrage.”

Senn looked at him. For the first time, something like shame crossed his face—not shame for Ilyra, but for the ease with which the words settled into place.

Pell struck the gavel.

“Recess until the second bell.”

The guards closed around Ilyra. As they led her beneath the painted figures, she saw the dockworker’s child’s shoe still lying near the testimony rail. No clerk had removed it. No one had entered it into evidence.

Outside, the towers began broadcasting the first day’s conclusion.

The trial had established that Ilyra Voss planned the flood, executed it, and refused to repent.

It had not established who knew the gates were failing.

It had not established why the protected districts were reinforced first, why the evacuation orders were sealed, or where the uncounted dead had gone.

But grief had been admitted in the chamber. It had been permitted to speak when it accused Ilyra, and expelled when it accused the city.

Ilyra understood then that the court did not fear her interruptions because they were disruptive. It feared them because each interruption threatened to return the dead to their proper number and the living to their proper questions.

As the chain pulled her toward the holding corridor, Senn remained at the testimony rail. He was staring at the abandoned shoe.

Pell watched him from beneath the lens.

The machine had begun to move, and every person inside it was being taught which direction counted as forward.

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: held in the Hall of Civic Judgment's custody corridor after the first public trial session. Goal: establish the Council's prior knowledge, restore the uncounted dead to the record, and protect the names and fate of those lost, while resisting her old need to control every sequence of facts. Relationships: openly opposed to Pell and the Council; fears for Nera, Hobb, and Lio; Senn remains hostile but has shown discomfort with Pell's manipulation; Maret is conflicted. Knowledge: knows the Council has issued a solitary-terrorist narrative, that Pell sealed her maps and evacuation orders, and that the trial admits her actions while excluding the Council's records; she has seen grief accepted as evidence against her and removed when it accuses officials. Possessions: torn white-and-bronze engineer's coat, chains, and no access to her maps, tools, forged order, civic seal, or keys. Condition: exhausted, bruised, publicly humiliated but lucid; increasingly aware that her interruptions can be turned into evidence of instability.

set.name: Oren Pell
set.description: Location: presiding over Ilyra Voss's public trial in the Hall of Civic Judgment beneath the central surveillance lens. Goal: preserve the Council's authority by making Ilyra the memorable solitary cause of the flood and suppressing records of protected routes, district reinforcement, and evacuation planning. Relationships: aligned with Dault and the Council; adversarial toward Ilyra; commands the guards, clerks, witnesses, and broadcast machinery. Knowledge: knows Ilyra entered North Barrage Four, disabled surveillance, opened the sluice, withheld information from assistants, and continued operating after workers called for help; knows the Council's records could implicate it and now uses sealed status and procedural control to exclude them. Possessions: judicial robes, repaired bronze chain, gavel, red report folder, Ilyra's confiscated maps and reports, sealed evacuation orders, procedural authority, and surveillance access. Condition: composed, calculating, publicly confident, and adept at converting interruptions, incomplete testimony, and public grief into prosecutorial evidence.

set.name: Maret
set.description: Location: on guard duty in the Hall of Civic Judgment after escorting Ilyra through the opening trial session. Goal: follow custody orders while determining whether Lessa's death and the devastation are being used to conceal the Council's responsibility. Relationships: works under Pell with Senn; grieves Lessa and remains conflicted toward Ilyra, while increasingly distrustful of official claims; has begun quietly resisting dehumanizing procedure by retrieving a removed survivor child's shoe. Knowledge: knows Ilyra has been branded the sole terrorist, that protected districts remained dry while the Low Quarter drowned, that official evidence is controlled, and that Pell suppresses survivors who accuse officials. Possessions: civic uniform, keys, and the child's abandoned shoe until it can be returned. Condition: tired, guarded, grieving, and morally unsettled; her distrust of Pell is becoming active.

set.name: Senn
set.description: Location: serving as a witness and guard in the Hall after the first public trial session. Goal: make Ilyra answer for Lessa's death while resisting Pell's suppression of evidence and questioning the solitary-villain narrative. Relationships: grieving over Lessa and hostile toward Ilyra, but increasingly distrustful of Pell and the Council; works alongside Maret and has begun recognizing how his own testimony is being weaponized. Knowledge: knows Lessa's testimony identified Ilyra's conscious refusal to help a child, knows Ilyra asked about the missing lower crew after arrest, and has seen Pell recast nuanced answers as proof of extremism while excluding accusations against the Council. Possessions: civic uniform, keys, and access to testimony and surveillance areas. Condition: angry, grieving, suspicious, and ashamed of how easily Pell converted his testimony into a predetermined narrative.

The public trial of Ilyra Voss opens before a packed Hall and a citywide broadcast; Pell presents her confirmed actions while excluding sealed records concerning the Council's prior knowledge and protected-district plans.
Archive clerk Veylan testifies from altered copies of Ilyra's warnings, while Pell blocks her attempt to introduce the missing reserve-capacity notation and other sealed technical evidence.

A survivor who accuses the Council of abandoning the eastern storage fields is removed with her child and labeled part of an organized agitation, demonstrating that grief is admitted only when directed at Ilyra.
Senn testifies that Ilyra showed concern for the missing lower crew but did not express remorse, and Pell recasts Senn's nuanced answers as proof of her extremism when she objects.

At the next stage of the trial, Lessa's sister testimony and other coerced survivor accounts will be used to turn sincere but incomplete grief into apparently definitive proof against Ilyra, while witnesses who accuse the Council will remain vulnerable to removal or punishment.
Senn's discomfort at Pell's manipulation of testimony will deepen his conflict between seeking Ilyra's punishment and resisting the Council's version of justice.

chapters.name: Names on the Record
chapters.content:
The clerk began with the dead.

Not the story of the dead. Not the shape of the water, or the hour the bells stopped, or the names shouted from roofs while the current carried furniture, doors, children. Only the names, arranged in the Council’s approved order, each one placed into the record like a stone set into a wall.

“Abren, Sol. Registered household, Crown allotment twelve.”

A pause. The clerk’s finger moved down the page.

“Alsen, Jori. Merchant district, temporary residence.”

Ilyra sat beneath the central lens with her wrists chained to the iron ring in the table. The chain had been polished for the broadcast. It caught the light whenever she moved, making each small motion visible in the galleries.

The clerk read on.

Some names she knew from work ledgers. Some from petitions. Some had never belonged to any official list at all until the flood made their absence inconvenient. She had seen them in the pump station, on smudged scraps and soaked ration books, written by survivors who did not know whether they were recording the living or the dead.

“Hobb, Renn.”

Her breath stopped.

The clerk did not look up. “Maintenance worker. Barrage Four service designation.”

A stir passed through the chamber. It was not grief. Grief made no sound in the Hall unless Pell permitted it. This was recognition, the quick intake of a hundred people discovering that a name had been promoted from rumor to fact.

“Hobb,” Ilyra whispered.

The magistrate lifted his eyes. “If the accused wishes to speak, she may do so after the witness testimony.”

“I did not—”

“After.”

The word fell with the weight of a shut gate.

The clerk continued. Nera Vale was not among the names. Neither was Lio. Ilyra kept her face still while the list moved past the lower crew and into the districts where the Council’s records were cleaner. Clean records had fewer people in them.

When the reading ended, Pell folded his hands over the red report folder.

“Call Tavia Senn.”

The name reached Ilyra before the woman did. Senn, standing beside the eastern rail in his civic uniform, went rigid. His sister came through the side door wearing a gray survivor’s coat with the sleeves cut short. Her hair had been shaved on one side, perhaps by fire, perhaps by a surgeon. A pale seam crossed her jaw.

Senn did not look at her.

Tavia looked at him.

For one instant the courtroom was not a chamber, and the lens was not watching. They were children on a stair, perhaps, before the city learned how to turn every private wound into public property. Then Tavia faced the bench.

“Do you swear that your testimony is true?” Pell asked.

“I swear I will tell what I saw.”

The distinction was careful. Pell smiled as though she had made a mistake.

“Tell the court where you were during the Feast of Renewal.”

“In the eastern storage fields. My husband had a stall there. We slept in the loft above it with the children.”

“The fields were marked abandoned.”

“They were not abandoned.”

A murmur rose behind Ilyra. Pell waited until it faded.

“Were you aware that you were occupying restricted civic land?”

“We were aware that the rent collectors came every month.”

Several people laughed before they remembered where they were. Pell’s expression did not change.

“And then the water came.”

“Yes.”

“Did you see the accused?”

Tavia’s fingers closed around the edge of the witness rail. “I saw a woman in an engineer’s coat. White and bronze. She was above the lower gate.”

“Did you know it was Ilyra Voss?”

“Not then.”

“But you know now.”

“I know what she looks like.”

Pell turned toward the gallery. “The accused has admitted that she entered North Barrage Four, disabled the surveillance relays, and opened the central sluice. Is that the woman you saw?”

Tavia looked at Ilyra.

“Yes.”

The answer was soft. It struck harder than the clerk’s reading.

Pell approached the witness rail. “What happened next?”

“The water rose through the field. People climbed onto carts and roofs. There was a child on the west platform. A little boy. He was calling for someone.”

Ilyra’s hands tightened beneath the table.

“Did the accused hear him?”

“Yes.”

“How do you know?”

“She turned toward him.”

“And did she help him?”

“No.”

The chamber seemed to tilt. Not from water. From the terrible simplicity of the answer.

Pell let the silence lengthen until it became an accusation with no speaker.

“What did she do?”

“She took hold of a brass key. She went the other way.”

Ilyra saw the roof again, though it was not Tavia’s roof. It was the old roof, the broken one near the south pump, and the child’s hand lifted against the rain. The brass valve key had been cold against her palm. Behind her, the district line had been filling. Ahead, the pump station waited. She had told herself that one life could not be weighed against a whole quarter. She had told herself the same thing in the barrage chamber, with Lio’s voice coming through the tube.

The child on the west platform was not the child on the roof. The courtroom made them one.

“Did you hear the accused say anything?” Pell asked.

Tavia swallowed. “She said the gate had to remain open.”

“Did she say she was sorry?”

“No.”

“Did she ask whether anyone had reached the families in the fields?”

“No.”

Ilyra turned toward her. “You were behind the grain shed. You couldn’t have heard—”

Pell struck the table with his palm.

“Let the record show that the accused attempts to intimidate the witness.”

“I am asking where she stood.”

“Your questions are not permitted.”

“You asked what she saw.”

“And she answered.”

Tavia’s face had gone gray. Ilyra wanted to tell her that the answer was not false, only unfinished. She wanted to tell her about the broken western assembly, the missing pressure valves, the lower feeder, the workers calling through the maintenance line. She wanted to put every piece on the table until no one could pretend that a brass key explained a flood.

But explanation had become another kind of control. She felt it gathering in her, the old impulse to seize the sequence and force each fact into its proper channel. Pell knew it. The clerk knew it. Perhaps even Tavia knew it. The more Ilyra resisted the shape of the story, the more visibly she became the shape they had given her.

Pell asked, “Were you offered anything in exchange for appearing today?”

“No.”

“Were you promised protection from eviction?”

“No.”

“Were you promised ration credits?”

“No.”

Pell turned to the chamber. “The witness has no interest but truth.”

Tavia flinched.

Ilyra noticed then that the gray coat was new. Its buttons bore the mark of the Civic Relief Office. A folded ration voucher showed beneath the cuff. Tavia followed her gaze and pulled the sleeve down.

Pell saw it too. He did not need to mention it. The chamber understood.

When Tavia was dismissed, Senn stepped aside to let her pass. Their shoulders almost touched. He looked at the voucher. She looked at the floor.

“You told me you had nothing,” he said.

“I have three children.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“No,” she said. “It is what they asked.”

She left through the side door. Senn remained at the rail, his jaw clenched so tightly the scar beside his mouth whitened.

Pell called the next witness.

A cooper from the flooded workshops testified that Ilyra had spoken of cleansing the city. He had not heard the word, but another man had told him she used it. In return for his testimony, the Civic Relief Office would restore his ration allotment. A laundress said Ilyra laughed when the first roofs vanished. She had not seen the laugh herself; she had seen another woman cover her mouth. Her eviction notice was withdrawn before she left the Hall.

A boy no older than fourteen said the engineers had discussed making the Crown District pay. His mother stood behind the gallery rail, clutching a stamped paper that guaranteed their room for one more month.

Pell never called these bargains. He called them assistance.

Each witness spoke something that could be true. That was the cruelty of it. The lie did not need to replace the truth. It only needed to stand in front of it.

During the recess, a clerk brought another list.

This one was longer.

The names were read by districts, beginning with the Low Quarter and proceeding upward. Ilyra sat with her eyes lowered, listening as the dead were sorted according to their civic value.

“Bera, Noll. Unregistered.”

“Cask, Vey. Foundry laborer.”

“Deren, Ma. No household record.”

“Etrin, Sol and two dependents. Temporary shelter.”

She remembered Sol Etrin. He had come to the pump station with a cracked lantern and asked whether the water would reach the foundry floor. She had told him to move his family to the eastern terraces. The terraces had been marked safe on the old map. The eastern gate had opened first.

“Falk, Jessa. Laundry worker.”

“Garn, Toma. Child.”

The clerk’s voice remained even. The lens above them hummed.

Ilyra had believed in totals because totals could be defended. Four thousand eight hundred and twelve dead, and behind the number a chain of choices: one gate, one pressure, one district against another. If she had opened the emergency door, the surge would have taken thousands more. If she had saved the child on the roof, the lower line might have failed. If she had left the key and gone to the trapped workers, the fields and workshops would have drowned faster.

She had built an arithmetic in which every refusal was a rescue.

But the names would not stay in columns.

Hobb Renn was not a unit of pressure. Nera was not an unavoidable loss. Lio was not the remainder after a district had been saved. Tavia’s child on the platform was not made less dead by the families Ilyra had hoped to protect. Nor did the families become less abandoned because Ilyra had chosen the wrong map for reasons the Council had helped create.

The numbers mattered. They described the reach of the water. They did not describe the weight of a hand withdrawing from a child.

“Voss, Tomas,” the clerk read.

Ilyra looked up sharply.

The chamber had gone quiet. Tomas’s name was not on the flood rolls. He had died years before in civic custody, under a different fiction, but the clerk had found him in an appended household record. A dead man entered late, carried forward by a sister who had once insisted that every omission was deliberate.

Pell glanced at her. He understood what had happened. Perhaps he had even ordered the name included.

“Voss, Tomas,” the clerk repeated. “Temporary detention. Prior civic record.”

Ilyra’s throat closed.

For a moment she saw Tomas at the ration office, his fingers black with ledger ink, laughing because he had finally found the missing entries. Then the cell door. Then the winter window in their mother’s room, filmed with ice from the inside.

The city had taught her that a person could disappear through a sentence. Now it was teaching her that a name could be used as a weapon without being false.

She lowered her head.

Pell leaned toward the microphone. “The accused appears affected by the inclusion of a relative’s name.”

Ilyra said nothing.

“Let the record show—”

“Let the record show his name,” she said.

The magistrate paused.

She lifted her face to the lens. “Not that I am affected. Not that I am unstable. Tomas Voss. He died in civic custody. Write that.”

Pell’s voice sharpened. “This proceeding concerns the Barrage disaster.”

“Then read the names as people, not as material.”

A guard moved behind her chair. Senn’s hand twitched near his belt, though whether toward his weapon or away from it, she could not tell.

Pell looked to the clerk. “Continue.”

The clerk did.

Ilyra listened until the list ended. She did not count. She did not calculate how many might have lived if she had chosen differently, because the answer would become another excuse. She had caused deaths. The Council had designed the basin. The governors had protected their districts. The witnesses had been pressed into the shape of the court’s hunger. All of these things could be true at once.

Responsibility was not a scale with her guilt on one side and the Council’s on the other. It was a net. Every hand had caught somewhere in it. Some hands had pulled. Some had cut holes. Hers had tightened the knots.

When the guards came to take her back to the custody corridor, Senn did not meet her eyes.

At the door, he said, “Tavia saw what you did.”

“Yes.”

“She didn’t see everything.”

Ilyra stopped.

Senn’s expression was raw with anger, but beneath it lay something worse: the fear that a partial truth might be all that remained of his sister’s life.

“No,” Ilyra said. “She didn’t.”

“Then why didn’t you say so?”

Ilyra looked toward the courtroom, where Pell was already speaking to the next clerk, restoring order to the record.

“Because what she saw was true.”

Senn’s mouth tightened. “That doesn’t make it enough.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “It doesn’t.”

The door opened. The corridor swallowed her, the names following like footsteps she could not command.

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: being returned from the second public trial session to the Hall of Civic Judgment custody corridor. Goal: restore the names and circumstances of the dead to the record, establish the Council’s prior knowledge, and resist both Pell’s narrative and her own urge to control every fact. Relationships: openly opposed to Pell and the Council; now recognizes Tavia Senn’s testimony as sincere but incomplete; Senn remains hostile yet has begun questioning Pell’s manipulation; Maret remains conflicted. Knowledge: heard Hobb Renn listed among the dead while Nera Vale and Lio remain unaccounted for; knows witnesses accepted civic relief tied to their testimony; publicly stated that Tomas Voss died in civic custody; understands responsibility cannot be reduced to totals or used to erase either her choices or the Council’s design. Possessions: torn white-and-bronze engineer’s coat, chains, and no access to maps or tools. Condition: exhausted, bruised, publicly exposed, lucid, and newly sobered by the names of the dead.

set.name: Oren Pell
set.description: Location: presiding over the ongoing public trial in the Hall of Civic Judgment beneath the central surveillance lens. Goal: preserve Council authority by making Ilyra the solitary cause of the flood and converting sincere grief, incomplete testimony, and procedural interruptions into proof of vengeance and instability. Relationships: aligned with Dault and the Council; adversarial toward Ilyra; controls guards, clerks, witnesses, relief arrangements, and broadcasts. Knowledge: knows Tavia Senn saw Ilyra turn away from a child with a brass key; knows the account is incomplete but presents it as definitive; knows witnesses receive civic aid and that casualty records can expose inconvenient deaths, including Tomas Voss’s custody death. Possessions: judicial robes, repaired bronze chain, gavel, red report folder, Ilyra’s sealed maps and reports, evacuation orders, procedural authority, and surveillance access. Condition: composed and calculating, though increasingly forced to manage the danger of names that connect civic violence to the Council.

set.name: Maret
set.description: Location: on guard duty in the Hall of Civic Judgment after the second public trial session. Goal: follow custody orders while discovering whether Lessa’s death and the wider devastation are being used to conceal Council responsibility. Relationships: works under Pell with Senn; grieves her sister Lessa and remains conflicted toward Ilyra; increasingly distrusts official procedure.
