Condition: blistered, exhausted, physically weak but lucid; increasingly willing to share knowledge and reject sole control, though still tempted by decisive command.

set.name: Oren Pell
set.description: Location: flooded execution chamber and Hall galleries, attempting to restore control after the Ember Descent interruption. Goal: seize Elian’s archival copies, suppress their transmission, seal the western passages, arrest participants, and preserve Council authority while the new flooding remains hidden. Relationships: adversarial toward Ilyra and Elian; commands the ceremony and officials; openly challenged by Senn and Maret and losing reliable obedience from clerks and maintenance crews. Knowledge: knows Elian’s packet exposes Council sacrifice orders and Dault’s escape; now knows the packet and pressure readings are circulating and that western districts face a new flood. Possessions: white judicial robes, repaired bronze chain, execution orders, broadcast authority, and guards under command. Condition: angry, publicly destabilized, urgent, and increasingly reliant on coercive orders.

set.name: Maret
set.description: Location: moving through Hall checkpoints and service passages after helping Ilyra escape the basin, carrying a divided section of the western pressure plan. Goal: get warnings and evacuation help toward Sable Ward while preventing Pell from converting the crisis into concealment or vengeance; protect the memory of Lessa. Relationships: conflicted toward Ilyra but cooperating with her; cautiously allied with Senn, Elian, and Jorren; openly resistant to Pell. Knowledge: understands private reservoirs are being drained to protect Crown property, Sable Ward lacks evacuation notices, Gate W-seven may have a relief vent, and no gate should open on Ilyra’s authority alone. Possessions: civic uniform with pins removed, keys hidden beneath her sleeve, one divided section of readings. Condition: frightened, grieving, morally resolute, and moving under risk of arrest.

set.name: Senn
set.description: Location: traveling through the western service passages toward survivor routes after leaving Ilyra and Elian, carrying a divided section of pressure readings. Goal: help evacuate Sable Ward and protect Tavia and other residents while ensuring Ilyra remains accountable; prevent Pell from using emergency powers to conceal the Council’s guilt. Relationships: still hostile toward Ilyra but cooperating with her plan; allied cautiously with Elian, Maret, and Jorren; distrustful of Pell. Knowledge: knows private reservoirs are redirecting pressure toward Sable Ward, coded notices favored wealthy households, forty-three survivors are in the tunnels, and Gate W-seven’s relief vent may be critical. Possessions: civic uniform, baton, keys, and one divided section of readings. Condition: angry, vigilant, morally unsettled, and prepared to disobey Pell.

set.name: Elian Dault
set.description: Location: hidden service corridors beneath the Hall with Ilyra after interrupting the Ember Descent, carrying archival copies and the remaining section of pressure readings. Goal: expose the Council’s planned sacrifice and her father’s escape while helping prevent Sable Ward’s flooding; keep Ilyra’s responsibility visible and prevent either woman’s evidence from becoming a simple heroic story. Relationships: tense alliance with Ilyra; adversarial toward Pell and the Council; cautiously cooperating with Senn, Maret, and Jorren; estranged from Governor Dault. Knowledge: possesses copied Council minutes, reservoir routing orders, coded evacuation notices, Dault’s signed lower-basin order, and the hidden escape route; now knows private reservoirs are being drained into western channels, Sable Ward has no warning, forty-three survivors are trapped in tunnels, and resistance must be distributed. Possessions: leather case, blue-threaded archival packet, dark traveling coat, gray scarf, and one section of pressure readings. Condition: exhausted, grief-stricken, controlled, politically endangered, and increasingly committed to practical rescue alongside the archival exposure.

set.name: Jorren Pell
set.description: Location: departing through the old drainage tunnels toward Sable Ward with a divided pressure-reading section and a rescue group. Goal: evacuate at least forty-three survivors and other trapped residents, reach the abandoned tram embankment, and test or open Gate W-seven’s concealed relief vent without causing another surge. Relationships: rescue diver and survivor organizer; blames Ilyra for the deaths of his wife and children and refuses her apology, but accepts her technical guidance; allied cautiously with Elian, Senn, and Maret. Knowledge: knows the civic crews are blocking east stairs, three work skiffs and a damaged barge are available, the western channels are rising, and local survivor knowledge must guide the response. Possessions: diver’s harness, rope coil, knife, copper rings, patched coat, and one divided section of pressure readings. Condition: soaked, driven, grieving, wary, and under immediate physical danger.

Ilyra identifies Elian’s smuggled reservoir readings as a deliberate sequence draining private Crown and Merchant reservoirs into western channels while the Crown gates remain sealed, directing pressure toward Sable Ward.
Elian reveals coded evacuation notices sent to wealthy Crown and Merchant households while Sable Ward receives no warning, confirming an imminent second sacrifice.

Rescue diver Jorren Pell enters the Hall with news that forty-three survivors are sheltering in old tunnels and begins organizing their evacuation through the abandoned tram embankment and possible relief vent at Gate W-seven.
Ilyra divides the pressure readings among Elian, Jorren, Senn, and Maret and refuses to authorize any gate opening on her word alone.

The distributed survivor network must obtain current pressure readings and coordinate local engineers, evacuation routes, and relief-vent access in Sable Ward without allowing Ilyra sole control of any gate.
The Council will attempt to seal the western service passages and arrest or suppress the engineers, clerks, guards, and survivors carrying the divided plan.

chapters.name: The People Beneath
chapters.content:
Senn found the first false death roll beneath a dead man’s coat.

The coat belonged to a prison porter who had been swept from the eastern stair during the first surge. His name was stitched inside the collar, along with the number of the cell block he served. Senn had known him by sight: a narrow man called Urek, who complained about his knees and kept sugared fennel in his pocket. Urek had not been one of the four thousand eight hundred and twelve. He had been absent from every list Senn had seen.

Now his coat lay across a table in the old drainage station, and a packet of papers rested inside it.

“Read the bottom,” Jorren said.

Senn held the page close to the blue flame of the lamp. The ink was fresh enough to shine. It recorded the names of prisoners, detainees, and civic laborers who had supposedly died during the flood. Beside each name was a date, a place, and a classification: drowned, crushed, missing presumed dead.

Urek’s name appeared third.

His death was dated two days before the flood.

Senn lowered the page. “He died on the eastern stair.”

“He died after he carried three children out of the records tunnel,” said a woman sitting opposite him. “I saw him do it.”

“What is your name?”

“Pella Rusk. Former night clerk in the prison infirmary.”

Former. The word had become a warning in Veyr. It meant that someone had either dismissed you, hidden you, or expected you not to survive long enough to object.

Pella tapped the page. “The officials are closing the rolls before the water reaches the cells. They mark people dead while they are still alive. Then the number of missing falls.”

“Why?” Senn asked, though he already knew the shape of the answer.

“So the Council can say the second flood killed no one who mattered,” Jorren said.

The drainage station had once controlled the lower channels beneath the Hall. Its walls were round and damp, built from old brick that sweated even when the river was low. People crowded around the tables: foundry workers, two nurses, a boatman with a bandaged ear, three prisoners Jorren had pulled from a collapsed holding tunnel, and a girl who held a brass cup in both hands without drinking from it. They were not an army. They were people who had found one another below the city because there was nowhere else to go.

Senn recognized the arrangement. Veyr’s officials called such gatherings disorder when they occurred aboveground. Below, they called them necessary.

Jorren spread a damp map across the table. “The prison officials have ordered the western passages sealed. They want the survivors in the tunnels counted, transferred, and erased from the route records.”

“Not erased,” Pella said. “Disposed of. There is a difference.”

Senn looked again at Urek’s name. Beneath it, someone had written a total: 117.

“Who are the others?”

“People who can no longer answer,” Pella said. “Some are dead. Some are trapped. Some are in cells the guards have not opened because the lower blocks are already taking water.”

“And the list reduces the count?”

“It removes uncertainty.”

Pella’s voice was flat, but her hand trembled beside the page. “Every name marked dead is a name they do not have to search for. Every body they do not recover becomes proof that the water was mercifully limited.”

Senn thought of Tavia and her children, of the relief clerk who had weighed her sister’s death against a ration voucher. He thought of Lessa’s red scarf caught in a grate and of the court treating that scrap as a complete account of what happened at the barrage.

“Give me the roll,” he said.

Pella looked at Jorren.

Jorren nodded once. “He is with us.”

Senn almost objected. He had not said he was with them. He had followed them through two passages, carried a pressure strip beneath his uniform, and struck a Hall officer who tried to close the tram route behind a group of children. He had done those things because Pell’s orders had become indistinguishable from another flood.

But the words remained in the room, and no one took them back.

“Not with her,” Senn said.

Jorren’s mouth tightened. “No one asked you to be.”

“I am with the people beneath. I am not with Ilyra Voss.”

“Then you are in the right place,” said the boatman. “Most of us are not with her either.”

A pressure tremor passed through the station. Dust shook from the ceiling. The girl with the brass cup looked toward the tunnel mouth.

“How long?” she asked.

“Before the lower wall gives?” Jorren said. “We do not know.”

“That is what she said.”

Senn looked at the girl. “Who?”

“The engineer.”

“She gave us the readings,” Jorren said. “She said no gate opens on her word alone.”

“And yet we are using her numbers.”

“We are using what is true in them.”

“Can you separate that from her?”

Jorren’s eyes hardened. “Can you separate the water from the wall that directs it?”

The question went around the table and found no easy place to stop.

Jorren pointed to a narrow service corridor on the map. “The records cell beneath the Hall is isolated from the main galleries. Ilyra knows the routes. Elian says she can read the old system better than anyone alive.”

“She built the system that killed us,” said Pella.

“She opened one gate,” said the nurse. “The Council built the rest of the city.”

“And she knew what would happen when she opened it.”

Senn felt the old anger rise, clean and familiar. It was easier when anger had one face. He had seen Ilyra turn away from the child. He had heard her admit that she carried the key instead. No map could alter that. No Council order could place the child back on the roof.

“Freeing her is not the same as trusting her,” he said.

Jorren leaned over the table. “I have no intention of freeing her so she can take a master lever and decide who drowns. I want her alive because the Council is still using the same channels, and because I want her to answer the people she harmed.”

“Alive for how long?”

“Long enough.”

“That is not a sentence.”

“It is more honest than calling her execution justice.”

Senn stared at him.

Jorren’s hand moved to the copper rings at his belt. “My wife and children are dead. I know what I want to do to Ilyra. I want to put her in a room with every family that lost someone and make her listen until she cannot turn their lives into numbers. That is not mercy.”

“No,” Senn said.

“It may not be justice either.”

The station quieted. Even the water seemed to listen through the brick.

Jorren continued, “But if we leave her to Pell, he gets the death he designed. He gets to call the records a lie and the survivors a mob. He gets another spectacle. I will not help him drown the truth inside her.”

Senn thought of the execution basin: the mirrored lenses, the heated water, the crowd leaning forward to see whether Ilyra would scream. He had wanted her to live then, though he had not known why. Not because she deserved comfort. Because death would let everyone stop asking questions.

“Keeping her alive could be vengeance,” he said.

“So could killing her.”

No one spoke for several breaths.

Pella lifted a small iron case from beneath the table. Inside lay fragments of metal: a broken hinge, two lengths of copper wire, a triangular plate punched with numbered holes, and a brass cylinder no longer than a finger.

“These came from the western maintenance crews,” she said. “They were going to melt them down and recast the gate housings. The markings match the old plans.”

Jorren picked up the triangular plate. “Can she use this?”

“She can tell us what it was,” Pella said. “That may be enough.”

Senn examined the edges. A strip of blue gasket cloth clung to one corner, dark with oil. He thought of the divided pressure readings in his pocket. Ilyra had torn the plan apart so no one person could own it. It was the first thing she had done that did not look like conquest.

“Who takes these to her?” he asked.

“I do,” said Pella.

“You cannot pass the Hall checkpoints.”

“I used to file the prison inventories. They still expect me to carry things no one wants to inspect.”

“They are searching everyone.”

“Then I will carry something they believe they have already searched.”

She opened a second bundle. It contained a folded map hidden between sheets of blank execution forms.

Senn almost laughed. “You are smuggling maps to a condemned prisoner inside her own sentence.”

“The city has always hidden its machinery in paperwork,” Pella said. “It seems fair to return the favor.”

Jorren pointed at Senn. “You know the Hall’s guard routes.”

“I know the public routes.”

“You know Pell’s habits.”

“I know he prefers people to think he has habits.”

“Can you get her a message?”

Senn looked toward the tunnel leading upward. He could picture the records cell: narrow drain, iron door, the window too high to see through unless one stood on the cot. Ilyra had spent forty-one days measuring places like that. She would have measured the distance between stones and the interval between footsteps. She would have turned confinement into a problem she could solve.

He wondered whether she had ever understood that the people below were not pieces waiting to be arranged.

“I can get a message,” he said. “Not a promise.”

“Good.”

Senn took the papers. Pella wrapped the metal fragments in oilskin and tied them with cord. The bundle was light enough to conceal beneath a jacket, but its contents felt heavier than the baton at his hip.

As they prepared to leave, the nurse stopped him.

“If you see her,” she said, “tell her the names are not numbers.”

Senn looked at the false roll. “She knows that.”

“Knowing is not the same as hearing it from us.”

He folded the list and placed it inside his uniform.

The ascent to the Hall ran through a shaft abandoned after the first flood. Senn went first with the lamp. Jorren followed, carrying rope and the damaged pressure gauge. Pella came last, holding the oilskin bundle beneath her blouse.

At the top, they separated.

Jorren touched Senn’s sleeve. “If Pell catches you?”

“He will say I acted alone.”

“Then do not give him the courtesy.”

Senn climbed into a records passage where the air smelled of wet paper and hot stone. Somewhere beyond the wall, officials shouted about sedition. A bell rang for the Crown line, then stopped halfway through its second strike.

He waited until the footsteps passed.

The records cell door had a viewing slit at eye level. Senn raised his hand to knock, then stopped. Through the slit he saw Ilyra sitting on the floor in her soaked white robe, her blistered feet extended toward the drain. Elian stood beside the wall, sorting scraps of paper by the light of a candle stub.

Ilyra looked up before he made a sound.

“Guard Senn,” she said. “Have you come to arrest us?”

“Not today.”

“An encouraging schedule.”

He unlocked the outer grille but left the cell door barred. “The Council is falsifying the death rolls.”

Elian’s hands went still.

Ilyra’s face did not change. Only her fingers tightened against the floor. “How many?”

“An initial list contains one hundred seventeen names entered before their deaths. Some are trapped. Some are alive. The officials are reducing the number of people they must search for.”

“Who has the roll?” Elian asked.

“I do.”

“Why bring it here?”

Senn met Ilyra’s eyes through the slit. “Because you should hear what the people beneath think of your numbers.”

He slid the folded list through the opening. Ilyra did not reach for it immediately.

“Are you joining Jorren?” she asked.

“I am helping him.”

“That was not my question.”

“No,” Senn said. “It was yours.”

She accepted the answer. “What does he want?”

“To keep the survivors alive. To expose Pell. To make you listen.”

“I have been listening.”

“Not to everyone.”

The words struck harder than he intended. Ilyra lowered her head.

Elian stepped forward. “What do you need from her?”

“Maps. Mechanical fragments. Anything that identifies the relief vent at W-seven.”

Ilyra opened the false roll. Her eyes moved down the names. Senn watched her search for something and feared she would find a way to turn the list into a calculation.

Instead she said, “Give me the metal.”

He passed the oilskin bundle through the grille. She unwrapped it piece by piece. The triangular plate caught the candlelight.

“That is not from W-seven,” she said.

“Then what is it?”

“A locking plate from the old common-release basin. The Council converted the basin into a private garden after the first flood.”

Elian stared at her. “A garden?”

“Stone terraces, imported soil, ornamental channels. The plans would still show a basin if they admitted what it had been.”

Ilyra turned the plate over. “The relief vent may connect to it. If the basin is intact beneath the garden, it can receive the western surge.”

“May?” Senn asked.

“The plate is damaged. I need the map.”

Pella appeared at the end of the passage, breathless but upright. She handed the folded forms to Elian through the grille. “There are guards above. Pell is sealing the archive tower.”

Ilyra spread the map on the cell floor. It was old, stained, and marked with channels that crossed beneath the Hall and traveled west toward Sable Ward. She placed the metal plate over one intersection.

For a moment the cell became what she had always wanted: a surface, a set of lines, a problem with an answer hidden inside it.

Then she looked at the false roll beside her hand.

“Who is making the decisions below?” she asked.

“Jorren,” Senn said. “Local workers. Nurses. Whoever knows the tunnels.”

“Good.”

“You sound surprised.”

“I am.”

He watched her mark the map with a piece of charcoal. “If you find a way to open the gate, do not do it alone.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

Ilyra’s gaze lifted. It held exhaustion, anger, and something less familiar—the discomfort of being required to trust people whose names she did not know.

“No,” she said. “But I am learning.”

Below them, a deep metallic groan moved through the Hall. The floor shifted. Water whispered inside the walls.

Senn gripped the bars. “How long?”

Ilyra looked at the map, then at the names on the false roll.

“Long enough to ask the people beneath,” she said. “Not long enough to decide for them.”

Pella began copying the marked channels onto the backs of the execution forms. Elian gathered the fragments. Senn kept watch while the condemned engineer drew a route no single hand could command.

Above, Veyr prepared to watch her die.

Below, the uncounted gathered around the water and began, imperfectly and in fear, to choose together.

set.description: Location: last known in the flooded lower control chamber of North Barrage Four, with fate unknown after the feeder failed and communication stopped. Goal: keep machinery from producing another surge while reaching trapped workers and child if possible. Relationships: allied with Nera and the lower crew but deeply distrustful of Ilyra’s priorities. Knowledge: knows feeder pressure was redirected through the eastern channel, the emergency door failed, and the lower crew’s condition is unknown. Possessions: tool case, bypass wires, damaged lantern, maintenance instruments, cutter, and burns from hot spray. Condition: unknown, presumed endangered.

set.name: Pellis
set.description: Location: traveling between the old drainage station, Hall records passages, and Ilyra’s records cell. Goal: preserve documentary evidence of manipulated death rolls, reservoir routing, and Council authority while helping the survivor network reach Ilyra. Relationships: allied with Ilyra’s intervention and the underground survivors; fearful of Pell and the Council; cooperating with Senn, Jorren, Elian, and Maret. Knowledge: knows at least 117 death entries were falsified before actual deaths, the common-release basin was converted into a private garden, and old maps and mechanical fragments may expose the western water network. Possessions: retired civic forms, copied false death roll, stained basin map, access knowledge, and smuggled mechanical fragments. Condition: anxious, breathless, isolated from official protection, and increasingly committed to risking discovery.

set.name: Governor Arven Dault
set.description: Location: away from Veyr after escaping by concealed private barge. Goal: survive, preserve authority, and protect private reservoir and evacuation decisions that exposed the Low Quarter. Relationships: aligned with Pell and the Council while estranged from Elian and abandoned citizens and officials on the platform. Knowledge: knows the Council is blaming Ilyra alone, the private evacuation route existed, and western channels are being used to protect Crown property; likely knows the concealment of casualty records. Possessions: ceremonial knife, torn white cloak, access to private barge and protected reservoirs, political connections. Condition: shaken, wet, politically endangered, and focused on survival and narrative control.

set.name: Tavia Senn
set.description: Location: outside the Hall with her three children after testifying in Ilyra’s trial. Goal: secure food, housing, and safety while preserving her honest memory of the flood. Relationships: sister of Senn; distrustful of Pell’s framing and not aligned simply with Ilyra or the Council. Knowledge: saw Ilyra at North Barrage Four turn away from a child while carrying a brass key, but did not witness the full barrage crisis or the trapped workers; may now be endangered by the western flooding. Possessions: gray survivor’s coat and civic ration voucher or relief document. Condition: grieving, frightened, physically marked by disaster, and dependent on unstable relief.

set.name: Elian Dault
set.description: Location: records cell beneath Veyr’s Hall with Ilyra, sorting archival copies and helping interpret the smuggled basin map. Goal: expose the Council’s planned sacrifice and her father’s escape while preventing Sable Ward’s flooding; keep Ilyra’s guilt visible and support distributed rescue. Relationships: tense alliance with Ilyra; allied cautiously with Senn, Maret, Jorren, Pellis, and the survivor network; adversarial toward Pell and Governor Dault. Knowledge: possesses copied Council minutes, reservoir routing orders, coded evacuation notices, Dault’s signed lower-basin order, the hidden escape route, and now the false death rolls and evidence of the converted common-release basin; knows the network is coordinating local action rather than obeying Ilyra alone. Possessions: leather case, blue-threaded archival packet, dark traveling coat, gray scarf, divided pressure readings, and copied channel markings. Condition: exhausted, grief-stricken, controlled, politically endangered, and committed to practical rescue and complete archival exposure.

set.name: Jorren Pell
set.description: Location: old drainage station and western survivor tunnels, directing an underground network toward Sable Ward and the abandoned tram embankment. Goal: evacuate at least forty-three survivors and other trapped residents, verify the W-seven relief route and buried common-release basin, expose the Council, and keep Ilyra alive to answer the harmed while preventing another mass death. Relationships: blames Ilyra for his wife and children’s deaths and rejects her remorse as useful; allied with Senn, Elian, Maret, Pellis, local workers, nurses, and survivors; opposed to Pell and the Council. Knowledge: knows prison officials falsified death rolls, the Council is sealing western passages, the western channels are rising, and the smuggled locking plate may identify a route to the converted basin. Possessions: diver’s harness, rope coil, knife, copper rings, damaged pressure gauge, and divided pressure-reading section. Condition: soaked, driven, grieving, wary, and struggling to distinguish justice from prolonged vengeance.

Senn secretly joins Jorren’s underground survivor network after learning that prison officials entered at least 117 people as dead before their actual deaths, reducing the number the Council must search for.

The survivors debate freeing Ilyra: Jorren wants her alive to expose the Council and face those she harmed, but rejects both her execution as civic justice and his own desire to prolong her suffering as simple mercy.

Pellis and the underground network begin smuggling a buried common-release basin map and mechanical fragments to Ilyra’s records cell, revealing that the basin was converted into a private garden and may receive the western surge.

Ilyra identifies a damaged locking plate as belonging to the converted common-release basin and marks a distributed route on the smuggled map, requiring local workers to verify and act rather than granting herself sole gate authority.

The falsified death rolls and the converted common-release basin will provide evidence for the later archive broadcast and inquiry, while the survivor network must verify whether the buried basin can receive the western surge.
Senn has joined Jorren’s network while keeping Ilyra accountable, and his unresolved desire to make her listen will continue complicating whether his actions are mercy or vengeance.

chapters.name: A Second Barrage
chapters.content:
The first thing Ilyra did with the map was turn it upside down.

Elian watched her rotate the stained sheet until the Hall sat at the bottom edge and the western channels rose toward her like branching veins. The old common-release basin had been drawn as a pale oval beneath what was now the Council garden. Its feeder ran east, under the execution galleries, then divided: one branch toward Sable Ward, another toward the private reservoirs beneath the Crown District.

“The basin is not a basin anymore,” Elian said.

“It is still a basin.”

“It has trees planted over it.”

“Trees do not change the slope.”

“People do.”

Ilyra’s charcoal paused. Her robe had dried in stiff white folds, bronze edging blackened by steam. Blisters rose along her wrists where the ceremonial restraints had rubbed her skin. She seemed not to feel them. The false death roll lay beside the map, weighted by the damaged locking plate.

“The garden terraces were built on fill,” she said. “Imported soil, stone retaining walls, decorative channels. The Council wanted the basin erased from the surface without losing its storage capacity. Water does not care what officials call a place.”

“Nor does a dead person,” Elian said.

Ilyra looked at her.

Elian had learned to recognize the moment when Ilyra’s mind gathered speed. Her eyes sharpened, her breathing became almost inaudible, and the room disappeared behind a sequence only she could see. It was not calm. It was possession—the old hunger finding a shape it could enter.

Ilyra drew a line from the western channels to the execution basin.

“The Ember Descent uses the central flood controls,” she said. “Not the public ones. The Hall’s ceremony requires heated water, pressure regulators, and a discharge route large enough to drain the basin between demonstrations. The control chamber is directly below the platform.”

“The execution was interrupted.”

“The machinery was not dismantled. Pell would never permit that. He wants the option of completing the sentence as soon as he regains the galleries.”

Elian bent over the map. “You think the ceremony can open the central controls.”

“I think it already has.”

The words came with a flash of excitement. Ilyra seized the brass cylinder and fitted it against the locking plate. The cylinder clicked once, then slipped free.

“Partial key,” she said. “The ceremony’s pressure line is a maintenance access to the central chamber. When they bring the water up, the Crown reservoirs must equalize through the Hall network. If we reverse the flow at the right moment—”

“We?”

Ilyra ignored the interruption. “The private reservoirs can be emptied into the Crown District. The pressure will fall in the western channels. Sable Ward will have time to evacuate through W-seven and the old basin.”

“And the Crown?”

“Water will enter the lower terraces first. Warehouses, gardens, the governor’s residences. The galleries above the execution platform may flood if the discharge is too rapid.”

Elian straightened. “The galleries are full.”

“Not yet.”

“They were filling when we broke the ceremony. People are still there. Officials, guards, spectators, clerks.”

“Then they will have to leave.”

Ilyra said it with such brisk certainty that Elian felt the cold beneath the Hall’s damp air.

“You are proposing to flood the people who came to watch you die.”

“I am proposing to stop the Council from flooding Sable Ward.”

“You said the galleries may flood.”

“Only if the pressure window closes.”

“And if it does?”

Ilyra’s charcoal resumed its path. “Then the water takes the galleries instead of the ward.”

Elian placed her hand over the map.

Ilyra stopped.

“Say it plainly,” Elian said. “You want the reservoirs emptied into the Crown District while Pell and half the Hall are gathered around your execution. You want them trapped by the water they directed at everyone else.”

“I want the gates opened.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only answer that matters to the people below.”

“No. It is the answer that gives you a lever.”

The cell seemed to contract. Somewhere beyond the door, a guard coughed and shifted his weight. The sound entered Ilyra’s calculations without disturbing them.

She drew three small circles around the ceremony platform.

“Guard rotation,” she said. “The west gallery changes at the second bell, because the viewing lenses need recalibration. Maret knows the service passage beneath the steam house. Senn can get through the records checkpoint if he carries the death roll. Pell will put his strongest men at the cell door and the public stairs. He will leave the mechanical corridors thinly guarded because he believes the machinery is more loyal than the workers.”

“Elian,” Ilyra said, “you can reach the broadcast tower from the archive stair. If the reservoir maps are transmitted while the gates move, they cannot call this a private attack. Every district will see where the water came from.”

“You are planning the broadcast too?”

“The records must travel with the water.”

“That sounds like one of your old reports.”

“It is better than an old report.”

“Because this time you have stolen the authority to make it true?”

Ilyra’s face tightened. “Because this time I know the Council will not permit a warning.”

The answer should have sounded like fear. Instead it sounded like vindication.

Elian lifted her hand from the map. “What happens to the people in the galleries?”

“Evacuate them before the release.”

“Through which passage?”

“The north stairs are open.”

“Pell sealed them an hour ago.”

“Then the service ramp.”

“Collapsed at the lower landing.”

Ilyra’s eyes flicked toward the fragments. “The maintenance shaft.”

“Too narrow for a crowd.”

“Crowds move when they are frightened.”

“Sometimes they trample one another.”

“Then the guards must direct them.”

“The guards are part of the crowd.”

Ilyra pushed herself upright. Pain crossed her face and vanished. She took the copper wire and laid it along the map’s western edge.

“Listen,” she said. “The private reservoirs are already being drained toward Sable Ward. If we do nothing, the lower walls fail before dawn. Forty-three people are in the tunnels. There are children in the foundries, families in the tram embankment, and workers the Council has already declared dead. You are asking me to protect a hall full of spectators while the city repeats the first flood.”

“I am asking you not to decide that their lives are the acceptable remainder.”

“I am not deciding. The Council decided when it sealed the Crown gates.”

“You are choosing how to answer.”

The charcoal snapped between Ilyra’s fingers.

For a moment Elian saw the old image beneath the new plan: governors on the ceremonial platform, their white coats bright against the river, the first flood rising toward them. Ilyra had selected the Feast not only because the controls could be reached then. She had chosen it because the powerful would be present. She had wanted them to understand fear in their bodies.

“You are smiling,” Elian said.

“I am not.”

“You are.”

Ilyra touched her mouth as if surprised to find it there. The expression disappeared, but not before Elian saw what it contained: not joy exactly, but the pleasure of a locked mechanism yielding to the correct pressure.

“I can do this,” Ilyra said.

“That is what frightens me.”

Ilyra turned the map back and forth. “The first barrage had one hand at the controls. This one will have several. Senn carries the west reading. Maret carries the Crown line. Jorren confirms W-seven. Pellis verifies the basin plate. You transmit the records. I open the central lock only after the confirmations arrive.”

“And if a district refuses?”

“Then we calculate another route.”

“And if there is no other route?”

Ilyra looked at the false roll. “Then they hear the numbers before anyone moves.”

It was the right answer, and Elian hated that it was right. Ilyra had learned to distribute the map, but she still wanted to be the mind at its center. Every route returned to her hand. Every uncertainty waited for her judgment.

A dull impact sounded above them. Dust fell from the ceiling into the candle flame.

“They are moving the execution apparatus,” Elian said.

Ilyra gathered the scraps of map. “Pell is trying to restart the ceremony.”

“He may be trying to kill you before we can act.”

“Then we use the ceremony before he uses me.”

Elian caught her arm. Ilyra flinched, more from surprise than pain.

“If the release threatens the galleries, you stop it,” Elian said.

“I stop it if stopping it does not drown Sable Ward.”

“No. You stop it because there are people there.”

“They are the people who came to watch.”

“Some are. Some were brought by work orders. Some are clerks. Some are children whose parents thought the Hall was safer than the streets. You do not get to turn all of them into the Council.”

Ilyra stared at her hand on her sleeve. “You think I do not know the difference?”

“I think you know the difference until the pressure rises.”

The words entered the cell like a blade from the old flood. Behind Ilyra’s eyes, the emergency door appeared: black water pushing through its seams, Nera’s voice in the maintenance tube, the child on the roof calling over the bells. A key in her hand. A calculation waiting to be preserved.

Her fingers began to tremble.

“I know what I did,” she said.

“Knowing afterward is not the same as yielding beforehand.”

Ilyra looked toward the barred door. “If I yield every decision because I once made the wrong one, the Council keeps deciding for everyone.”

“No one is asking you to disappear. We are asking you to remain one voice among the others.”

“One voice may be too slow.”

“Then let the slowness belong to all of us.”

A third voice came from the passage. “That depends how much time the water gives us.”

Senn stood beyond the grille, soaked to the knees, one hand wrapped around the folded death roll. Behind him, Maret carried a ring of keys and a narrow pressure strip under her coat. Both looked as though they had come through a wall rather than a door.

Ilyra’s attention snapped to the strip. “Crown line?”

“Part of it,” Maret said. “The western reading is rising faster than your last estimate. Pell has ordered the Crown gates kept sealed.”

“Of course he has.”

Senn’s jaw hardened. “Do not sound pleased.”

“I sound unsurprised.”

“You sound like you have been waiting for him to make the correct mistake.”

Ilyra met his stare. “I have been waiting for him to make the mistake that kills people.”

“And you want to answer that by putting water through the galleries.”

“I want to put it through the district that owns the reservoirs.”

“People live there too.”

The words halted her more completely than Elian’s accusation had. Senn stepped to the grille.

“Tavia is outside the Hall with three children,” he said. “If you open the Crown line without a way to clear those terraces, you may drown families who never saw your face.”

Ilyra looked down at the map. “Then we need the evacuation routes before the release.”

“Yes.”

“Can Jorren supply them?”

“He can supply some. Not enough.”

Maret set the keys on the floor. “There are old service lifts beneath the Merchant terraces. They are locked, but the counterweights still work. If the water rises slowly, they can move people to the upper walks.”

“Slowly,” Ilyra repeated. “The Crown reservoirs will not empty slowly.”

“Then divide the release,” Elian said. “Not one opening. A sequence. Each district confirms the next.”

Ilyra stared at the channel markings. Her mind raced through the alternatives, but now every line contained a face someone had placed before her.

Another impact shook the Hall. This time a bell rang: one deep note, then a second. The sound traveled through stone and water.

Ilyra closed her eyes, counting the interval.

“Three minutes until the steam regulators open,” she said. “Seven until the first pressure rise. At the second bell, the west gallery changes guards. At the third, Pell begins the sentence again if he can.”

She opened her eyes. The feverish confidence had returned, but it was no longer untouched by doubt.

“Elian,” she said, “send word that the ceremony is the access point. Not the command point. No gate opens until its district confirms.”

“And you?”

“I will get us to the controls.”

“Us?”

Ilyra looked at the map, the false names, and the fragments spread across the floor. “If I go alone, it becomes my barrage.”

The admission cost her. Elian could hear it in the roughness of her voice.

“And if you are tempted?” Elian asked.

“I will say so.”

“That is not enough.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “It is the first thing.”

Senn took the folded roll from his coat and held it against the bars. “Then hear this before you touch the controls. The names are not numbers.”

Ilyra reached for the roll. “I know.”

“Knowing is not the same as hearing it from us.”

She accepted the paper. Her thumb rested over Urek’s name, then moved down the column of the falsely dead.

Through the wall came the hiss of steam entering the execution machinery. The Hall was preparing its spectacle again. Above, officials gathered in white and bronze to watch a condemned woman descend into heated water. Below, the private reservoirs strained against their sealed gates, and Sable Ward waited in the dark for the next decision made on its behalf.

Ilyra placed the damaged locking plate at the center of the map.

“Then let them open the ceremony,” she said. “We will open the city.”

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: records cell beneath Veyr’s Hall with Elian, Senn, and Maret nearby, preparing to use the renewed Ember Descent machinery as access to the central flood controls. Goal: halt Sable Ward’s engineered flooding through a carefully sequenced release of the Council’s private reservoirs, expose the hidden water network, and preserve distributed decisions while accepting responsibility for the first flood. Relationships: tense alliance with Elian, who challenges her vengeance and demands evacuation safeguards; cautiously cooperating with Senn and Maret and the underground survivor network; opposed by Pell and the Council. Knowledge: knows the common-release basin lies beneath the Council garden, the ceremony’s pressure system connects to central controls, private reservoirs can be redirected toward the Crown District, Sable Ward’s pressure is rising, the Crown gates remain sealed, and the galleries and terraces may be endangered by a counter-release; understands that local confirmations must precede each gate opening. Possessions: soaked, heat-damaged white robe edged in bronze, false death roll, smuggled basin map, damaged locking plate, copper wire, hinge, and brass cylinder. Condition: blistered, exhausted, physically weak but animated and feverishly confident when solving the hydraulic problem; emotionally unsettled by Elian’s accusation that she wants powerful people to feel helpless, and beginning to admit that the ceremony must be an access point rather than her personal command.

set.name: Maret
set.description: Location: records passage and Hall service routes with Senn, carrying keys and a Crown-line pressure strip while preparing for the renewed execution ceremony. Goal: get warnings and evacuation help to Sable Ward, identify usable service lifts beneath the Merchant terraces, prevent Pell from converting the crisis into concealment or vengeance, and protect Lessa’s memory. Relationships: conflicted toward Ilyra but cooperating with her; allied cautiously with Senn, Elian, Jorren, Pellis, and local survivors; openly resistant to Pell. Knowledge: understands private reservoirs are draining toward Sable Ward, coded notices favored wealthy households, the Crown gates remain sealed, the ceremony provides access to central controls, and old service lifts may evacuate Crown and Merchant residents if the release is slow enough. Possessions: civic uniform with pins removed, keys hidden beneath her sleeve, divided pressure readings, and a narrow Crown-line pressure strip. Condition: frightened, grieving, physically strained, morally resolute, and willing to violate Hall orders to create evacuation routes before the counter-release.

set.name: Senn
set.description: Location: records passage outside Ilyra’s cell after moving between the Hall and Jorren’s underground survivor network, carrying the false death roll and a western pressure reading. Goal: evacuate Sable Ward and Tavia’s children, expose Pell’s concealment, prevent the counter-release from killing uninvolved residents, and keep Ilyra accountable without allowing her sole control; still uncertain whether his persistence is mercy or vengeance. Relationships: hostile toward Ilyra but secretly allied with Jorren, Pellis, Elian, Maret, and local survivors; openly resistant to Pell and the Council. Knowledge: knows at least 117 people were entered as dead before their actual deaths, private reservoirs are redirecting pressure toward Sable Ward, the Crown gates are sealed, the Ember Descent can provide access to the controls, and each release requires evacuation and local confirmation. Possessions: civic uniform, baton, keys, false death roll, and divided pressure readings. Condition: soaked, angry, vigilant, morally unsettled, and committed to helping the network while insisting to Ilyra that the names are not numbers.

set.name: Elian Dault
set.description: Location: records cell beneath Veyr’s Hall with Ilyra, coordinating archival evidence and the planned broadcast. Goal: expose the Council’s planned sacrifice and her father’s escape, prevent Sable Ward’s flooding, broadcast the reservoir records during the counter-release, and force rescue planning to include spectators and uninvolved families. Relationships: tense but practical alliance with Ilyra; allied cautiously with Senn, Maret, Jorren, Pellis, and the survivor network; adversarial toward Pell and Governor Dault. Knowledge: possesses copied Council minutes, reservoir routing orders, coded evacuation notices, Dault’s signed lower-basin order, the hidden escape route, false death rolls, and evidence of the converted common-release basin; knows the Ember Descent machinery can access central controls and that Ilyra’s plan risks the execution galleries and Crown terraces. Possessions: leather case, blue-threaded archival packet, dark traveling coat, gray scarf, divided pressure readings, copied channel markings, and stained basin map. Condition: exhausted, grief-stricken, controlled, politically endangered, and determined to restrain Ilyra’s decisive instincts without surrendering the urgent rescue.

Ilyra identifies that the Ember Descent's heated-water machinery provides maintenance access to the central flood controls beneath the execution platform and designs a counter-release through the Council's private reservoirs.
Elian confronts Ilyra over her willingness to endanger the execution galleries, exposing that the rescue plan also appeals to Ilyra's desire to make the powerful experience helplessness.

Ilyra revises the counter-release into a distributed sequence: Elian will broadcast the records, local groups will confirm routes and gates, and Ilyra will enter the controls without acting as sole authority.

Ilyra and the survivor network will use the interrupted Ember Descent as an access point to the central flood controls, requiring sequential district confirmations before releasing private reservoir water and preventing any single authority from commanding the gates.

The execution galleries, Crown terraces, and other populated districts must receive evacuation routes before the reservoir release, since the rescue plan could otherwise turn spectators and uninvolved families into new flood victims.
Elian must broadcast the reservoir maps and Council records while the counter-release occurs so the Council cannot recast the operation as Ilyra's solitary terrorist attack.

chapters.name: The Shape of Vengeance
chapters.content:
The first thing Ilyra did with the new plan was draw a line through it.

Not across the map. Across the Crown District.

Her charcoal stopped at the gardens above the Hall, where the private reservoirs lay beneath tiled courtyards and glass-roofed winter rooms. Beyond them, the river channels narrowed toward the ceremonial platform. If the western pressure came through the common-release basin and the Crown gates opened in the proper order, the water would pass beneath the terraces, strip the gardens, drown the lower warehouses, and spare Sable Ward from the full force of the Council’s discharge.

If the order was wrong, the execution galleries would become a bowl.

If she opened the Crown gates too quickly, the water would climb the Hall steps before the spectators understood that the ceremony had changed.

If she opened them too slowly, Sable Ward would be lost.

Ilyra wrote the times beside each gate, then rubbed them out and wrote them again.

The records cell smelled of wet wool, hot metal, and the sour mineral breath rising through the drain. Somewhere beyond the walls, the Hall’s machinery groaned as men tried to restore the interrupted Ember Descent. Each shudder passed through the floor and into her blistered feet. The city was preparing to kill her with the same system she meant to enter.

Elian watched from the opposite side of the table. She had removed her coat and wrapped it around her shoulders, but the fabric was still dark at the hem from the water in the execution basin. The blue-threaded packet lay open beside her. Its pages curled in the damp.

“You have made the Crown District into a number,” Elian said.

“It is a pressure body.”

“That isn’t what I said.”

Ilyra looked down at the map. “The water does not care what I call it.”

“No. You do.”

The charcoal snapped between Ilyra’s fingers. A black splinter lodged beneath her nail. She pushed it deeper without noticing.

Behind Elian, Senn stood with his shoulder against the stone wall, his baton hanging from one hand. He had said little since returning from the passage. Maret was farther down the cell, listening at the door for the change in guard rotation. Her civic pins had been removed, leaving small pale marks in the cloth of her uniform. Even stripped of insignia, she looked like someone who had once belonged to an order and had not yet decided whether to mourn it.

“Read the figures,” Ilyra said. “Sable Ward has six thousand people in the lower streets. More if the count is honest. The Crown terraces have evacuation lifts, sealed stairways, private boats, and three levels of stone above the first surge.”

“Those are not the figures you wrote first.”

Ilyra’s gaze moved to the edge of the table.

Elian had found the earlier sheet beneath the basin map. The paper was creased from being folded and unfolded too many times. On it, in Ilyra’s hand, the sequence was simpler: Crown release, western diversion, gallery breach if necessary.

If necessary.

There were other words beneath the erased line. Elian had held the page near the lamp until the pressure of the old writing showed through.

Let them see.

The phrase had been written before the first flood.

Ilyra remembered the pen in her hand. Remembered the neat black letters. Remembered thinking that the governors would be gathered on the platform in their white coats, beneath the bronze banners, while the Low Quarter waited behind walls they had declared expendable. She had imagined the river rising around their shoes. She had imagined Governor Dault reaching for a railing and finding no servant close enough to catch him.

She had not imagined the people in the storage fields.

She had imagined the governors.

“I wrote it in anger,” she said.

“You selected the day in anger.”

“I selected the day because the Council would be assembled.”

“You selected the day because the Council would be assembled where you could see them.”

The cell seemed to contract. Ilyra measured it instinctively: eleven paces from wall to wall, three and a half from table to drain. The ceiling was low enough that Elian’s head nearly touched the hanging pipe. A drop of water formed at the pipe’s joint, trembled, and fell.

Ilyra waited for it to strike the floor.

“One drop,” she said.

Elian’s expression tightened. “What?”

“Nothing.”

The drop spread on the stone in a dark circle.

For forty-one days she had counted everything that could be counted. Breaths between footsteps. Hinges in the lock. The interval between Senn’s visits and Maret’s. The exact time it took for a guard to descend the eastern stair. Control was not comfort, but it had edges. It could be held.

Memory had no edges.

It came when she closed her eyes: the North Barrage chamber, the pressure needle trembling, the copper taste of fear in the air. Nera’s face under the maintenance lamp. Hobb shouting that the feeder was buckling. Beyond the upper grates, festival lights moving like stars over black water.

She had told herself the ceremony made the intervention visible. If the governors were present, they could not deny the danger. If the water rose beneath their platform, they would have to listen.

But underneath the argument had been another thought, bright and private:

They will know what it is to wait for a door to open.

She had not spoken that thought to Nera. She had not spoken it to Hobb. She had not spoken it even to herself in a voice she would recognize as confession.

“I did not open the barrage to frighten them,” Ilyra said.

Elian leaned over the map. “No?”

“I opened it to lower the pressure.”

“You did both.”

“The second was not the purpose.”

“Purpose is not a magic word. You can have two.”

Ilyra pushed back from the table. Her chair scraped the floor, and Maret turned from the door.

“You want this to be simple,” Ilyra said. “You want my anger to explain everything because then your father’s orders can explain everything else. The Council chose the lower basin. I opened the gate. You can put those facts on opposite sides of a page and call the page balanced.”

“I want the page not to lie.”

“It will lie if you make my motive the center of it.”

“Then stop making it the center.”

The words landed harder than an accusation. Elian took the earlier sheet and turned it so that Ilyra could see the faded writing.

“Do you want justice for the dead?” Elian asked.

Ilyra stared at the words.

“Or do you want an audience for your moral triumph?”

Senn shifted against the wall. “Elian.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “Let her finish.”

Elian’s fingers remained on the page. “You keep saying the powerful must be made helpless. You say the records must be shown while the water moves, that the galleries must watch the Crown gardens drown, that no one should be allowed to mistake the cost of their protection. Some of that is necessary. Some of it is theater.”

“The records are necessary.”

“The records are. Your satisfaction is not.”

Ilyra laughed once. It came out thin and without humor. “You think I am satisfied?”

“I think you are alive when you describe the gates.”

The cell fell silent except for the buried pumps.

It was true. When Ilyra spoke of pressure windows, the weakness in her body receded. Her hands steadied. The world became a system of forces that could be anticipated if she looked closely enough. Elian’s accusation had become another variable, and variables could be solved.

She reached for the damaged locking plate.

“Here,” she said. “The basin plate is warped, but the old teeth are intact. The release will need confirmation from the basin workers. The western channel requires a second confirmation from Sable Ward. The Crown line cannot open until the evacuation lifts are cleared. Those are not gestures. They are safeguards.”

“You designed them because I insisted.”

“I designed them because they are sound.”

“You designed them after I told you that if you controlled every gate, you would become the Council with better mathematics.”

Ilyra’s hand closed around the plate.

The Council with better mathematics.

In the first flood, she had believed the difference between herself and the men who dismissed her was that she knew the numbers. She had believed knowledge made her honest. They had chosen who could be sacrificed because it preserved property. She had chosen who could be sacrificed because the equations demanded it—or because she had made equations into a place where no one could challenge her grief.

She remembered Nera through the maintenance tube.

Not the words first. The sound. A wet, ragged breathing between shouts. Then: “You said there would be a way back.”

Ilyra had answered that the pressure was falling.

Nera had asked, “For whom?”

At the time, Ilyra had heard defiance. Now she heard the question beneath it. Who had she included in the word we?

“I was right about the danger,” Ilyra said.

Elian did not soften. “You were.”

“And I was wrong about what being right permitted me to do.”

Senn looked at her then. Maret turned fully from the door.

The admission did not relieve Ilyra. It made the room larger and less stable. If she had been wrong about everything, she could have surrendered the whole memory to error. But the Council had known. The lower basin had been designed. The valves had been removed for Dault’s private line. Families had been placed in the fields she marked empty. Truth and guilt occupied the same machinery.

Elian folded the sheet with the faded words.

“Say it plainly,” she said.

Ilyra’s throat tightened. “I wanted them afraid.”

“Which them?”

“The governors. The Council. Anyone who had decided that fear belonged only to us.”

“And now?”

“Now Sable Ward is being flooded.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “It is the emergency.”

Elian waited.

Ilyra looked at the map again. The Crown gardens were pale beneath the charcoal. The Sable channels were dark with repeated marks. Between them ran the common-release basin, buried under soil and ornamental stone, a shared safeguard converted into a private garden. Someone had planted flowering trees over the place where the city was meant to release its excess water.

“I want the Council exposed,” Ilyra said. “I want the dead counted. I want Sable Ward evacuated. I want the people who ordered this to answer for it.”

“And you want them to know you did it.”

Ilyra could have denied it. The denial rose easily, practiced by years of trial and interrogation.

Instead she said, “Yes.”

Elian’s face changed—not into forgiveness, but recognition.

“I want them to know I was not a mistake they could erase,” Ilyra continued. “I want them to hear the names. I want them to stand where I stood and understand that the water was never an accident.”

“That is vengeance.”

“It may be.”

Senn’s jaw tightened. “May be?”

Ilyra turned toward him. “What would you call it?”

He looked at the false death roll in his hand. “I don’t know. I wanted you to live long enough to hear what you did to my sister. I told myself that was accountability. Some days it felt like I wanted you to hurt because I hurt.”

Maret lowered her eyes.

Senn continued, “Wanting a thing for the right reason doesn’t keep the want clean.”

The pump beneath them gave a violent knock. Dust sifted from the ceiling. Somewhere above, people began shouting. The sound traveled through the Hall’s stone ribs, distorted but unmistakable: a crowd no longer cheering.

Ilyra bent over the map.

“The first confirmation must come from the basin,” she said. “Then Sable Ward. Then the evacuation lifts. No release before all three.”

Elian studied her. “And if one refuses?”

“Then we explain the pressure and wait.”

“We may not have time.”

“I know.”

“And if waiting costs thousands?”

Ilyra’s fingers hovered above the Crown line. The old instinct was immediate: seize the master controls, calculate the lesser loss, act before fear became debate.

She withdrew her hand.

“Then the loss will belong to the decision we make together,” she said. “Not to me alone.”

Elian nodded once, though doubt remained between them.

Ilyra gathered the charcoal, the locking plate, and the map. The metal was cold despite the heat in the room. She could still feel the imagined terror of governors beneath her palm, a bright shape that had survived every correction she had made to herself.

She did not mistake its disappearance for redemption.

At the door, Maret whispered that the guards were moving.

Ilyra folded the map and gave half of it to Elian.

“Keep the Crown route,” she said.

“You trust me with it?”

“No. I trust the route not to belong to one person.”

For the first time, Elian almost smiled.

Then the locks above them began to turn, and Ilyra felt the old command rise inside her like floodwater: open, close, decide.

She named the command before it could become an order.

Vengeance.

Then she waited for the others to speak.

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: records cell beneath Veyr’s Hall with Elian, Senn, and Maret nearby, waiting for guards to move while preparing to use the renewed Ember Descent machinery as access to the central flood controls. Goal: halt Sable Ward’s engineered flooding through a carefully sequenced release of the Council’s private reservoirs, expose the hidden water network, preserve distributed decisions, and accept responsibility for the first flood without turning accountability into a personal spectacle. Relationships: tense alliance with Elian, who confronts her desire to make the powerful helpless and now shares control of the Crown route; cautiously cooperating with Senn and Maret and the underground survivor network; opposed by Pell and the Council. Knowledge: knows the common-release basin lies beneath the Council garden, the ceremony’s pressure system connects to central controls, private reservoirs can be redirected toward the Crown District, Sable Ward’s pressure is rising, the Crown gates remain sealed, the galleries and terraces may be endangered by a counter-release, and local confirmations must precede each gate opening. Possessions: soaked, heat-damaged white robe edged in bronze, false death roll nearby, smuggled basin map divided with Elian, damaged locking plate, charcoal, copper wire, hinge, and brass cylinder. Condition: blistered, exhausted, physically weak but animated when solving hydraulic problems; emotionally unsettled after admitting she wanted the governors to fear her and recognizing vengeance within her rescue plan, yet determined not to take sole command.

set.name: Maret
set.description: Location: records passage and Hall service routes outside Ilyra’s cell, listening for guard movement and preparing for the renewed execution ceremony. Goal: get warnings and evacuation help to Sable Ward, identify usable service lifts beneath the Merchant terraces, prevent Pell from converting the crisis into concealment or vengeance, and protect Lessa’s memory. Relationships: conflicted toward Ilyra but cooperating with her; allied cautiously with Senn, Elian, Jorren, Pellis, and local survivors; openly resistant to Pell. Knowledge: understands private reservoirs are draining toward Sable Ward, coded notices favored wealthy households, the Crown gates remain sealed, the ceremony provides access to central controls, old service lifts may evacuate Crown and Merchant residents if the release is slow enough, and Ilyra has admitted that personal vengeance is entangled with her plan. Possessions: civic uniform with pins removed, keys hidden beneath her sleeve, divided pressure readings, and a narrow Crown-line pressure strip. Condition: frightened, grieving, physically strained, morally resolute, and alert to the guards’ approach while willing to violate Hall orders to create evacuation routes.

set.name: Senn
set.description: Location: records passage outside Ilyra’s cell after moving between the Hall and Jorren’s underground survivor network, carrying the false death roll and western pressure reading. Goal: evacuate Sable Ward and Tavia’s children, expose Pell’s concealment, prevent the counter-release from killing uninvolved residents, and keep Ilyra accountable without allowing her sole control; he now openly recognizes that his own wish to make her hear the harm may contain vengeance. Relationships: hostile toward Ilyra but secretly allied with Jorren, Pellis, Elian, Maret, and local survivors; he has admitted his motives are morally mixed; openly resistant to Pell and the Council. Knowledge: knows at least 117 people were entered as dead before their actual deaths, private reservoirs are redirecting pressure toward Sable Ward, the Crown gates are sealed, the Ember Descent can provide access to the controls, each release requires evacuation and local confirmation, and Ilyra selected the first intervention partly to frighten the governors. Possessions: civic uniform, baton, keys, false death roll, and divided pressure readings. Condition: soaked, angry, vigilant, morally unsettled, and committed to helping the network while insisting that names are not numbers and that accountability must not become another appetite for suffering.

set.name: Elian Dault
set.description: Location: records cell beneath Veyr’s Hall with Ilyra, Senn, and Maret, holding the Crown route while guards begin moving above. Goal: expose the Council’s planned sacrifice and her father’s escape, prevent Sable Ward’s flooding, broadcast the reservoir records during the counter-release, and force rescue planning to include spectators and uninvolved families. Relationships: tense but practical alliance with Ilyra; she directly challenges Ilyra’s desire for moral triumph and shares route information so control cannot belong to one person; allied cautiously with Senn, Maret, Jorren, Pellis, and the survivor network; adversarial toward Pell and Governor Dault. Knowledge: possesses copied Council minutes, reservoir routing orders, coded evacuation notices, Dault’s signed lower-basin order, the hidden escape route, false death rolls, evidence of the converted common-release basin, and the newly acknowledged truth that Ilyra wants the Council to know she acted; knows the Ember Descent machinery can access central controls and that Ilyra’s plan risks the execution galleries and Crown terraces. Possessions: leather case, blue-threaded archival packet, dark traveling coat, gray scarf, divided pressure readings, copied channel markings, stained basin map with the Crown route, and the folded sheet bearing Ilyra’s erased words. Condition: exhausted, grief-stricken, controlled, politically endangered, and more wary than ever of Ilyra while recognizing her willingness to admit vengeance.

Elian confronts Ilyra with the faded words “Let them see,” forcing her to admit that she selected the first Feast intervention partly to make the governors afraid and that she still wants the Council to know she acted.

Ilyra acknowledges that being correct about the flood’s danger did not grant her the right to decide who would be sacrificed, and recommits the second operation to shared confirmations rather than sole control.
Senn admits that his wish to keep Ilyra alive to hear what she did to his sister sometimes feels like a desire to make her hurt, explicitly linking accountability with his own unresolved vengeance.

Ilyra’s admission that she wants the Council to know she acted, and her recognition that vengeance remains inside the rescue plan, will complicate her later public address and testimony; she must neither deny the harm she caused nor turn accountability into self-glorifying spectacle.

chapters.name: Pell’s Bargain
chapters.content:
The locks turned in sequence.

One above the door. One inside the wall. One beneath the floor, where the old records cell had once held flood ledgers and confiscated maps. Ilyra counted the intervals between them because counting was easier than imagining who had ordered the movement.

Three breaths.

A scrape of iron.

Two breaths.

The final bolt withdrew with a sound like a tooth being pulled.

Maret stepped away from the door. Senn lifted his baton, though the passage beyond was too narrow for him to swing it properly. Elian folded the Crown route beneath her coat. The others had taken their places around Ilyra without deciding to do so, as if the cell had become a small defensive machine and each of them a necessary part.

Magistrate Oren Pell entered alone.

He wore the white judicial robe from the interrupted ceremony, but its lower hem was dark with water. A bronze chain crossed his chest. One link had been repaired with wire, and the crude join caught the lamplight whenever he moved. He carried no guard’s weapon. That was the first sign that he had come to speak rather than command.

The second was the man behind him.

A clerk stood in the passage with a writing board pressed against his ribs. His face was pale, his eyes lowered. Pell turned his head slightly.

“Wait outside.”

The clerk obeyed. The door remained open.

Ilyra looked at Pell’s hands. Empty.

“You have been busy,” Pell said.

“Have you?”

“Restoring order.”

“Is that what you call the water in Sable Ward?”

His expression did not change, but his gaze flicked toward the map table. He knew. Of course he knew. The Council had never been blind to water. It had only been selective about whose drowning counted as information.

“Your associates have mistaken movement for power,” he said. “The Hall is secured. The broadcast relays are being isolated. The western passages are sealed.”

“Then why are you here?” Elian asked.

Pell looked at her with the weary contempt of a man forced to acknowledge an inconvenient relative. “Because you have made yourself a criminal rather than a daughter.”

“I was a daughter before I was a criminal.”

“And now you are both.”

Senn shifted his grip on the baton. “Say what you came to say.”

Pell’s eyes returned to Ilyra. “Gladly.”

He removed a folded document from inside his robe. It was not an execution order. The paper was thinner, cream-colored, with a blue seal pressed into the corner. He set it on the table beside the basin map.

Ilyra did not touch it.

“An amended declaration,” Pell said. “To be read over the civic network before the Ember Descent resumes.”

“You’ve already had my statement.”

“Your statement was a list of grievances dressed as responsibility. This is cleaner.”

“Clean for whom?”

“For the city.”

The phrase had been used by Pell before, in court, in the interrogation chamber, in the quiet corridor outside the Flood Cells. The city was always invoked as if it were a single frightened animal, and Pell alone knew how to keep it from biting itself.

Ilyra opened the document.

The first line named her as the sole architect of the North Barrage disaster. The second described her as suffering from “a prolonged fixation born of district resentment.” The third stated that no official, engineer, clerk, or civic department had known of her intentions or contributed to the conditions she exploited.

She read the page twice.

The words were calm. That was their cruelty. No insult. No theatrical accusation. Only the soft administrative language that turned a city into a witness and a woman into a malfunction.

“What do you want?” she asked.

Pell sat in the chair she had left near the drain. He did not ask permission. “A confession.”

“I have confessed.”

“Not the useful part.”

His voice was almost kind. Ilyra had learned to distrust kindness more quickly than anger. Anger announced its appetite. Kindness concealed the hand that selected the portion.

“You will read this declaration publicly,” Pell said. “You will state that you acted alone, that your reports were inventions created to justify a private campaign, and that the Council had no prior knowledge of the pressure conditions at North Barrage Four. You will say the flood was the product of your irrational intervention, not a consequence of policy.”

“And in return?”

“A painless death.”

Maret made a small sound behind him. Not a gasp. Something closer to disgust.

Pell continued. “The basin will be heated to the proper threshold. The descent will be brief. No prolongation, no public questioning, no attempt to extract names from you while the crowd watches. You will be permitted a sedative before the ceremony.”

Ilyra looked again at the document.

Painless.

The word entered her with the precision of a hook. She imagined the heated basin, the steam closing over her, the mirrored lenses multiplying the moment. She imagined no pain, or as little as the Council could define by regulation. A body reduced to an event. A final breath measured and approved.

Pell leaned forward.

“And the engineers from your department will be spared prosecution.”

Ilyra’s eyes lifted.

“Who?”

“Those still under investigation. Halvek. Venn. Sorell’s deputies. The mechanics who signed your access logs. The archive staff who failed to report your map theft. Their charges will be withdrawn if you establish that they were deceived by you.”

“Halvek dismissed the reports.”

“Perhaps. But he need not be tried for the consequences of your response.”

“Venn’s seal was stolen from his office.”

“Then he need not be tried for failing to guard it.”

“Pellis?”

Pell paused. “The clerk who assisted you will be transferred and released.”

That was the first true bargain in the room. Pellis had copied forms, carried fragments, risked the Hall’s records to get the maps through. He had not opened the barrage. He had not chosen the Feast. But the Council could still make his life a warning to every clerk who thought paper belonged to the public.

“And Nera?” Ilyra asked.

Pell’s gaze did not waver. “The surviving engineers.”

“She is not confirmed dead.”

“I know.”

“Then say her name.”

“I am offering you the lives of people who may yet be saved from a prosecution that will otherwise follow them for years.”

“You know where she is?”

“I know what the records say.”

“The records say Hobb is dead.”

“The records say many things.”

For an instant, the room lost its dimensions. Ilyra heard the maintenance tube instead of Pell’s voice. Nera breathing through water. Nera asking, For whom? Hobb shouting at the feeder. Lio crying behind the emergency door.

Pell watched her face.

“You see?” he said. “You can still protect them.”

The old memory shifted. She was no longer before the sealed door. She stood in the records cell with a pen in her hand, and the page beneath it was blank. One sentence could be written. One version could be fixed. The engineers would walk away. Pellis would keep his name. Nera, if alive, would not be dragged into a courtroom and made to answer for a decision she had opposed.

Ilyra imagined the declaration entering every district through the civic towers.

I acted alone.

The words would travel over Sable Ward while water rose through its streets. People would hear that the disaster had no parent but her. The Council’s hands would disappear into the sentence. Dault’s order would become a forgery. The private reservoirs would become irrelevant. The dead would belong to one woman, and the city could return to sleep.

But the names of the engineers would remain.

Nera Vale: spared because Ilyra had lied convincingly.

Pellis: alive because the truth had been narrowed.

Hobb: dead, perhaps, and protected by a false record.

For one breath, the arrangement seemed almost merciful.

Elian watched her. She knew before Ilyra spoke what was happening.

“You’re considering it,” Elian said.

“I am considering the people he named.”

“That is how the offer is built.”

“Do not make their lives into an argument against saving them.”

“I’m not.” Elian’s voice lowered. “I’m asking what you think you are saving them into.”

Pell smiled faintly. “Your friend has inherited the luxury of purity.”

Elian stepped toward the table. “No. I have inherited a house full of records proving what your bargains cost.”

“You have inherited grief and mistaken it for authority.”

“I have inherited your father’s signature.”

The smile vanished.

Ilyra barely heard them. She was reading the declaration again, but this time she read it as an engineer. The structure was elegant. Every sentence removed a support from the next. If she acted alone, her reports became invention. If her reports were invention, the Council had no reason to prepare for the flood. If it had no reason to prepare, the lower-basin design became innocent. If the design was innocent, the deaths became the consequence of her mind.

Pell had not written a confession. He had designed a load-bearing lie.

She touched the blue seal with one finger.

“And if I sign?”

“You read it.”

“Then the Council releases the engineers?”

“On the same broadcast.”

“Before my death?”

“During the ceremony.”

“So they hear that their freedom depends on my guilt.”

“Their freedom depends on your honesty.”

Ilyra laughed softly. “You have learned to call obedience honesty.”

Pell rose. “You are in no position to lecture anyone about the difference.”

The words struck because they were not wholly false. Ilyra had called necessity what she wanted. She had called calculation what had sometimes been pride. She had asked Nera to trust a map whose omissions she knew existed. She had sealed a door and defended the machinery with the vocabulary of lives saved elsewhere.

Pell saw the hesitation and stepped closer.

“You want authorship,” he said.

Ilyra’s hand tightened on the page.

“You want to write the final account yourself,” he continued. “Even now. You would rather die as the woman who revealed the Council than live as the woman who admitted she was merely consumed by resentment. You call that truth because it preserves your chosen shape.”

“You want me to become your shape.”

“I want you to stop pretending that your motives are nobler than your acts.”

“Then why offer me a lie?”

“Because the city needs an ending.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “You need one.”

Behind Pell, the clerk shifted in the passage. From above came a dull vibration, followed by a burst of voices. The Hall’s machinery had begun moving again. Somewhere, heated water was being forced into the execution system. The sound traveled down through the walls, a pulse beneath the stone.

Pell placed both palms on the table.

“Sign, and the engineers live.”

Ilyra closed her eyes.

The first memory came not as water but as ink. Her childhood hand copying ration figures beside Tomas. Twelve measures promised, seven delivered. A clerk’s neat correction. A permit denied. Tomas saying, “If it is written, they can say it was never so.”

Then the pump station. The child on the roof. The brass key hot in her palm.

Then Nera behind the emergency door.

She had wanted to control the water because the city had taught her that whoever controlled the record controlled the dead. She had believed a perfect account could force justice into existence. Now Pell offered her the opposite power: to protect the living by corrupting the account.

It was tempting because it would still be her choice.

That was the trap.

She opened her eyes.

“Give me the pen,” she said.

Elian took one step forward. “Ilyra.”

“I need to write the names.”

Pell reached inside his robe and produced a narrow black pen. He set it beside the declaration.

“Only the signature,” he said.

“Of course.”

She picked it up. The metal was warm from his body. On the first line beneath the declaration, she wrote her name.

Ilyra Voss.

Pell exhaled.

The relief in him was small but unmistakable. It was the relief of a man watching a gate begin to close.

Ilyra let the ink glisten.

Then she drew the pen through her name.

Pell’s face hardened. “What are you doing?”

“Correcting the record.”

“You accepted the terms.”

“I examined them.”

She folded the declaration once, carefully, and held it over the lamp. The paper caught at the corner. Blue flame ran along the edge. Pell lunged, but Senn moved between them. Maret seized the document with a pair of tongs from the table and dropped it into the drain basin.

The burning sheet hissed. Black letters loosened and broke apart in the water.

Pell stared at her. “You have condemned those engineers.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “You have.”

“They will be prosecuted.”

“Then let them testify.”

“They will be tortured into testimony.”

“Then let the city hear that too.”

“You think the city wants your truth?”

“No.” Ilyra’s voice shook, but she did not lower it. “I think it wants a story it can consume. You want to give it one where I am the only meal.”
