Condition: soaked, bloodied at the cheek, angry, vigilant, morally unsettled, and committed to accountability without allowing vengeance or emergency authority to dictate the rescue.

set.name: Mara Quill
set.description: Location: moving from the opened prison wing into the Hall’s service routes with the released prisoners, seeking the Crown stairs and alternate receiving paths for Sable Ward evacuees. Goal: use her knowledge of the tram and service routes to reach survivors and prevent twelve-place capacity from becoming a death sentence for everyone else. Relationships: distrustful of Ilyra and Senn’s uniforms but cooperating with both; aligned provisionally with Pellan, released prisoners, district representatives, workers, and survivors; opposed to Pell and the Council. Knowledge: knows official maps omit or misstate local routes, understands that the tram route is collapsed below the third landing and the boiler route is flooded, and has heard the three-confirmation rule and the current capacity limit at Old Foundry School. Possessions: prisoner’s gray clothing, a civic wrench, bandaged hands, and local route knowledge. Condition: scarred, wary, angry, physically tense, and unwilling to grant Ilyra forgiveness while choosing rescue work over passive revenge.

set.name: Pellan
set.description: Location: moving with Mara Quill and the other released prisoners through the Hall’s service routes toward alternate Crown stairs and receiving paths. Goal: use his former tram-mechanic knowledge to identify safe routes, assist evacuations, and keep the released group from becoming an uncontrolled mob. Relationships: provisionally allied with Mara, Senn, Ilyra, workers, district representatives, and survivors; distrustful of the Council and Pell; cooperating despite the danger of being labeled a rioter. Knowledge: knows the tram embankment has collapsed below the third landing, the service lift is unsafe until confirmed, and no person should carry a gate key without a second witness under Ilyra’s protocol. Possessions: prisoner’s work clothes and a civic wrench. Condition: physically strained, cautious, resentful, and focused on practical rescue rather than vengeance.

Ilyra formalizes a three-part gate protocol requiring an engineer’s pressure confirmation, a worker’s route confirmation, and a district representative’s receiving-capacity confirmation before any gate opens; she rejects faster variants that would restore her unilateral authority.

Senn opens the old prison wing and releases Mara Quill, Pellan, and other prisoners, including people with route and mechanical knowledge; the group accepts paired tools and distributed decisions for the rescue.
Baret, Vennik, and Rusk publicly refuse Pell’s order to sever the western tower line, and their names and refusal enter the continuing archive broadcast.

Mara Quill and the released prisoners will work with Senn, district representatives, and route workers during the rescue, carrying local knowledge while remaining subject to paired tools and distributed confirmations rather than a single commander.

chapters.name: The Last Night
chapters.content:
The last night began with the Hall pretending it was still a place of law.

At the seventh bell, clerks carried warmed lamps through the service galleries. At the eighth, the execution basin was drained and scrubbed, though the bronze beneath the platform remained dark with heat. At the ninth, the mirrored lenses were turned toward the empty galleries and tested one by one. Each lens gave back a small, pale room in which no one stood.

Ilyra watched the reflections from the records cell.

She had been moved there after the relay workers’ refusal, when Pell decided that a prisoner awaiting death should not remain close to the machinery of public communication. The cell had no window, but the wall sweated with the Hall’s weather. Water ran down the stone in fine threads. Somewhere below, a pump labored, stopped, and labored again.

She sat on the floor with her back against the wall and arranged the objects she had left: charcoal, copper wire, the damaged locking plate, the brass cylinder, and the burned edge of Pell’s declaration. The white robe was no longer white. Heat had yellowed its bronze border, and one sleeve was stiff with dried water. Her blisters had opened beneath the bandages. When she flexed her fingers, pain traveled up her arms in bright, clean lines.

Pain was useful. It marked the boundary between her and everything else.

She placed the charcoal parallel to the wall.

Then she began to write names on the floor.

Nera.

Hobb Renn.

Lio.

The names did not arrive in order. Hobb came first because the court had read his name as if it were a line in an inventory. Nera came because her voice had remained behind the door. Lio came because the child had said, very calmly, that the water was at her chest.

Ilyra added the workers whose names she had heard through the maintenance tube. Some were only sounds now, broken by the metal and the flood. Jase. Orlin. Sef. A woman who had called herself Mother without giving another name. The child on the west platform, if Lio was not that child. The child on the roof, whose name Ilyra had never known.

She stopped.

The charcoal trembled between her fingers.

In memory, the roof was not a roof but a dark island rising through brown water. A small body stood beside a chimney, hair pasted to the face. The child had one hand lifted. In Ilyra’s other hand, the brass valve key pressed a hard circle into her palm.

“Please,” the child had said.

The pump station bell had been ringing behind her. Pressure was still rising. If she carried the key to the station, she could open the drainage line. If she left it, the lower streets would fill another foot, perhaps two. The figures in the water had become indistinct. She had told herself that a key could save a street, while a hand could save only one life.

She had not told herself the other thing.

That the child’s fear made the decision feel clean. That choosing the key allowed her to remain the engineer and not become the woman who had to choose a particular face.

The memory changed, as it always did. The roof tilted. The child became Nera. Nera became Tomas. Tomas became a crowd without names, all of them reaching toward the hand that held the tool.

Ilyra put down the charcoal.

“Not evidence,” she said.

The cell returned the words to her in a thin echo.

She gathered the names into a list on the burned declaration. It was easier there. The paper had already been used for a lie. She could give it something that was not true merely because she wanted it to be true.

Nera Vale—sealed behind the lower door.

Hobb Renn—listed dead.

Lio—unconfirmed.

The workers behind the door.

The families in the eastern storage fields.

The child on the roof—unknown.

She wrote Anja Meret and, beneath it, Leth, Ovan, Suri. She had not met them. Their names had come through Senn’s relay in a voice that shook only once. She wrote them because the Council would not. She wrote Lessa, with the red scarf and brass pin. Tomas Voss, died in civic custody. The unnamed. The unregistered. The people whose last records were wet enough to blur.

By the time she finished, the list filled both sides of the declaration.

It looked like a confession.

That was what frightened her.

Not that the names were false. Not that she had invented a single one. But that the list could be carried into the morning and held up before the lenses. Look, the dead could say. Look how much I remember. Look how deeply I have suffered. Look how my suffering proves that I am changed.

She imagined the crowd receiving it. Some would weep. Some would cheer. Pell would let the silence grow until her remorse became another civic ornament. The city would use the names to measure her heart and never ask who had chosen the lower basin, who had removed the valves, who had sealed the evacuation orders.

Even grief could become a lever.

Ilyra folded the paper once. Twice.

Then she fed it to the lamp.

The flame took the corner. Names curled black, lifted, and became ash. She watched until Nera’s name disappeared. She watched until Tomas’s name became a glowing thread. When the last scrap fell into the lamp, she opened the vent and scattered the ash into the damp air.

A key turned in the outer lock.

Ilyra reached for the charcoal, but the door opened before she could hide it.

Maret stood there without her civic pins. Her uniform was dark at the shoulders with water, and one hand gripped the frame as if the Hall were moving beneath her. She had a narrow pressure strip tucked into her belt and a ring of hidden keys at her waist.

“You’re not supposed to have visitors,” Ilyra said.

“I’m not visiting.”

“Then you’re disobeying an order.”

“Yes.” Maret stepped inside and shut the door. “Pell has issued several tonight. It’s difficult to choose which one to break first.”

She looked at the floor. The charcoal marks remained where the paper had been, a scatter of names and fragments. Ilyra had not thought to erase them.

Maret read the first three. Her face tightened at Hobb’s name.

“I thought he was missing,” she said.

“The court listed him among the dead.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“No.”

Maret looked toward the ceiling, where a dull tremor passed through the stone. “He’s ordering the list clerks to close the missing rolls. Anyone not confirmed alive by dawn is to be entered as dead. It will make the numbers cleaner.”

“Cleaner numbers make uglier graves.”

“Pell doesn’t care about graves.”

“He cares about what can be counted.”

Maret’s mouth pulled tight. “He cares about what can be blamed.”

For a moment neither spoke. The Hall breathed around them: a distant shout, a wheel clattering along a service track, the long metal groan of a gate under pressure.

Then Maret said, “My child is in Sable Ward.”

Ilyra looked at her.

The guard’s expression did not change, but the hand on the door frame had begun to shake.

“Where?”

“Foundry Row. A room above a cooper’s shop. The upper floor is still dry, according to the last message.”

“Name?”

“Rian.” Maret swallowed. “Seven years old. He has a cough that worsens in damp weather. His grandmother is with him. I sent word for them to take the Crown road, but the guards closed it before they reached the stairs.”

Ilyra’s first thought was the map. Foundry Row lay beside the channel the Council was filling. Its route toward Old Foundry School might still carry groups of six. The school could receive twelve. The west lift was unsafe until the lower shaft was read.

Her second thought was that she had begun calculating before she had said the child’s name.

“Rian,” she repeated.

Maret nodded.

“I can’t promise he’ll be reached.”

“I didn’t come for a promise.”

“What did you come for?”

“To tell you where the lift is.” Maret drew the narrow pressure strip from her belt and unfolded it. “The west service stair descends to the lift brake. The lower shaft is taking water, but not steadily. If Jorren confirms the bottom is clear and I release the upper brake at the right pressure, it can rise to the service court. If I release it early, it becomes a piston.”

“A piston against the people below.”

“Yes.”

“And Pell knows?”

“He knows there is a route. He doesn’t know I kept the divided readings.”

Maret touched the strip with one finger. “He ordered me to release it for the execution officials. He wants the upper court clear before dawn. He also ordered the arrest of Baret, Vennik, and Rusk. Pellis is on the list. So are two relay apprentices and every engineer who refuses to certify that the western pressure is accidental.”

The words entered Ilyra like cold water.

“Then he’s preparing the story before the flood ends.”

“He’s preparing the silence.”

From somewhere above came three dull knocks. A signal through the service pipes.

Maret answered with two.

Ilyra stared at the charcoal marks on the floor. Until now, Maret had been a uniform, a key, a body between Ilyra and the controls. An obstacle with a mother’s face only when the past required one. But there was a child in Foundry Row, seven years old, coughing in damp air, waiting for a route that had been closed by an order written somewhere dry.

The child on the roof had been nameless because Ilyra had permitted that. A nameless child could become a variable. Rian could not.

“Take the lift only after Jorren confirms the shaft,” she said. “Not before.”

Maret’s eyes sharpened. “Even if Pell’s men reach the court?”

“Especially then.”

“If Rian is trapped—”

“I know.”

“No, you know the pressure.” Maret’s voice broke against the words and hardened again. “You know the height, the basin, the number of bodies the channel can carry. You don’t know what it is to hear your child coughing while someone tells you the route is unsafe.”

Ilyra accepted the blow. “You’re right.”

That seemed to unsettle Maret more than an argument would have.

“I know what it is to choose a tool,” Ilyra said. “I know what it is to call a person one life and a street many lives until the person disappears inside the arithmetic. I will not tell you that waiting is mercy. I will tell you the lift must have two confirmations before it moves.”

Maret looked down at the names. “And if the confirmations don’t come?”

“Then we say that aloud. We do not turn uncertainty into permission.”

A second lock turned outside.

Maret stepped back. “Pell’s moving the execution crews.”

“Already?”

“He wants the basin reheated before the first public bell. The lenses will be tested at midnight. At dawn he’ll call it a continuation of the lawful rite, even if half the Hall is underwater.”

“Who is with him?”

“Enough guards to make a corridor. Not enough to control the building if the workers refuse.”

“And the witnesses?”

Maret’s gaze went flat. “He ordered the old trial witnesses confined in their homes. Tavia Senn’s ration voucher has been revoked. The survivor from the storage fields was taken from the relief ward. He says they are being protected from agitation.”

Ilyra felt the familiar pressure gather behind her ribs. A command would have been easier. Open this. Break that. Force the gate. Force the truth into the air until no one could deny it.

Instead she picked up the copper wire.

“Tell Senn the names must go out with the orders,” she said. “Not after. The engineers’ refusals, the missing rolls, Rian’s location, all of it.”

“Maret,” a voice called from the corridor. “Report.”

She moved to the door but did not open it.

Ilyra held out the wire. “For the brake signal.”

Maret took it. Their fingers touched. The contact was brief, practical, and more intimate than any forgiveness.

“If Rian is reached,” Ilyra said, “put his name on the live roll.”

“If he isn’t?”

“Put his name on the missing roll.”

Maret looked at her for a long moment. “And yours?”

“I won’t be missing.”

“No,” Maret said. “You’ll be on the platform.”

She opened the door and went out.

The lock closed.

Ilyra remained on the floor until the lamps outside dimmed. Then she took up the charcoal and drew three circles on the stone: pressure, route, receiving space. Beneath them she wrote no names. Names could be burned, counted, concealed. But the circles required voices beyond hers.

Through the wall, the Hall began to heat the water.

She heard the machinery wake in stages. First the boilers. Then the feed pumps. Then the iron valves, turning with a sound like teeth grinding in sleep.

Nera’s voice came back from the sealed corridor.

You don’t get to call it necessary because you were the one who chose it.

Ilyra closed her eyes.

“I know,” she said.

The answer did not come from the wall. It came from memory, from the roof, from the drowned streets, from the child whose name she had never learned.

At midnight, the first lens brightened.

Ilyra placed both hands on the floor and waited for the confirmations to arrive.

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: in the records cell beneath Veyr’s Hall at midnight on the final night before the Ember Descent, after Maret’s visit; waiting for distributed confirmations while the execution machinery reheats. Goal: halt Sable Ward’s engineered flooding, protect named residents and threatened engineers, expose Pell’s suppression through broadcasts and distributed gate commands, and refuse sole authority even under pressure. Relationships: tense practical alliance with Elian, whose challenge restrains her; cooperating with Senn, Maret, Jorren, Mara Quill, Pellan, relay workers, and survivors; opposed by Pell and the Council; now sees Maret as a parent and collaborator rather than merely a guard or obstacle. Knowledge: has formalized the three-confirmation protocol requiring pressure, route, and receiving-capacity confirmations; knows Foundry Row may route toward Old Foundry School, the west lift requires lower-shaft confirmation and upper brake release, and Maret’s child Rian is trapped there; knows Pell is suppressing witnesses, closing missing rolls, and targeting resistant engineers and relay workers. Possessions: soaked, heat-damaged white robe edged in bronze, charcoal, copper wire, damaged locking plate, brass cylinder, central and basin maps, false death-roll material, and burned remnants of Pell’s declaration. Condition: blistered, exhausted, lucid, grieving, and still tempted to seize the master controls; has written and burned a list of names to avoid converting remorse into spectacle, and is waiting for confirmations instead of acting alone.

set.name: Oren Pell
set.description: Location: elsewhere in Veyr’s Hall directing the reheating of the Ember Descent basin and movement of execution crews before dawn. Goal: restore the public rite, force a narrative isolating Ilyra, suppress witnesses and records, close the missing rolls, seize or prosecute resistant engineers and relay workers, and preserve Council authority through coercion. Relationships: adversarial toward Ilyra, Elian, Senn, Maret, Jorren, Pellis, relay workers, survivors, and named witnesses; increasingly challenged by clerks, guards, and maintenance crews. Knowledge: knows Ilyra rejected his bargain, the archive records and worker refusals can expose Council policy, the west lift and flood controls are unstable, and Maret and other workers retain divided readings and route knowledge. Possessions: white judicial robes with repaired bronze chain, execution orders, broadcast authority, suppression and arrest orders, manipulated death-roll instructions, and guards under command. Condition: angry, hurried, publicly destabilized, and increasingly dependent on confinement, prosecution, and manipulated counts as he prepares the spectacle before the flood and resistance can make his orders evidence against him.

set.name: Maret
set.description: Location: moving through the Hall’s service routes toward the west lift and upper brake beneath the execution complex after visiting Ilyra’s records cell. Goal: reach and evacuate her seven-year-old child Rian and his grandmother from Foundry Row, open a usable route to Sable Ward, warn residents, and prevent Pell from converting the crisis into concealment or vengeance. Relationships: conflicted toward Ilyra but cooperating with her; allied cautiously with Senn, Elian, Jorren, Maret’s fellow workers, Pellis, released prisoners, and survivors; openly resistant to Pell. Knowledge: Rian is trapped above a cooper’s shop in Foundry Row, the Crown road is closed, the west lift requires a lower-shaft pressure confirmation and upper-landing brake release, and releasing it early could turn the shaft into a deadly piston; Pell has ordered witness confinement, missing-roll closure, and arrests or prosecution of resisting relay workers and engineers. Possessions: civic uniform with pins removed, hidden keys, divided pressure readings, narrow Crown-line pressure strip, copper wire for the brake signal, and service access knowledge. Condition: frightened, grieving, physically strained, shaken by the threat to Rian, and resolute as she risks disobedience while accepting that the lift cannot move without confirmation.

Maret reveals that her seven-year-old child Rian and his grandmother are trapped above a cooper’s shop in Foundry Row, with the Crown road closed and the west lift available only after lower-shaft confirmation.

Pell orders missing rolls closed at dawn, threatened witnesses and relay workers confined or arrested, and resisting engineers prosecuted while he reheats the Ember Descent and prepares to suppress evidence before the public rite.

Maret’s seven-year-old child Rian and his grandmother remain trapped above a cooper’s shop in Foundry Row; their status must be confirmed through evacuation or the missing roll, and Rian must be placed on the live roll if reached.

Pell’s midnight suppression order targets Tavia Senn, the storage-field survivor, Baret, Vennik, Rusk, Pellis, relay apprentices, and resisting engineers; the coalition must protect or publicly expose these threatened witnesses before the execution spectacle restores the official narrative.

chapters.name: White and Bronze
chapters.content:
By the first bell, Veyr had dressed itself for renewal.

White cloth hung from the bridges. Bronze ribbons crossed the streets above the rising water. The Feast banners had been washed in perfumed steam and stretched between towers whose foundations were already sweating. In the Crown District, servants carried trays of sugared river-pears through houses with sealed windows. In Sable Ward, people climbed tables, shelves, and the roofs of foundries while guards turned them back from the upper stairs.

The city made two arrangements for the same water.

Ilyra saw neither arrangement directly. She heard it through the Hall.

The records cell opened before sunrise. Two attendants came for her, both wearing the white sleeves of the civic cleansing service. One was old enough to remember the first Feast after the flood; the other watched Ilyra with the fixed fascination of someone who had purchased a lens-seat and wanted to know whether the condemned looked different at close range.

“Stand,” the younger attendant said.

Ilyra stood.

Her knees trembled. She refused to let them see it.

The older attendant carried a basin of heated water. Steam rolled over the rim, smelling of bitter herbs and metal. The younger held a chain coiled in both hands. Its links were whitewashed, but beneath the paint the bronze showed through like old bruises.

“Arms,” he said.

“Your seal is wrong.”

He looked down. A small civic mark had been stamped into the clasp: a crown over a descending wave. The lower point of the wave leaned left.

“It is the execution seal,” he said.

“It is a service seal.”

His expression tightened. “You know the difference?”

“I designed the plate.”

The older attendant glanced toward the door. In the corridor, someone called for more coal. Water struck a lower gate with a deep, repeating boom.

The younger man’s thumb brushed the clasp. “Will you cooperate?”

“No.”

He raised the chain.

Ilyra smiled without warmth. “That was cooperation.”

The older attendant almost smiled back. Almost. Then she poured the hot water over Ilyra’s shoulders.

It was not hot enough to burn. That was the first cruelty. The water had been measured to redden the skin, open old blisters, and leave her capable of standing when the lenses came alive. The second cruelty was the scent. Rosemary, salt, and the faint copper odor of the basin carried her backward.

A roof under brown water.

A child beside a chimney.

The brass key in her hand.

Please.

Ilyra shut her eyes.

The attendant scrubbed her hair with a rough cloth. Water ran down her back and between her shoulder blades. The old woman worked with professional care, cleaning the soot from Ilyra’s neck, removing dried blood from beneath her fingernails, washing away every visible trace of the cell.

“Does the Feast always require so much polishing?” Ilyra asked.

“It requires the condemned to be recognizable,” the woman said.

“Recognizable as what?”

The cloth paused.

“Whatever they have printed.”

The younger attendant laughed once. “They printed your face on the sweetcakes.”

“I know.”

“Have you seen one?”

“I have eaten one.”

He stared.

“On the forty-first day,” Ilyra said. “A guard dropped it. It tasted of flour and ash.”

The old woman resumed scrubbing. “Hold still.”

The water rose another inch somewhere beyond the cell. The Hall answered with a groan.

For a moment Ilyra was not in the cleansing room. She was in the North Barrage chamber, watching the pressure needle fall exactly as she had promised. Nera’s sleeve had been blue with gasket dust. Hobb had laughed when the central sluice opened. Above them, the Feast lamps trembled in the dark river.

We have it, Ilyra had thought.

Not saved. Not yet. But mastered.

That word had been the hidden pleasure. Not correction. Not rescue. Mastery.

The younger attendant pulled her arms behind her and fastened the chain.

The clasp clicked.

Ilyra felt the thin metal pin beneath her tongue.

She had taken it from the hem of the old records ledger after the last night’s lamps went out. It was no longer than a fingernail, sharpened at one end, and its taste had become part of her mouth. She had hidden it there because Pell searched hands, sleeves, hair, and shoes. He had not searched the place where speech began.

The pin was not enough to free her. It could lift a spring in the service collar, if she found the right angle. It could score a wire, open a narrow panel, or break the seal on a maintenance cover. It could also cut her tongue and fill her mouth with blood before the first public bell.

A tool was never a promise.

The chain ran from her wrists to a bronze belt at her waist. Two attendants checked the links. The younger tugged hard.

“Comfortable?” he asked.

“No.”

“Good.”

The old woman brought the robe.

White, with bronze edging. It had been cut to make her body seem taller and more severe. The sleeves ended above the wrists so the marks of the chain would remain visible. A narrow strip of crimson had been sewn inside the collar, where the cameras could not see it but the execution clerk could identify the garment as final issue.

Ilyra lifted her arms as they dressed her.

In the mirror above the wash basin, she saw a pale stranger. The face was thinner than the one on the sweetcakes. Her hair had been combed back. Her eyes looked black with exhaustion.

The robe made her look clean enough to condemn.

The younger attendant fastened the collar. He wore a coded seal at his throat, a small bronze disk engraved with three nested lines. Ilyra had seen the same pattern on the service orders Pell used to move crews through locked passages.

“Turn your head,” she said.

“Why?”

“Your seal is upside down.”

His hand rose automatically.

Ilyra moved before he could understand. She twisted against the chain, caught the disk between two fingers, and pressed her thumb into the soft wax beneath its rim. The seal lifted with a faint wet sound. She turned it half a degree and pressed it back.

“There,” she said. “Now it reads as a descent order.”

The younger attendant looked down.

The older woman had gone still.

“What did you do?” he whispered.

“Corrected your insignia.”

He touched the disk. The wax had taken the imprint of her thumbnail across the lower line. To a door reader, it would register as an authorized descent crew rather than a prisoner escort. One compromised seal. One narrow opening in Pell’s wall.

Not enough.

But no gate opened from one force alone.

A bell rang in the upper galleries.

The old woman stepped away from Ilyra. “They’re filling the seats.”

“Already?”

“They began before dawn.”

The doors opened. Sound poured in.

Crowds in the Hall’s galleries shouted, laughed, argued over wagers. The noise rose and fell in waves, not unlike a river negotiating an obstruction. Someone called, “Barrage Butcher!” Someone else answered with a chant from the old flood trials. Children were lifted onto shoulders. Vendors moved along the aisles selling bronze masks shaped like sluice gates.

The younger attendant seized Ilyra’s chain.

She stepped into the corridor.

The Hall had been transformed. White banners fell from the ceiling, each stamped with the Council’s crest. Bronze braziers burned along the walls. Steam climbed through grates in the floor, making the air damp and bright. On either side, mirrored lenses turned in their housings, finding her.

Each lens held a room.

A room in the docks, where workers stood beside a flooded loading platform.

A room in Merchant Row, where women in festival white leaned toward a viewing glass.

A room in Sable Ward, where no one had arranged seats because the water had entered through the doors.

The lenses multiplied her until she seemed to walk beside herself: Ilyra in the corridor, Ilyra in the galleries, Ilyra reflected in the eyes of people who had never seen the barrage.

An announcer’s voice rolled through the Hall.

“Citizens of Veyr, witness the completion of civic justice. Witness the woman who seized the river and return her to the water she weaponized.”

The crowd answered with applause.

Ilyra kept walking.

At the end of the corridor, a side door stood beneath a bronze placard: DESCENT CREW—AUTHORIZED. The younger attendant moved toward it without hesitation. Ilyra looked at the seal at his throat. Her thumbnail mark caught the light.

The door opened.

Beyond it, two maintenance workers were arguing over a pressure board. They saw the altered seal, saw the white robe, and stepped aside. One looked at Ilyra’s face, then at the chain.

“Is the basin ready?” the younger attendant asked.

“Ready enough,” one worker said. “The west feed is surging.”

“Surging?”

The worker glanced toward the floor. “Water’s backing through the old service channels. Pell ordered the lower grates closed.”

“Why?” Ilyra asked.

The worker’s eyes flicked toward her. “To keep the galleries dry.”

There it was. The entire city reduced to an instruction.

Keep the galleries dry.

Not keep the ward alive. Not open the receiving basins. Not confirm the routes. Keep the galleries dry.

The worker turned back to the board. “They say the flood is from the old channels. They say it has nothing to do with the Council.”

“Who says?”

He gave her a frightened look. “Everyone who wants to keep working.”

The guard pulled her onward.

A service stair descended toward the execution platform. Along its walls, the mirrored lenses had been set at regular intervals. Their bronze backs clicked and rotated. A child in one gallery pressed both hands to the glass. Her mother pulled her away, but not before the child saw Ilyra and waved.

Ilyra did not wave back.

At the bottom, the platform waited over the basin.

Heated water churned below it, white with steam. Bronze rails enclosed the descent square. Beyond the rails, galleries climbed in tiers, already packed. Pell stood on the far dais in white judicial robes, his bronze chain repaired and polished. Around him gathered the officials: Councilors in feathered collars, district governors with ceremonial knives, reservoir commissioners wearing silver gloves.

They had come dressed for a beginning.

Ilyra recognized Governor Pellan’s aide, Director Sorell’s replacement, and three men whose signatures had appeared on the evacuation orders. None looked toward the lenses. They looked toward one another, checking that they had arrived before the story began.

Pell raised one hand.

The crowd quieted by degrees.

“Magistrate,” Ilyra said.

His gaze settled on her. “Ilyra Voss.”

The lenses brightened. Her face appeared in every district.

Behind Pell, a clerk held the sentence. Another held a ceremonial cord. A third kept glancing at the doors, where the rising water had begun to show beneath the threshold.

Pell smiled for the city.

“Today,” he said, “Veyr witnesses the final purification of a civic traitor.”

The crowd roared.

Ilyra looked past him to the sealed control grates beneath the dais. She could feel the machinery through the soles of her shoes: the pulse of the heated basin, the pressure in the old channels, the constrained force searching for a path. Somewhere beyond the walls, Foundry Row was filling. Somewhere, Maret was waiting for the lift confirmation. Somewhere, Elian carried the records toward the towers, and Senn carried names that Pell wanted erased.

The city had been invited to watch her die.

That was the point of the platform. Not merely punishment. Substitution. Let them watch one woman descend. Let them cheer at the visible body while the invisible hands turned the gates.

Pell gestured to the clerk.

The clerk began to read the sentence.

Ilyra felt the pin beneath her tongue and tasted iron.

She could spit it into the basin. She could use it on the collar. She could wait.

Pressure. Route. Receiving space.

Three circles, none of them hers alone.

The first drop of heated water struck the bronze below.

The mirrored lenses carried the sound outward, district by district, until all Veyr heard the water begin.

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: chained on the Ember Descent platform beneath Veyr’s Hall at the first public bell of the Feast, with heated water beginning below her and mirrored lenses transmitting her to every district. Goal: halt Sable Ward’s engineered flooding, protect named residents and threatened engineers, expose Pell’s suppression through the broadcast and distributed gate commands, and refuse sole authority even while using the execution machinery as access. On the morning of the Feast, civic attendants wash Ilyra, chain her to a bronze execution belt, and dress her in the white robe with bronze edging prepared for the Ember Descent.
Ilyra conceals a sharpened metal pin beneath her tongue and compromises a guard’s coded descent-crew seal, creating a narrow unauthorized opening in Pell’s execution security.

The Ember Descent galleries fill while rising water backs through the Hall’s service channels; mirrored lenses transmit Ilyra’s procession and the first sound of heated water to districts across Veyr.

At the execution platform, Ilyra recognizes that the public rite is designed to substitute her visible punishment for scrutiny of the officials controlling the gates, while Pell and Council officials gather to perform civic closure.

The compromised descent-crew seal and concealed metal pin must provide Ilyra a narrowly timed means of accessing or disrupting the execution machinery without restoring her sole control over the flood gates.

The Ember Descent platform and mirrored broadcast must be used by the coalition to redirect public attention from Ilyra’s punishment toward the Council’s gate orders, reservoir routing, and threatened witnesses before Pell can restore the official narrative.

chapters.name: The Names She Carries
chapters.content:
The clerk read the sentence as though it were a blessing.

“Ilyra Voss, formerly appointed engineer of the civic water service, you are found guilty of unlawful seizure of barrage authority, civic mass murder, destruction of public infrastructure, and sedition against the lawful districts of Veyr. By order of the Council and under the Ember Statutes, you are sentenced to descent through the heated basin until life leaves you.”

The final words vanished beneath the applause.

Ilyra stood inside the bronze rails with her wrists chained before her. Steam gathered on her lashes. The platform trembled under the pressure of water moving through the old channels below. Every mirrored lens in the Hall had turned toward her, and beyond those lenses the city waited for a body to confirm what it had already decided.

Pell let the applause crest.

He had learned the timing of spectacle. He knew when the crowd wanted cruelty, when it wanted solemnity, and when it wanted the brief silence in which a condemned person might appear to understand the honor of being destroyed.

When the noise thinned, he stepped closer to the platform.

“By civic custom,” he said, “the condemned may make a final statement.”

A murmur passed through the galleries. Some people called for confession. Others called for the water. A man near the front shouted, “Tell us you enjoyed it!”

Another voice answered, “Make her beg!”

Pell lifted his hand again. The city quieted because it had been trained to quiet for him.

“You may speak,” he told Ilyra. “But understand that this is not another hearing. The judgment is complete. Nothing you say can alter the sentence.”

“Then why ask?”

A slight pause. It was almost invisible, but the nearest lens caught it and enlarged it across a hundred viewing panes.

“Because Veyr deserves to hear the truth from your mouth.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “Veyr deserves to hear what you fear from it.”

The crowd stirred.

Pell’s expression did not change. “This is precisely the sort of theatrical evasion that brought you here.”

Ilyra looked at the lenses. At their polished bronze rims. At the people crowded behind them: dockhands with wet cuffs, merchants in dry festival clothes, families pressed into halls where the water had not yet reached, and residents of Sable Ward standing in darkness because their district’s viewing relay had failed or been cut.

She imagined their faces receiving her voice through wires and towers. She imagined Pell receiving it too, deciding which sentence to preserve and which to call delirium.

For once, she did not begin by arranging the order of facts.

“I opened North Barrage Four,” she said.

The words were small. The Hall carried them anyway.

A hiss ran through the galleries, followed by delighted whispers. The crowd had been promised a denial or a confession. It had received the first stone of either structure.

“I opened it knowingly,” Ilyra continued. “I stole the seal. I forged the order. I entered the control chamber during the Feast because the Council had chosen to protect the Crown and Merchant districts while directing the pressure toward the lower basin. I knew the barrage was unstable. I knew the old maps were incomplete. I knew the storage fields might contain people who were not recorded in the civic plans.”

Pell’s clerk lowered his eyes to his page.

Ilyra saw the movement. The sentence had not included the storage fields. It had included sabotage, sedition, unlawful entry. It had not included the knowledge that made the act monstrous and the city culpable at once.

“I opened the gate,” she said, “and I understood that people would die.”

This time the silence held.

The heated water struck the basin below with a hollow rush. Steam folded around her knees.

A woman in the third gallery began to weep. Someone near her hissed for quiet. Somewhere farther back, a child asked why the people were cheering yesterday if she had known.

Pell leaned toward the speaking horn. “The condemned admits the central fact. Let the record show—”

“Let the record show the whole sentence,” Ilyra said.

He looked at her.

“The Council knew the lower basin was the planned pressure sink,” she said. “The Council removed the western valves to preserve a private reservoir line. The Council reinforced the districts that could pay for protection and called everyone else an acceptable discharge. I brought that evidence to the engineers who outranked me. They dismissed it. I sent warnings through the announcement network. My access was cut. Governor Dault removed me from duty and signed orders that kept the Crown line sealed.”

Pell made a gesture toward the clerk. “These are allegations already rejected by the court.”

“They were excluded by the court.”

The lenses clicked. One of them shuddered, then steadied.

Pell’s voice sharpened. “You are attempting to distribute your guilt among men who were not present when you committed the crime.”

“I am not distributing it.”

The answer surprised him. It surprised the crowd more.

“I am carrying it,” Ilyra said. “Mine is not lighter because theirs exists.”

A sound moved through the Hall—not applause, not outrage. Recognition, perhaps, though recognition did not mean agreement. It was the sound of people hearing a door unlatch in a room they had believed sealed.

Ilyra lowered her eyes to the water.

“Nera Vale,” she said.

The name entered the broadcast and traveled beyond the Hall.

“She was an apprentice engineer. She trusted my judgment. I did not tell her everything I knew about the uncertainty in the old channels. I told myself that delay would endanger the city. I told myself that she would understand once the pressure fell. When the western gate failed, she and the lower crew were behind the emergency door.”

Her mouth had gone dry around the metal pin. Its edge pressed against her tongue.

“I could have opened that door,” she said. “Opening it would have flooded the control chamber and destroyed the feeder machinery. It might have sent a surge into the lower districts. I chose the machinery. I sealed the door. I told them to wait.”

No one shouted now.

“Hobb Renn was there,” she continued. “A pump mechanic who knew the lower works better than I did. The child called Lio was there, rescued from the west platform. I heard them. I knew the water was rising. I kept my hands on the controls.”

In the gallery, a man covered his face.

“I do not know whether Nera survived. I do not know whether Lio did. Hobb’s name was read among the dead, but a name in a civic list is not the same as a body recovered. The city called that uncertainty an accounting problem. It was a room. It was a voice behind a door. It was a choice I made.”

For a moment she saw Nera as she had been beneath the barrage: blue gasket dust on her sleeve, one hand lifted toward the maintenance tube, eyes bright with disbelief.

You said the pressure would fall.

Ilyra had wanted to answer that it had fallen. The needle had moved. The calculation had held for three minutes and seventeen seconds. She had wanted those facts to become a shield.

They had never been a shield. They had been the shape of the door she closed.

“And the child on the roof?” Pell asked.

His tone was mild. He had found the wound and placed a finger inside it.

The crowd shifted. Some had heard the testimony. Some had bought the sweetcakes printed with the image of a brass key. Some knew only that the Barrage Butcher had watched a child drown and chosen to carry on.

Ilyra tasted iron.

“Yes,” she said.

Pell turned to the lenses. “The condemned confirms—”

“Do not use my confirmation as your conclusion.”

His jaw tightened.

“I heard the child,” Ilyra said. “The roof was already surrounded. I had the valve key. If I went to the child, I could not reach the pump station in time to stabilize the drainage line. I chose the key. I carried it away. I told myself that saving the larger district required one unbearable refusal.”

The memory came not as an image but as a pressure in her hands: wet brass, the key biting her palm, the child’s voice cracking against the rain.

She had not known the child’s name.

That ignorance had made it easier to write the event as a necessary loss. A person without a name could be placed in a column. A column could be balanced.

“I did not know the child,” she said. “That was part of my failure. I knew the calculation and not the life. I knew the number of gates and not the names of the people beneath them.”

A woman near the front cried out, “Her name was Sella!”

Another voice said, “No, it was Mina!”

The names struck each other and fell into the steam.

Ilyra bowed her head.

“If you know the child’s name, say it,” she said. “Do not say mine instead.”

Pell stepped onto the first bronze stair. “This performance of remorse cannot erase the fact that you selected the Feast because the governors were present. You wanted them afraid.”

“Yes.”

The answer stopped him.

Ilyra raised her face. “Partly. I wanted the Council to feel the danger it had assigned to others. I wanted them trapped above the river. I wanted them to understand. That desire was vengeance. I will not polish it into strategy.”

The crowd had expected repentance to bend her low or defiance to make her proud. Instead she stood between them, refusing the posture each required.

“I am responsible for opening the barrage,” she said. “I am responsible for withholding the full danger from Nera. I am responsible for the workers behind the door. I am responsible for the child on the roof. I am responsible for believing that correct calculations gave me the right to choose who would be lost.”

Pell waited, perhaps for the sentence that would make him safe.

Ilyra gave it to him only in part.

“But I did not act in a vacuum. I acted inside a city built to make some lives into reservoirs for others. I acted after warnings were erased, after scarcity was engineered, after officials decided which districts could be sacrificed and called the decision law. The Council’s guilt does not absolve me. My guilt does not absolve the Council.”

The first gallery began to applaud.

Pell snapped, “Silence them.”

No guard moved.

Senn stood at the edge of the platform, baton lowered. Maret was visible beyond him among the service crew, one hand closed around the rail. Elian did not appear in the Hall, but Ilyra imagined her somewhere beneath the city carrying the records toward the towers. The names had gone out. Nera. Hobb. Lio. The child without a settled name. The trapped workers. The people the plans had called empty space.

Pell turned toward the guards. “I gave an order.”

Senn looked at him. “They heard her.”

The sentence was not defiance yet. It was a fact.

Ilyra felt the pin shift beneath her tongue. A drop of blood slid down her throat. She could use it now, perhaps. She could cut the collar, strike the nearest lock, seize the mechanism beneath the platform. The old desire rose with familiar clarity: one hand on the control, one will above the water, every consequence made legible by her decision.

Then she heard the workers behind the emergency door.

Not their words. The silence after them.

She had believed that carrying responsibility meant taking control of everything. It had taken years, and a city drowned twice, to learn that responsibility might instead mean refusing the power to make the next sacrifice alone.

Pell faced the lenses again. “The statement is concluded.”

“No,” Ilyra said.

She turned toward the nearest mirrored lens. Its glass held her face, enlarged and trembling in the steam.

“I carry the dead,” she said. “Not as proof that I was right. Not as weights to force the living into obedience. I carry them because I chose, and because others chose, and because no sentence spoken by one mouth can make those choices disappear.”

The water below her surged.

Across Veyr, the lenses received her voice. In Sable Ward, where the relay still held, people heard the names. In the Crown District, servants stopped beside dry windows. In the Hall, the crowd looked first at Ilyra, then at Pell, and finally at the grates beneath the dais.

For the first time, the city was not watching only the condemned.

It was listening for the machinery.
