chapters.name: The Towers Speak
chapters.content:
The machinery answered before the crowd did.

Beneath the execution dais, a relay wheel turned with a slow metallic cough. The sound passed through the bronze rails and into Ilyra’s feet. Somewhere below, a maintenance lock released. Then another. The Hall’s mirrored lenses flickered, not with the pale reflection of her face but with black squares, white lines, and the blue thread of an archival packet being opened.

Pell spun toward the nearest lens.

“What is that?”

No one answered him.

The image steadied. A civic seal appeared first, followed by a date, a reservoir designation, and a signature written in a hand Ilyra recognized from the old orders.

GOVERNOR ARVEN DAULT.

Below it, in a clerk’s narrow script, were the words: LOWER-BASIN DISCHARGE ACCEPTABLE IF CROWN LINE REMAINS SECURE.

The crowd made a noise like wind entering a cracked window.

At the bottom of the image, a second line appeared.

REINFORCEMENT PRIORITY: CROWN, MERCHANT, CEREMONIAL PLATFORM.

SABLE WARD: NO ADDITIONAL CREWS AUTHORIZED.

Pell climbed the bronze stair. “Cut the lenses.”

The clerk beside him reached for the control box. Its cover had been sealed with red wax. He broke the wax, pushed the lever, and received a spark that threw him backward. The lens remained lit.

A woman’s voice began reading the order.

It came from the Hall’s civic announcer, the same measured voice that had once declared ration changes, curfew hours, and Ilyra’s conviction. It spoke without anger or pity. That was what made it terrible.

“By instruction of Governor Arven Dault, dated the third day before the Feast of Renewal: ‘In the event of eastern pressure exceeding reserve tolerance, discharge may be directed through the lower basin, provided the Crown line and Merchant reservoirs remain protected.’”

The voice paused.

“‘Residents of the lower basin are not to be notified before discharge. Premature evacuation may obstruct the ceremonial route and create unacceptable congestion.’”

No one in the galleries cheered.

Ilyra looked at the lens and saw, behind the written order, a wavering image of Elian in a tower chamber. Her hair was wet at the temples. Blue-threaded packets lay open across a brass console. A relay worker stood on either side of her, one with a hand pressed to a bank of fuses and the other watching a stairwell where footsteps approached.

Elian lifted one packet toward the lens.

“This is the Council reservoir map,” she said. “The red channels are private lines. They lead from the Crown gardens, the Governor’s reservoirs, and the Merchant cisterns into the western network. The black channels are the public gates. Notice which ones were kept closed.”

The map widened across every lens.

The city saw itself from above.

Veyr’s districts appeared as colored blocks around the river. The Crown sat high and pale. Merchant terraces lay behind thick retaining walls. Sable Ward spread below them, a dark fan of foundries, workers’ courts, old tram sheds, and narrow streets. Arrows converged upon it from the protected districts, each marked with a pressure value and a time.

At the edge of the image, someone had written: ACCEPTABLE LOSS.

A man in the upper gallery whispered, “That is my street.”

“It is mine,” another answered.

The announcer began reading names from the packet. Engineers. Clerks. Relay apprentices. Workers who had refused to sever the towers. Residents denied evacuation permits.

“Baret of the heating works. Vennik of the dock relay. Rusk of the western maintenance crew. Pellis, archive clerk, designation suspended. Mara Quill, former tram worker. Anja Meret, resident of Foundry Row, with children Leth, Ovan, and Suri.”

The names crossed the Hall and went outward along the wires.

In Sable Ward, a woman standing on the roof of a flooded cooperage heard Anja’s name and dropped the bucket she was holding. In a Crown kitchen, a servant stopped beside the speaking horn. At the western tower, an engineer who had spent the night expecting arrest leaned toward the sound and heard his own name read into the city.

Pell reached the control box again.

“Shut down the western tower,” he ordered. “Then the north and dock relays. Use the emergency severance code.”

A guard ran to the service stair.

From somewhere beneath the Hall came a bell: one strike, two, three. Not the alarm for fire. The old civic signal for a relay interruption.

The image of Elian shivered. Her mouth moved, but for a moment only static came through. Then a different voice spoke.

“This is Tower Three,” said an older man. “The severance order has been received.”

Pell turned toward the lens.

“Execute it.”

“We will not.”

The words were quiet. They traveled farther than Pell’s command.

In the tower chamber, the older man placed both hands on the console. His uniform had no district pins. Behind him, two apprentices held open the maintenance panel.

“The order is signed by Magistrate Pell,” he said. “It carries no district confirmation and no witness from the relay office. Under the emergency provisions, we are required to preserve an active public line while evacuation is in progress.”

“You are required to obey the Council,” Pell said.

“We are obeying the written route law.”

“That law has been suspended.”

“Then read the suspension to the city.”

A ripple moved through the galleries.

Pell’s face tightened. “You presume your position gives you authority.”

“No,” said the engineer. “We presume your position does not erase ours.”

The lens cut briefly to another tower. Workers in dock coats forced open a bronze maintenance hatch. A woman with a bandaged wrist threaded copper wire around a bypass pin while a boy held a lamp over her shoulder. Their hands shook. They worked anyway.

Ilyra felt the old hunger rise—not for the lever now, but for the sequence. Tower Three holding. Dock relay open. Western line carrying the maps. If the common-release basin received the pressure, if the lower shaft was confirmed, if the receiving districts—

She stopped herself.

The map was not a command. It was an invitation to people who could see what she could not.

“Where is Elian?” Maret asked from beyond the platform.

“Tower One,” Ilyra said.

Maret stared at her. “You can see that?”

“The lenses are carrying her image.”

A second image appeared. Elian stood in a narrower chamber, its walls sweating with condensation. She had one hand on the main relay and the other around a folded notice.

“Tower One is active,” she said. “Tower Three is active. The dock line is active. The Crown relay is attempting to overwrite us.”

As she spoke, a white sheet appeared over the map.

PUBLIC INFORMATION WITHHELD DURING SECURITY OPERATION.

A seal flared beneath it. The message tried to cover the reservoir routes.

Then a new line cut across the sheet.

WORKERS REFUSE CENSORSHIP.

The words were followed by the names Baret, Vennik, and Rusk.

The crowd turned toward the Council officials. Some of the governors had begun backing away from the dais. Their ceremonial sashes were bright against faces gone gray. One man whispered to another and received a sharp shake of the head. There was nowhere to retreat without passing the galleries.

Pell saw it too.

“Seize the relay workers,” he said.

A captain beside him hesitated. “Which workers?”

“All of them.”

“They’re in the towers.”

“Send the city guard.”

“The guard cannot reach Tower Three. The west stair is flooded.”

“Then use their families.”

The words came too quickly. Pell seemed not to hear himself until the nearest lens caught them.

“Bring their families into the Hall,” he said. “Baret’s wife. Vennik’s sons. Rusk’s mother. Pellis’s brother, if he has not already fled. Put them before the lenses. Tell the workers that every minute of refusal will be marked against the people they leave behind.”

Silence fell harder than before.

The civic announcer repeated the order.

“By direction of Magistrate Oren Pell: families of resisting relay workers are to be detained and displayed as material witnesses to civic disobedience.”

A guard near the platform lowered his spear.

Pell rounded on him. “You heard me.”

“I heard the announcer,” the guard said.

“Then obey.”

“My sister is in Sable Ward.”

It was Senn. He had not moved from the platform’s edge. His baton hung at his side, wet bronze catching the light.

Pell stared at him. “Your sister testified against this woman.”

“She testified to what she saw.”

“And you will protect the people who caused her death?”

Senn looked at Ilyra. His expression held no forgiveness.

“I will protect the people you are threatening now.”

Maret stepped down from the service platform. “My child is in Foundry Row.”

Pell’s gaze shifted to her. “Then you understand what is at stake.”

“I understand exactly,” she said. “That is why I am not moving for you.”

Another bell sounded through the Hall. This time it came from the western network.

Elian’s image returned. Behind her, the tower windows showed a city of rain and rising water.

“Foundry Row route is still blocked at the Crown road,” she said. “The west lift has not been opened. Lower-shaft confirmation pending.”

Maret gripped the rail. “Rian.”

“I know,” Elian said. “We are carrying his name on the live roll.”

The statement did not promise survival. Maret closed her eyes, then opened them.

“Tell the lower crew to confirm the shaft before the brake release,” she said. “No shortcuts.”

“I will.”

Pell shouted toward the lenses. “This broadcast is an unlawful seizure of civic communication. Any person assisting it will be charged with sedition. Any engineer who refuses a Council order will lose their charter, their housing, and their family’s ration status.”

The announcer carried his threat into every district.

For a heartbeat, the towers seemed to falter.

Then Tower Three answered.

“Record that as a threat,” said the older engineer.

The dock relay answered next. “Record it.”

A younger voice from Tower One said, “Recorded.”

The threat became part of the archive.

Ilyra watched Pell understand what had happened. His power depended on commands disappearing into obedience before anyone could examine them. But the towers were no longer carrying only orders. They were carrying refusals, names, signatures, and the sound of officials threatening children for the sake of a sealed gate.

The city was hearing the machinery speak in its own voice.

Elian lifted the final packet.

“This is Governor Dault’s evacuation instruction,” she said. “Private carts were assigned to Crown and Merchant households six hours before the first public warning. Sable Ward permits were suspended at the same hour. The Council knew. It planned the silence.”

The document filled the lenses.

At the bottom was Dault’s signature.

Ilyra’s breath caught—not from surprise, but from the sudden absence of distance. The old Governor had been a figure in testimony, a name on orders, a man who had escaped through a hidden route. Now his hand lay before the city, each stroke visible.

Pell approached the platform rail.

“You think this changes what she did?” he asked the crowd. “You think papers make the drowned rise? She opened the barrage. She chose the Feast. She wanted vengeance, and now her accomplices want to bury that truth beneath accusations.”

“No,” Ilyra said.

Pell looked at her.

“The papers do not make the drowned rise,” she said. “They stop you from drowning them a second time.”

The nearest lens tilted toward her. Beyond it, the map still showed pressure gathering in the western channels.

Ilyra placed both hands on the bronze rail. The metal was hot enough to hurt.

“To the engineers,” she said, “do not open a gate because I tell you to. Do not close one because Pell threatens you. Confirm the pressure. Confirm the route. Confirm who can receive the water. Put your names beside the decision.”

She heard her own words carried away through the Hall, up the towers, across the districts.

“To the workers,” she continued, “open only the maintenance locks you can witness. If a route is unsafe, say so. If a family is trapped, name them. Do not let anyone turn your silence into consent.”

Pell’s hand closed around the rail opposite hers.

“You are still trying to command them.”

“I am telling them not to make me their master.”

For the first time, he had no immediate answer.

Below the platform, heated water surged against the basin gates. Far away, another channel opened with a deep subterranean groan. On the lenses, the red arrows of the private reservoirs began to move.

Not yet toward the Crown.

Toward the receiving channels that workers, engineers, and district voices were still verifying.

In Tower Three, the old engineer raised a hand. In the dock relay, the woman with the bandaged wrist turned a key. At the Hall’s service stair, Maret took the copper wire and disappeared into the wet darkness with two witnesses behind her.

Pell remained before the city, surrounded by his orders and unable to make them vanish.

The crowd had come to watch a woman descend into boiling water.

Now it watched the towers, and the towers showed them who had built the basin.

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: chained within the bronze rails of the Ember Descent platform beneath Veyr’s Hall, with heated water surging below and mirrored lenses transmitting the tower broadcast and her words across the city. Goal: halt Sable Ward’s engineered flooding, protect named residents and threatened engineers, expose Pell’s suppression through the broadcast and distributed gate commands, and refuse sole authority even while using the execution machinery as access. Relationships: tense practical alliance with Elian, Senn, Maret, Jorren, Mara Quill, Pellan, relay workers, and survivors; opposed by Pell and the Council; publicly claims responsibility without accepting the Council’s solitary narrative. Knowledge: knows Elian has activated the towers, Dault’s orders and reservoir maps are broadcasting, workers in several towers have refused severance, Pell is threatening families and ration status, Foundry Row remains blocked, and the west lift requires lower-shaft confirmation before brake release. Possessions: soaked, heat-damaged white robe edged in bronze, bronze execution chain and belt, concealed sharpened metal pin beneath her tongue, compromised descent-crew seal, charcoal, copper wire, damaged locking plate, brass cylinder, central and basin maps, false death-roll material, and burned remnants of Pell’s declaration. Condition: blistered, exhausted, lucid, grieving, publicly exposed, and tempted to seize machinery, but reaffirming the pressure-route-receiving-space confirmations and refusing to become anyone’s master.

set.name: Oren Pell
set.description: Location: on the judicial dais beside the Ember Descent platform, directing the failing execution spectacle while the surveillance towers broadcast Council records and heated water surges in the basin. Goal: restore the public rite, force a narrative isolating Ilyra, suppress witnesses and records, close the missing rolls, seize or prosecute resistant engineers and relay workers, and preserve Council authority through coercion. Relationships: adversarial toward Ilyra, Elian, Senn, Maret, Jorren, Pellis, relay workers, survivors, and named witnesses; increasingly challenged by guards, engineers, and the audience after the broadcast. Knowledge: knows the archive broadcast has exposed Dault’s signed orders, private reservoir routes, and planned Sable Ward sacrifice; knows Tower Three, Tower One, and the dock relay have refused severance; has ordered resistant workers’ families detained and threatened engineers with loss of housing and ration status. Possessions: white judicial robes with repaired bronze chain, execution orders, broadcast authority, suppression and arrest orders, manipulated death-roll instructions, and guards under command. Condition: angry, hurried, publicly confident but shaken, increasingly dependent on threats as commands fail to disappear into obedience.

set.name: Maret
set.description: Location: descending from the Ember Descent service platform into the wet Hall service routes with copper wire and two witnesses, after refusing Pell’s suppression order. Goal: reach and evacuate her seven-year-old child Rian and grandmother from Foundry Row, open a usable route to Sable Ward, warn residents, and prevent Pell from converting the crisis into concealment or vengeance. Relationships: conflicted toward Ilyra but cooperating with her; allied cautiously with Senn, Elian, Jorren, Pellis, released prisoners, relay workers, and survivors; openly resistant to Pell. Knowledge: Rian is trapped above a cooper’s shop in Foundry Row, the Crown road is closed, the west lift requires a lower-shaft pressure confirmation and upper-landing brake release, and releasing it early could turn the shaft into a deadly piston; Pell has ordered families of resistant workers detained and has broadcast threats; she has insisted that the lower crew confirm the shaft before the brake is released. Possessions: civic uniform with pins removed, hidden keys, divided pressure readings, narrow Crown-line pressure strip, copper wire for the brake signal, and service access knowledge. Condition: frightened, grieving, physically strained, and resolute as she risks disobedience while accepting that the lift cannot move without confirmation.

set.name: Senn
set.description: Location: at the edge of the Ember Descent platform, baton lowered while the tower broadcast exposes Pell’s orders and rising water threatens the Hall. Goal: evacuate Sable Ward, broadcast named residents and threatened engineers, expose Pell’s concealment, and prevent the counter-release from killing uninvolved people while keeping Ilyra accountable. Relationships: hostile toward Ilyra but cooperating with her; allied with Jorren, Maret, Elian, Mara Quill, Pellan, Baret, Vennik, Rusk, and survivors; openly resistant to Pell and has now refused to enforce threats against relay workers’ families. Knowledge: knows the western tower line is carrying worker refusals and names, Pell has ordered families detained and threatened ration status, Anja’s children remain on the live roll, and the west lift cannot be used until its lower shaft is confirmed safe. Possessions: civic uniform, baton, keys, false death roll, divided pressure readings, written names of Anja’s children, and relay access. Condition: soaked, bloodied at the cheek, angry, vigilant, morally unsettled, and committed to accountability without allowing Pell’s vengeance or emergency authority to dictate rescue.

set.name: Elian Dault
set.description: Location: inside Tower One’s relay chamber, operating the surveillance network with archival packets while rain and floodwater rise outside Veyr. Goal: broadcast Council orders, reservoir maps, evacuation evidence, and the names of threatened engineers and Sable Ward residents while preventing Ilyra from turning rescue into a solitary attack. Relationships: tense but effective ally of Ilyra; allied with Senn, Maret, Jorren, Pellis, workers, and survivors; adversarial toward Pell and Governor Dault. Knowledge: knows Dault’s signed lower-basin discharge order, private reservoir routes, and advance Crown and Merchant evacuations are now public; knows Tower Three and the dock relay have refused severance, the Crown relay is trying to overwrite the broadcast, and Foundry Row remains blocked pending lower-shaft confirmation. Possessions: leather case, blue-threaded archival packets, Council minutes, reservoir orders, Dault’s signature, false death rolls, basin map, pressure readings, and Crown route. Condition: exhausted, wet, politically endangered, controlled, and resolute as she keeps the archive alive under threat.

Elian activates the surveillance-tower network and broadcasts Dault’s signed lower-basin discharge order, private reservoir maps, evacuation instructions, and the names of resistant workers and threatened residents across Veyr.

Civic announcers read the Council’s written orders aloud, including its instruction to withhold Sable Ward evacuation and its planned acceptable loss, shifting the public spectacle toward the state’s flood machinery.
Engineers and relay workers in Tower Three, the dock relay, and Tower One refuse Pell’s severance order, open maintenance locks, and publicly attach their names to the continuing archive broadcast.
Pell orders the families of resistant relay workers detained and displayed, threatens engineers with loss of housing and ration status, and has the civic announcer broadcast those threats.
Senn and Maret openly refuse Pell’s command to enforce the suppression, with Senn declaring he will protect those Pell threatens and Maret insisting on witnessed confirmation for the west lift.
Ilyra publicly instructs engineers and workers to confirm pressure, routes, and receiving capacity rather than obeying her or Pell as a sole authority.

The distributed gate operation must continue through verified pressure, route, and receiving-capacity confirmations while Pell’s threatened families and resistant workers remain vulnerable to retaliation.
Maret and the lower crew must confirm the west lift’s lower shaft before releasing its upper brake, and Rian’s status must be entered on the live roll rather than assumed.

chapters.name: Everything Fails at Once
chapters.content:
The first confirmation arrived in three pieces.

A pressure reading, scratched onto a strip of copper by a hand that shook so badly the numbers climbed over one another. A route report from Sable Ward, carried through the tower line in a voice powdered with static. A receiving mark from the Old Foundry School, where twelve places had become eleven because one of the rooms had taken water through its floor.

Ilyra read the pieces beneath the white glare of the execution platform.

“Pressure?” she asked.

Elian’s voice came through the nearest lens, thin but distinct. “Confirmed by Tower Three. Western channel rising. Crown reservoir still sealed.”

“Route?”

Jorren answered from somewhere below the Hall. “Boiler room path open for four. Tram route gone. W-seven is sealed. We have three boats, and one is taking on water.”

“Receiving?”

A woman whose name Ilyra did not know said, “Old Foundry School can receive eleven if the injured are carried in pairs. No more.”

Eleven.

The number sat in Ilyra’s mind beside the thousands who had died at North Barrage Four, beside Nera’s voice in the maintenance tube, beside the child on the roof. Numbers never arrived alone anymore. They dragged names behind them.

“Do not open anything yet,” she said.

On the dais, Pell lifted his hand. The gesture had once been enough to silence a hall. Now it vanished beneath a burst of voices from the lenses. Civic announcers in three districts were reading Governor Dault’s discharge order. In another, workers were naming the detained families of the relay engineers. The crowd in the galleries had stopped chanting for the Ember Descent. Some shouted at the Council. Some shouted at Ilyra. Some shouted simply because the water had begun to show between the bronze floor plates.

Pell turned toward the lens that carried his face into every district.

“Sever the tower line,” he ordered. “Arrest the relay crews. Shut the galleries.”

No one moved.

Senn stood at the foot of the platform with his baton lowered. Behind him, one of the old bronze doors had been forced open, and a stream of prisoners came through it carrying blankets, ropes, civic stretchers, and whatever tools they had found in the abandoned wing. Mara Quill led them with a wrench tucked through her belt. Pellan followed, limping but upright, directing two men toward a woman who had fallen against the rail.

Pell saw them and seemed to age in the instant before his anger replaced surprise.

“You will return those prisoners to their cells.”

Senn did not look at him. “There are no cells dry enough to return them to.”

“That is not an answer.”

“It is the only one I have.”

A crack sounded from below.

Not the crack of timber or masonry. This was deeper: a metal complaint transmitted through the platform, a long shudder under the soles of Ilyra’s feet. The heated water beneath the execution basin lurched against its walls. Steam rolled up between the bronze ribs and blurred the mirrored lenses.

Elian’s voice cut through the haze. “The common-release basin isn’t receiving.”

Ilyra caught the copper strip from the messenger. “Why?”

“We found the inlet. It opens into a garden.”

“A garden?”

“Private. Walled. There are trees in it.”

For one absurd moment Ilyra imagined the old map as it had been drawn: a broad basin beneath the lower channels, designed to receive a sudden burden and spread it across reed beds before it reached the homes below. She saw the inked circles, the engineer’s careful notation, the words COMMON RELEASE written in a hand that believed the word meant something.

“What has been done to it?”

“Stone terraces. Ornamental pumps. The basin has been filled with soil.” Elian’s breath caught. “There’s a plaque. It calls the garden a gift to the governors.”

The next tremor threw water over the platform’s edge.

“Can the inlet be cleared?” Ilyra asked.

“Not by hand. The terraces have retaining walls. If we break the first one, the garden will go into the lower streets.”

“Which streets?”

“Crown gardens, then the west warehouse road.”

“Occupied?”

A pause.

“Of course,” Elian said.

The old instinct rose in Ilyra with such force it almost felt like relief. Take the control. Choose the channel. Put the pressure where the city’s bones could bear it. If people were in the way, calculate the number. If the number was ugly, call it necessary before anyone else could name it vengeance.

She pressed her tongue against the hidden metal pin until its edge cut her.

“Find another receiving space,” she said.

“We are looking.”

“Do not look. Ask the districts.”

Elian understood. The lenses flickered, and the voices began again.

Below the platform, Maret had been listening to the west-lift report. A copper wire ran from her hand to a small relay box bolted into the service rail. Its tiny indicator remained dark.

“Lower shaft?” she asked.

A voice answered from the wire, distant and breathless. “Not confirmed. Water in the pit. We can hear the brake, but not see the landing.”

“Then no release.”

“Your child is in Foundry Row,” Senn said quietly.

Maret’s face tightened. “I know where my child is.”

The Hall shook again. From somewhere beyond the eastern wall came a muffled roar, followed by the groan of stone settling under weight.

Maret looked toward the service passage. “If the lift does not move, Rian stays above the cooper’s shop.”

“If the brake releases before the lower shaft is confirmed,” Senn said, “the counterweight will drop through the flooded section. It will crush anyone below and drive the water up the shaft.”

“I know what it will do.”

“Then you know why we wait.”

For a heartbeat she seemed ready to strike him. Instead she tore the copper wire from the relay box.

“I am not waiting.”

She ran.

“Maret!” Senn called.

She did not turn. Her uniform vanished into the service route, pins removed, keys hidden, one hand closed around the narrow pressure strip as if it were a blade.

Ilyra watched her go and felt the old judgment form: abandonment of assigned post, unauthorized movement, compromised procedure. Then she saw Maret’s shoulders as she disappeared, carrying not a calculation but a child’s name.

“Let her pass,” Ilyra said.

Senn looked up at her. “The lift?”

“Still requires confirmation.”

“And if she reaches it?”

“Then she will have to decide whether she can obtain one.”

A shout rose from the western galleries. Water had reached the first stair. People pressed backward, trampling the viewing benches. The mirrored lenses swung on their brackets, no longer showing Ilyra’s face but the dark surge behind the gallery walls.

Pell seized a guard by the collar. “Get the descent crew to the lower controls.”

“The descent crew is carrying injured spectators,” the guard said.

“Leave them.”

The guard stared at him.

Pell slapped him. “Leave them and take the controls.”

Senn crossed the wet platform in three strides. His baton struck Pell’s wrist, not hard enough to break it, but enough to make him release the guard.

“Touch another worker,” Senn said, “and I will put you on the floor.”

Pell’s face whitened. “You are threatening a magistrate.”

“No. I am warning a man.”

Behind Senn, Mara and Pellan reached the eastern stair. A prisoner carried a boy whose hair was plastered to his forehead. Another dragged a woman with a broken ankle. The released prisoners had divided themselves without orders: some went toward the galleries, some toward the flooded service doors, some toward the archive room where Pell’s clerks were trying to tear down the broadcast equipment.

Mara saw Ilyra and stopped.

“This is your plan,” she said.

“It is the Council’s water.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “It is also mine.”

Mara’s grip tightened on the wrench. “Then make it work.”

The lens above them spat static. Elian’s voice returned, more urgent now.

“Another confirmation. Dock district can receive six. But their channel is narrow, and the workers say the lock is jammed.”

“Pressure?”

“Confirmed.”

“Route?”

“Unconfirmed. Their lower road is filling.”

“Then no release.”

“Unless we do nothing,” Elian said, “in which case Sable Ward floods through the foundry line in less than twelve minutes.”

The words went through Ilyra like cold water.

Twelve minutes. A narrow window. A perfect number for the old Ilyra, the woman who believed urgency proved authority. She could override the three confirmations from the central chamber. She knew the sequence. She knew which gates to force and which pressure locks to bypass. The execution machinery had been built around a master control, because the Council liked to call speed a virtue when speed protected the districts that mattered.

The master control was beneath the platform.

Only she could reach it quickly. Only she knew the damaged system’s old arrangement. Only she could decide which channel to sacrifice when the valves refused the commands sent through the distributed network.

She could save some districts.

She could also become the hand that chose the others.

“Elian,” she said, “what is failing?”

“Central relay is not accepting district confirmations.”

“Why?”

“Pressure spike. The receiving plate is warped.”

Ilyra looked down at the bronze belt still locked around her waist. The compromised seal had opened the maintenance collar, but the damaged locking plate hung from her chain like a small, blackened tooth. Beneath the platform, an access hatch stood open where Maret had freed her during the interrupted execution. Steam poured through it.

“I’m going below,” Ilyra said.

Senn caught her arm. “You’re chained.”

She drew the pin from beneath her tongue. Its sharpened end flashed between them.

“Not for long.”

She worked the pin into the belt’s small service catch. Her fingers slipped twice. On the third attempt, the catch yielded with a click.

Pell saw the movement. “Stop her.”

No guard obeyed.

The crowd had become a living barrier between the dais and the platform. Some people still wanted Ilyra dead. Others wanted the water stopped. Many wanted their relatives found. The city had discovered, all at once, that these desires could not be separated by a sentence read from a raised chair.

Ilyra lowered herself through the hatch.

The control chamber below was smaller than she remembered and more damaged than the maps allowed. The old master console occupied the far wall, its brass levers trembling in their sockets. Water drove through a cracked pressure window, spraying the floor in silver bursts. Three pipes had burst beneath the execution basin; the heated water that had been meant to kill her was mixing with the flood and turning the chamber into a scalding fog.

A red indicator burned above the master lever.

OVERRIDE AVAILABLE.

Her hand stopped inches from it.

In the red light, the chamber became North Barrage Four. The same metal. The same shudder beneath the floor. The same promise that if she only acted quickly enough, the people outside would become numbers she could protect.

Nera calling through the tube.

The child on the roof.

The brass key in her fist.

A voice came through the maintenance speaker. Elian, but faint now. “Ilyra, answer me.”

“I’m here.”

“The district confirmations are breaking apart. Sable Ward reports three routes open, one blocked. Old Foundry has eleven places. Dock has six if the lower road clears.”

“Can the network repair the relay?”

“Not in twelve minutes.”

The master lever shivered under her hand.

“Then I can override.”

“Yes.”

She waited for Elian to tell her not to. Elian did not.

“Tell me what happens if I do,” Ilyra said.

“You take every gate command.”

“For how long?”

“Until the pressure falls or the system tears itself apart.”

“Can you stop me?”

Another silence. “No.”

Above them, something heavy collapsed. The chamber ceiling shed dust and hot droplets. Through the speaker came the sound of people shouting, then the sharp ring of a bell from a district tower.

Ilyra imagined Maret reaching the lift. Senn carrying the wounded. Jorren below the streets, searching for four people in a boiler room while the tunnel folded around him. The garden wall holding back a basin that had once belonged to everyone. Pell standing above all of it, still believing command was the same as control.

Her fingers closed around the master lever.

The machinery woke beneath her palm. Every gauge on the wall sprang toward red. Far away, gates began to answer.

For one breath, the city was hers.

Then the speaker crackled.

“Ilyra,” Elian said. “The next command is yours alone.”

The lever pulled against her hand like a living thing.

She looked at the red light, at the trembling network beyond it, and understood the terrible seduction of being needed. If she took control, people might live. If she refused, people would certainly die. The difference between rescue and vengeance narrowed to the shape of her hand.

Above, the water struck the execution galleries.

Below, every gate waited.

And Ilyra had not yet decided whether refusing to rule was an act of responsibility—or merely another way to make the city pay for what it had made her.

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: in the damaged control chamber beneath the Ember Descent platform, hand on the activated master override while heated water and floodwater mix around the machinery. Goal: stop Sable Ward’s flooding, preserve lives, and choose between the failing distributed protocol and sole control without repeating North Barrage Four. Relationships: tense practical ally of Elian, Senn, Maret, Jorren, Mara Quill, Pellan, relay workers, and survivors; opposed by Pell and the Council; accountable to the dead and publicly exposed. Knowledge: Old Foundry School can receive eleven, the dock route is conditional, the common-release basin is a private garden, Jorren’s tram route collapsed, W-seven is sealed, the relay is failing, Maret has gone toward Foundry Row, and the master override can seize every gate command. Possessions: soaked heat-damaged white robe, bronze belt and chain, sharpened metal pin, compromised seal, charcoal, copper wire, damaged locking plate, brass cylinder, maps, pressure readings, and broadcast evidence. Condition: blistered, exhausted, lucid, morally frightened, and tempted by the power to save some districts through unilateral control.

set.name: Oren Pell
set.description: Location: on the flooded judicial dais above the Ember Descent platform, attempting to direct guards and restore the execution spectacle as water reaches the galleries. Goal: suppress the archive, isolate blame on Ilyra, seize resistant workers and witnesses, and preserve Council authority through threats. Relationships: adversarial toward Ilyra, Elian, Senn, Maret, Jorren, Mara Quill, Pellan, relay workers, and survivors; increasingly defied by guards and prisoners. Knowledge: knows the broadcast has exposed Council orders, the common basin is blocked, the countergate is failing, and his orders to abandon injured spectators are no longer obeyed. Possessions: judicial robes, execution orders, broadcast authority, arrest and suppression orders, manipulated death-roll instructions, and nominal command of the guards. Condition: furious, frightened, publicly isolated, and dependent on coercion.

set.name: Maret
set.description: Location: moving alone through the flooded service route toward the west lift and Foundry Row after abandoning the relay post. Goal: reach and evacuate her seven-year-old child Rian and grandmother while preventing an unsafe lift release. Relationships: conflicted but cooperating with Ilyra; allied cautiously with Senn, Elian, Jorren, Mara, Pellan, released prisoners, relay workers, and survivors; openly resistant to Pell. Knowledge: the west lift’s lower shaft remains unconfirmed and flooded, early brake release could kill people below, Rian remains above a cooper’s shop, and the Hall’s water is rising. Possessions: hidden keys, divided pressure readings, narrow Crown-line strip, copper wire, and service-route knowledge. Condition: frightened, physically strained, grieving, furious, and determined.

set.name: Senn
set.description: Location: on the flooded Ember Descent platform and Hall galleries, coordinating wounded evacuation with released prisoners while Pell’s authority collapses. Goal: protect threatened residents and workers, keep rescue from becoming vengeance, and prevent an unsafe gate release while holding Ilyra accountable. Relationships: hostile toward Ilyra but cooperating with her; allied with Jorren, Maret, Elian, Mara, Pellan, relay workers, prisoners, and survivors; openly defying Pell. Knowledge: the galleries are flooding, the distributed relay is failing, the west lift lacks lower-shaft confirmation, and Pell ordered guards to abandon injured spectators. Possessions: civic uniform, baton, keys, false death roll, pressure readings, names of threatened residents, and relay access. Condition: soaked, bloodied, angry, vigilant, and committed to rescue over command.

set.name: Elian Dault
set.description: Location: inside Tower One’s relay chamber, maintaining the archive broadcast while district confirmations fragment under pressure. Goal: keep Council evidence and threatened names public, coordinate district confirmations, and prevent Ilyra from becoming sole ruler of the gates. Relationships: tense but effective ally of Ilyra; allied with Senn, Maret, Jorren, Mara, Pellan, relay workers, prisoners, and survivors; adversarial toward Pell and Governor Dault. Knowledge: Old Foundry can receive eleven, dock capacity is conditional, the common-release basin is a private garden, Jorren’s route collapsed, the central relay plate is warped, and Ilyra has activated the master override. Possessions: archival packets, Council minutes, reservoir orders, false rolls, basin map, pressure readings, relay tools, and broadcast authority. Condition: exhausted, wet, politically endangered, controlled but urgently afraid.

set.description: Location: in the lower service and tunnel network near Sable Ward after the tram evacuation route collapsed. Goal: reach four survivors trapped in a boiler room and evacuate remaining residents without disguising impossible capacity as arithmetic. Relationships: blames Ilyra for his family’s deaths but cooperates with Senn, Elian, Maret, Mara, Pellan, workers, prisoners, and survivors; opposed to Pell and the Council. Knowledge: eleven survivors escaped the lower tram sheds, four remain in the boiler room, the tram route is gone, W-seven is sealed, only three boats remain, and one boat is damaged. Possessions: diver’s harness, rope, knife, copper rings, damaged pressure gauge, and pressure-reading section. Condition: soaked, bleeding, driven, grieving, and under severe time pressure.

set.description: Location: on the flooded Hall stairs with released prisoners, carrying wounded spectators and directing alternate service routes. Goal: move survivors toward usable receiving spaces and prevent limited capacity from becoming an excuse to abandon everyone else. Relationships: distrustful of Ilyra and Senn’s uniforms but cooperating with both; allied provisionally with Pellan, prisoners, district representatives, workers, and survivors; opposed to Pell. set.name: Pellan
set.description: Location: on the flooded Hall stairs with Mara Quill and released prisoners, helping carry wounded people from the galleries. Goal: identify safe routes, assist evacuation, and keep the released group from becoming an uncontrolled mob. Relationships: provisionally allied with Mara, Senn, Ilyra, workers, district representatives, prisoners, and survivors; distrustful of Pell and the Council. Knowledge: the tram route is collapsed, service routes are flooding, receiving capacity is limited, and no person should carry a gate key without a second witness. Possessions: prisoner’s work clothes and civic wrench. Condition: physically strained, cautious, resentful, wet, and focused on practical rescue.

The first countergate confirmations reveal that the Old Foundry School can receive only eleven injured residents, the dock district has limited conditional capacity, and the distributed relay is already failing under the pressure spike.

The common-release basin is discovered converted into a walled private governor’s garden with terraces and ornamental pumps, preventing it from receiving the western surge without dangerous demolition.
Jorren’s tram evacuation route collapses and W-seven remains sealed, leaving only three boats, one damaged, to reach the remaining Sable Ward survivors.
Senn and the released prisoners begin carrying wounded people through the flooded Hall, while Senn refuses Pell’s order to abandon them and strike for the controls.
Maret abandons the west-lift relay post to reach Rian and his grandmother in Foundry Row, while Senn insists the lift cannot be released before the flooded lower shaft is confirmed safe.
Ilyra reaches the damaged control chamber beneath the execution platform and activates the master override, discovering that she can seize every gate command but has not yet chosen whether to do so.

Ilyra must decide whether to use the master override, which would restore sole authority over every gate, or continue the distributed protocol while the damaged system and districts remain under immediate time pressure.
The converted common-release basin remains blocked by the governors’ private garden, forcing the coalition to find or create receiving capacity without simply sacrificing another occupied district.
Maret’s attempt to reach Foundry Row must establish whether Rian and his grandmother can be rescued, while the west lift remains locked until its flooded lower shaft is witnessed safe.

chapters.name: The Choice Below
chapters.content:
The master lever pulled against Ilyra’s hand like a living thing.

Every gauge on the wall had swung toward red. Behind the brass faces, needles trembled in their sockets, each one registering a district, a channel, a choice. The controls did not care who had built the city or who had been drowned beneath it. They answered pressure. They answered force. They answered the hand that claimed them.

For one breath, Veyr was hers.

Then the hatch above clanged open.

Elian dropped through the steam, caught the ladder with one hand, and struck the floor hard enough to slide across the wet metal. Her archive packets were tied beneath her coat. Water streamed from her hair and ran black with soot along her cheek.

“You came down,” Ilyra said.

“I was afraid you would mistake my voice for permission.”

A burst of heat crossed the chamber. Elian raised her sleeve over her mouth and crouched beside the relay cabinet. “Move your hand.”

“I can stabilize the western pressure.”

“You can command the western pressure.”

“The distinction is not useful in twelve minutes.”

“It was not useful at North Barrage Four either.”

The words struck more cleanly than the steam. Ilyra’s fingers tightened around the lever.

Above them, the flood hit the execution galleries with a sound like a building breathing its last. The chamber shook. A lamp tore loose from its bracket and burst against the floor. Darkness swallowed the room except for the red indicator over the master control.

Elian found the relay box by touch. “How much of the network can you still hear?”

“Enough.”

“Ask it.”

Ilyra looked at the speaker grille. “Sable Ward, report.”

Static answered first. Then a man’s voice, hoarse and close to breaking. “Foundry Row route open from the lower cooper’s lane. Water at the second stair. We have marked three roofs with white cloth. We need a receiving district.”

“Names?” Elian asked.

The voice hesitated. “Anja Meret and children Leth, Ovan, Suri. Six foundry workers. Two elders. More coming.”

Ilyra closed her eyes. The names entered the chamber and made it smaller.

“Route confirmation,” she said. “Sable Ward, give your witness.”

“Baret at the western relay,” another voice answered. “I see the lane. I see the roof marks. I confirm the route, not the capacity.”

“Receiving?”

A third voice burst in, distorted by static. “Old Foundry remains eleven, but we have eight bodies already and two cannot walk. Dock channel is narrowing. We may receive six if the lower road is cleared.”

“Who speaks for the dock?” Elian said.

“Rusk,” came the answer. “I have the lock crew with me. We can clear the road if the pressure drops.”

“If,” Ilyra repeated.

Elian’s hand disappeared into the relay cabinet. “We need the district representatives to say what they can receive, not what they hope to receive.”

“They are doing that.”

“No. They are offering themselves as basins. That is what the Council taught everyone to do.”

The sentence brought back the old maps: lower district as basin, homes as acceptable loss, bodies converted into a word that sounded clean when written in a margin. Ilyra had hated that language. She had also used it. A basin was only a district whose people had not been invited to call themselves anything else.

She released the master lever by a fraction.

The gauges lurched. A valve somewhere beyond the chamber slammed shut, then opened again with a shriek.

Elian looked up. “What did you do?”

“Nothing permanent.”

“That is not an answer.”

“I let the network breathe.”

“Then let it choose.”

“You heard the reports. The relay is failing.”

“And you heard the reports. The routes are changing. If you take control now, every district becomes an instruction you issue from a room they cannot enter.”

“I know the system.”

“You know the machinery.”

“It is the same thing.”

“No.” Elian’s voice rose above the pipes. “It is exactly the lie they used. They said knowing the channels meant they knew the people who lived beside them. They said a governor could decide what a neighborhood could lose because he had read the pressure tables. They said urgency made consent unnecessary.”

Ilyra turned on her. “You think consent will hold the wall?”

“No. Workers will hold it. Residents will hold it. Engineers will hold it. You will help them.”

“While we wait for a committee to agree?”

“While we wait for the people beneath the water to tell us where their doors are.”

Another tremor rolled through the chamber. The master lever jumped beneath Ilyra’s palm. A line of heated water broke from the ceiling and struck the floor between them. Steam blinded her. She heard Elian cry out and reached blindly, finding her wrist.

“Back,” Ilyra said.

“I’m not leaving.”

“Back!”

For an instant the word carried the old authority. She heard it as Pell would have heard it, as Nera had heard every order through the maintenance tube. A command made sharp by fear and defended as competence.

Elian did not move.

“Tell me,” she said, “which gate do you open?”

“The western relief gate.”

“And what floods?”

“Crown gardens and the warehouse road.”

“Who is there?”

“Workers, guards, families who received the evacuation notices late.”

“Which gate, Ilyra?”

The question stayed in the steam.

She saw the roof again. The child’s small hand lifted against the gray sky. The brass valve key had been heavy, warm from her grip. She had told herself the pump station would save more people. That had been true. It had also been true that she had not wanted to drop the key. She had wanted to be the person who carried the answer.

“I do not know,” she said.

Elian’s grip loosened on her wrist.

“That is the first honest thing you’ve said since I came down.”

“I know what happens if we wait.”

“Yes.”

“People die.”

“Yes.”

“If I act, people die differently.”

“That is not the same as saying you may choose them.”

Ilyra looked at the red indicator. The light reflected in the water around her boots, a small burning sun broken into ripples.

“North Barrage Four had no time for three confirmations.”

“Did it have time for one more person to know the full danger?”

Ilyra said nothing.

“Nera trusted you,” Elian continued. “You decided what she could bear to know. You called that protection. Then you made a choice she could not consent to and called it necessity. You may be right about the pressure. You may be right about the minutes. You may even save more people by taking that lever.”

The last admission was worse than accusation.

“But being right about the danger,” Elian said, “does not make you rightful over everyone’s sacrifice.”

The master control hummed. The chamber offered her the clean shape of an answer: seize, redirect, close, release. A sequence. A result. No argument, no delay, no witness who could say the gate should have opened elsewhere.

Ilyra removed her hand.

The red indicator flickered but did not go dark.

Elian exhaled once. “Can you disable the override?”

“No.”

“Can you prevent it from accepting commands?”

“Not without cutting the central relay.”

“Then leave it.”

“You want a temptation bolted to the wall?”

“I want the truth visible.”

The speaker crackled. A new voice entered, breathless and young. “Foundry Row to central. We have reached the cooper’s shop. There is a child and an elderly woman above the roofline. Water is through the upper windows.”

Ilyra knew before the speaker finished.

“Name the child,” she said.

“Rian.”

Maret’s voice broke through behind him. “Rian Senn. Grandmother alive. Lower lift shaft still flooded. We have rope access from the cooper’s roof. We can move them by hand if the current holds.”

Senn’s voice came over another line. “Maret, do not release the lift.”

“I’m not releasing it,” she answered. “I’m taking the roof route.”

“Confirm the route.”

“I confirm what I can see.”

“The receiving district?”

Silence. Water roared behind her.

“Foundry Row has no room,” Maret said. “The school is full. The dock road is blocked.”

“Then mark them live,” Elian said. “Do not let their absence become a death.”

A faint scratching followed, as if someone were writing on metal.

Ilyra pressed both palms against the relay cabinet. “Open the district channel.”

Elian stared at her. “You just said the relay was failing.”

“It is. We will use the failures.”

She pointed to the warped receiving plate. “The central confirmation is rejecting simultaneous signals because the plate is bent. Split the commands into staggered pulses. Pressure first. Route second. Receiving capacity third. No gate receives all three from one source.”

“Elian, I need the district voices on separate lines.”

“I can patch them.”

“You can patch what you can reach.”

“Yes.”

“Then do it.”

Elian seized the copper wire and stripped it with her teeth. “You will not touch the master control.”

“I won’t.”

“If a command fails?”

“We send it again through the district that owns the route.”

“If it fails again?”

“We do not replace their refusal with my order.”

Elian held her gaze. “Say it clearly.”

Ilyra looked toward the speaker, though the people listening were scattered through towers, tunnels, foundries, boats, kitchens, prison corridors, and roofs above the water.

“No gate opens on my authority,” she said. “No district is treated as an empty basin. Pressure, route, and receiving capacity must be confirmed separately by the people who bear them. If a confirmation fails, we wait for another answer. We do not make silence consent.”

Elian patched the first line.

The chamber filled with voices.

Tower Three confirmed the western pressure. Baret named the reading and the time. Sable Ward confirmed the white-marked roofs and the cooper’s lane, though the water had risen to the third stair. The dock workers reported that the lower road was obstructed by a fallen tram carriage. Old Foundry revised its capacity from eleven to nine, then to ten when two residents opened a dry classroom. A woman from Crown gardens said the ornamental wall could be breached from the north side, but only if the garden’s residents were moved first.

No voice sounded certain. That uncertainty was not a flaw in the room. It was the room.

“Send the first command,” Ilyra said.

Elian’s fingers moved over the relay contacts. “Which?”

“Western pressure to relief channel two. Sable route confirmed. Receiving pending.”

“Without receiving?”

“Not a gate opening. A preparation command. Lower the retaining lock by one mark. Let the workers know what pressure is coming.”

Elian nodded and transmitted.

Somewhere beneath Crown gardens, workers answered. A gauge on the wall shifted from red to amber.

The change was small. It did not save anyone. It did not absolve her. But it had passed through other hands before reaching the machinery.

“Next,” Ilyra said.

A new report came from Sable Ward. The white cloth on the cooper’s roof had vanished beneath the water. Maret and two prisoners were moving Rian and his grandmother by rope across the adjoining roof. The live roll had been marked: Rian Senn, present; grandmother, present. Anja Meret and her children remained at the foundry stairs. Jorren’s voice announced that the four survivors in the boiler room were still alive, but the only passage to them was narrowing.

Ilyra felt the master lever waiting behind her.

It would have been faster. She knew that now not as an argument but as a fact. It might have opened the relief channel before the confirmation arrived. It might have saved the boiler room. It might also have driven the western surge into the road where the named families were moving.

Facts did not become rights merely because they were urgent.

“Tell Jorren to mark the boiler room as a live obstruction,” she said. “No one calls them lost. Ask which wall can be opened from their side.”

Elian transmitted.

The answer came after a long interval. “North wall has a steam pipe. If we cut it, the room vents into the service trench. We need pressure lowered first.”

“Then that is the next command,” Ilyra said.

“Pressure confirmation?”

“Tower Three.”

“Route confirmation?”

“Jorren.”

“Receiving?”

The chamber went quiet.

Beyond the walls, Veyr groaned. The execution galleries were still filling. Pell was still above, issuing orders that fewer people obeyed. The Crown gardens still held the basin shut with stone and privilege. Maret still carried a child across a roof. Every answer had a cost. Every delay had a body inside it.

Elian touched the relay wire. “We wait for receiving.”

Ilyra nodded.

The master control shuddered unattended. Its red light burned over the water, over the damaged maps, over the woman who had once believed that responsibility meant taking the lever before anyone could stop her.

This time Ilyra stood beside it with empty hands.

She listened as the districts argued, contradicted themselves, revised their numbers, and named their living. She listened until waiting became an action shared with people she could not see.

Then, through the static, a worker from the service trench said, “We can receive the pressure if the foundry opens its east doors.”

A district representative answered, “The east doors lead through occupied homes.”

“Then ask them,” Ilyra said.

Elian looked at her.

“Ask them,” Ilyra repeated. “Do not decide for them.”

The question went out across the failing network.

Below the city, the gates waited. Above it, the water rose. And in the chamber beneath the place built for her death, Ilyra Voss did not take the master control. She sent the command outward and waited for the answer to come back in more than one voice.

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: in the damaged control chamber beneath the Ember Descent platform, standing beside the activated but unused master override while heated water and floodwater mix around the machinery. Goal: stop Sable Ward’s flooding, preserve lives, and coordinate a shared gate response without becoming sole ruler of the water. Relationships: tense practical ally of Elian, Senn, Maret, Jorren, Mara Quill, Pellan, relay workers, and survivors; opposed by Pell and the Council; accountable to the dead and publicly exposed. Knowledge: the Old Foundry and dock capacities are changing, the common-release basin is blocked by a private garden, Jorren’s route has collapsed, W-seven is sealed, the relay is failing, Maret has reached Foundry Row, Rian and his grandmother are alive and on the live roll, and staggered pressure-route-receiving confirmations can use the failing network without granting her sole authority. Possessions: soaked heat-damaged white robe, bronze belt and chain, sharpened metal pin, compromised seal, charcoal, copper wire, damaged locking plate, brass cylinder, maps, pressure readings, and broadcast evidence. Condition: blistered, exhausted, lucid, morally frightened, and choosing to keep her hands off the master control despite knowing unilateral action may be faster.

set.name: Maret
set.description: Location: on the roofs of Foundry Row after reaching the cooper’s shop, moving Rian and his grandmother by rope with two released prisoners while the west lift remains locked. Goal: evacuate her seven-year-old child and grandmother, keep them entered on the live roll, and prevent an unsafe lift release. Relationships: conflicted but cooperating with Ilyra; allied cautiously with Senn, Elian, Jorren, Mara, Pellan, released prisoners, relay workers, and survivors; openly resistant to Pell. Knowledge: Rian and his grandmother are alive, the roof route is currently usable, the lower lift shaft remains unconfirmed and flooded, Anja Meret and her children remain at the foundry stairs, and the distributed protocol requires witnessed route and receiving confirmations. Possessions: hidden keys, divided pressure readings, narrow Crown-line strip, copper wire, and service-route knowledge. Condition: frightened, physically strained, soaked, furious, and determined as she carries her child across the flooded roofs.

set.name: Senn
set.description: Location: on the flooded Ember Descent platform and Hall galleries, coordinating wounded evacuation and monitoring the west-lift and Foundry Row reports while Pell’s authority collapses. Goal: protect threatened residents and workers, keep rescue from becoming vengeance, and prevent an unsafe gate or lift release while holding Ilyra accountable. Relationships: hostile toward Ilyra but cooperating with her; allied with Jorren, Maret, Elian, Mara, Pellan, relay workers, prisoners, and survivors; openly defying Pell. Knowledge: the galleries are flooding, the distributed relay now uses staggered confirmations, the west lift lacks lower-shaft confirmation, Rian and his grandmother are alive and marked on the live roll, and Anja’s family remains threatened at the foundry stairs. Possessions: civic uniform, baton, keys, false death roll, pressure readings, names of threatened residents, and relay access. Condition: soaked, bloodied, angry, vigilant, and committed to rescue over command.

set.name: Elian Dault
set.description: Location: inside the damaged control chamber beneath the Ember Descent platform with Ilyra, patching the warped relay and transmitting staggered district commands. Goal: keep Council evidence and threatened names public, coordinate independently witnessed pressure, route, and receiving confirmations, and prevent Ilyra from becoming sole ruler of the gates. Relationships: tense but effective ally of Ilyra; allied with Senn, Maret, Jorren, Mara, Pellan, relay workers, prisoners, and survivors; adversarial toward Pell and Governor Dault. Knowledge: the master override can seize every gate, Ilyra has agreed not to use it, district capacities and routes are changing, Rian and his grandmother are alive in Foundry Row, and the relay can carry separated confirmation pulses despite its damage. Possessions: archival packets, Council minutes, reservoir orders, false rolls, basin map, pressure readings, relay tools, copper wire, and broadcast authority. Condition: exhausted, wet, soot-streaked, politically endangered, controlled but urgently afraid.

set.name: Jorren Pell
set.description: Location: in the lower service and tunnel network near Sable Ward after the tram evacuation route collapsed, coordinating access to four survivors in a boiler room. Goal: reach and evacuate the trapped survivors and remaining residents without disguising impossible capacity as arithmetic. Relationships: blames Ilyra for his family’s deaths but cooperates with Senn, Elian, Maret, Mara, Pellan, workers, prisoners, and survivors; opposed to Pell and the Council. Knowledge: eleven survivors escaped the lower tram sheds, four remain alive in the boiler room, the tram route is gone, W-seven is sealed, only three boats remain with one damaged, and the boiler room’s north wall can vent into the service trench if pressure is first lowered and receiving capacity confirmed. Possessions: diver’s harness, rope, knife, copper rings, damaged pressure gauge, and pressure-reading section. Condition: soaked, bleeding, driven, grieving, and under severe time pressure.
Elian enters the damaged control chamber and confronts Ilyra’s attempt to use the master override, comparing her urgency to the Council’s justification for deciding sacrifices at North Barrage Four.
Ilyra acknowledges that technical correctness and urgency do not grant her the right to choose everyone’s sacrifice, removes her hand from the master control, and leaves the override unused.

Elian and Ilyra adapt the failing relay into staggered pressure, route, and receiving-capacity pulses, requiring district witnesses to confirm each part separately rather than allowing Ilyra to command a gate alone.

Maret reaches Foundry Row and confirms Rian and his grandmother alive; both are entered on the live roll while Maret and prisoners begin moving them across the roofs without releasing the unconfirmed west lift.

The staggered district protocol must produce a verified pressure, route, and receiving-capacity sequence for at least one relief command while the central relay continues failing and the Crown garden remains an obstruction.
Rian and his grandmother have been marked present while crossing the Foundry Row roofs, but their evacuation remains incomplete and must be confirmed without releasing the unsafe west lift.
Anja Meret and her children remain live at the flooded foundry stairs and must be evacuated or accurately recorded among the missing before the Council can erase them.

chapters.name: The Flood Divided
chapters.content:
The first confirmation arrived as three separate knocks in the relay.

Pressure.

Route.

Receiving.

Then the line broke into a hiss.

Ilyra stood with both hands braced against the edge of the control table and listened to the silence that followed. Beneath the platform, the chamber shook with the force of water moving through passages never meant to carry it. Heated water from the execution basin ran in silver threads along the floor, mixing with the colder flood rising through the service grates. Steam drifted beneath the ceiling, turning the relay lamps into blurred stars.

“Again,” Elian said.

“I heard it.”

“You heard the pressure pulse. Not the receiving confirmation.”

“I heard enough to know the west channel can take the load.”

Elian’s face tightened. “That is not the same thing.”

Ilyra looked at the master override. Its brass handle trembled in its housing, waiting for the hand that would make every district a subordinate instrument. She had left it untouched. The choice had not made the chamber safer. It had only made every delay visible.

A fresh pulse struck the relay. This time the voices came through together, ragged and overlapping.

“Foundry route open—”

“—lower stairs taking water—”

“—receiving space at Old Foundry reduced to—”

“—Crown channel refuses—”

The last voice was clear enough to stop the others.

“Crown District refuses release.”

Elian seized the speaking tube. “Identify the witness.”

A woman answered. “Engineer Sel Vey. Crown irrigation station. We have received the pressure figures. We will not open the channel.”

“Your channel is the only one that reaches the eastern industrial trench,” Elian said. “Without it, the west surge will remain against Sable Ward.”

“We know what it reaches.”

Ilyra leaned toward the tube. “Then say it.”

There was a pause. In the background, someone was shouting. Another voice called out that the gardens were already flooding.

“Crown’s lower terraces,” Sel said. “The warehouse court. The glasshouses. Three residential streets.”

“Mostly occupied by servants and warehouse families,” Elian said.

“Occupied by people,” Sel replied. “We are not opening a channel that drowns them to save Sable Ward.”

Ilyra felt the old answer rise in her, clean and immediate: open the gate. The numbers had already arranged themselves in her mind. If Crown remained closed, the pressure would climb through Sable’s foundry drains. The first industrial row would fail. Then the tenements behind it. The water would meet the packed streets and carry fire from the furnaces into the flood. If Crown opened, the channel would take a portion of the surge, but the low terraces would be lost.

A choice made by geometry.

A choice made by someone.

She reached for the charcoal and wrote figures across the damp table. Elian watched her, not stopping her, not trusting the motion.

“How many?” she asked.

Sel’s answer came after a delay. “We have no current census.”

“Use the live roll.”

“The roll is incomplete.”

“So is every roll.” Ilyra pushed the speaking tube closer. “Tell me what you have.”

“Four hundred and twelve in the lower terraces. Two hundred and six in the warehouse court. Ninety-three in the glasshouses and adjoining quarters. More unregistered workers may be there.”

“And Sable?”

Jorren’s voice broke in from another relay. “At least three thousand in the pressure path. Six hundred in the foundry blocks. More moving toward the stairs. Four in the boiler room still alive. Anja Meret and her children are at Foundry Stair Four. We have a rope route, but the next rise may cut it.”

Senn’s voice followed him. “Rian and the grandmother are off the cooper’s roof. Alive. Maret has them at the receiving shed.”

For one breath, Ilyra allowed herself relief. It felt indecently bright.

Then the relay carried Maret’s voice. “The shed is taking water. We need the eastern channel or we lose the route.”

The voices fell silent again.

Ilyra looked at the map. The Crown channel was drawn in blue, a decorative line beneath orchard symbols and the names of estates. Its old purpose had been to carry emergency overflow toward the industrial trench. At some point, the Council had turned its first basin into gardens, its second into warehouses, its third into a walled promenade. The city had not eliminated the flood path. It had placed wealth on top of it and called the danger solved.

Sel spoke again. “If we open, Crown will flood. People are moving into the upper streets, but the stair gates are locked. We need time.”

“Unlock the stair gates,” Ilyra said.

“The wardens will not.”

“Then name them.”

“Their families are in the district.”

Ilyra closed her eyes. The old machinery of fear was everywhere: at the gates, in the records, inside the mouths of people trying to save one another. Pell had built it so thoroughly that even refusal could become an act of protection.

“Sel,” she said, “I am going to give you the figures. You will repeat them to the station, and you will let the residents hear them. No order. No command. Only the projected outcomes.”

Elian glanced at her. “Ilyra.”

“I know.”

“You do not know the numbers precisely.”

“I know the range.”

“That is not precision.”

“It is more honest than calling the deaths acceptable.”

She drew two columns on the table. “If Crown remains closed, the pressure reaches Sable’s foundry line in twelve minutes. The first collapse is likely within four. The water depth in the lower blocks will rise above the second floors in nine. We project between eighteen hundred and twenty-four hundred people trapped before rescue access fails. If Crown opens within three minutes, the terraces flood to the upper gardens. The warehouse court loses its lower levels. We project between two hundred and five hundred people endangered, depending on how quickly the stair gates open.”

Jorren cut in. “Those are not deaths.”

“No,” Ilyra said. “They are people we may be able to move.”

“And if the routes fail?”

“Then the number changes.”

“Into what?”

She stared at the wet charcoal. “Into names.”

The word traveled through the relay. Perhaps the station heard it. Perhaps the whole city did. The archive broadcast had not stopped, and somewhere above them the civic announcers were still reading Council orders into the rising noise.

A new voice entered the channel, a man’s, breathless and furious. “You want us to drown for people who have never paid a Crown levy? Sable Ward took the water for generations. Let the gates hold.”

Another voice answered him. “My sister is in the warehouse court.”

“Then get her out.”

“The stair gates are locked.”

“Because opening them lets the flood into the upper streets.”

“Because you built your streets over the basin.”

The argument broke apart into shouting.

Ilyra’s fingers tightened around the charcoal until it snapped. For an instant she was back at North Barrage Four, hearing Nera through the maintenance tube, hearing the child’s voice behind the door. She had known the mathematics. She had known the alternatives. She had also known which lives she could bear to make abstract.

“Elian,” she said, “put the projected paths on the broadcast.”

“Elaborate.”

“Not just the figures. The map. Crown channel to eastern trench. Sable pressure line. The garden basin. Show what blocks what.”

“The Council will call it an incitement.”

“Let them call a map whatever they need.”

Elian turned to the relay board. Copper wire flashed between her hands as she patched the damaged circuit. “Sel, can you open local speakers?”

“I can open them if the station power holds.”

“Do it.”

The Crown channel filled with a harsh burst of static. Then Elian’s voice, carrying through the district, began to describe the water. She did not say sacrifice. She did not say necessary. She said: here is the pressure; here are the routes; here are the occupied buildings; here is what remains unconfirmed.

For a moment, no one spoke.

Then a worker said, “The lower garden wall is already cracking.”

A woman answered, “My children are in Glasshouse Three.”

“Move them to the north arcade.”

“The arcade is closed.”

“Break it.”

“Who confirms the route?”

“I do.”

“Who receives them?”

“The schoolhouse on Crown Rise.”

“The schoolhouse is full.”

“Not full,” another voice said. “The Council’s guards are using it for stores.”

Senn came over the line. “Mara, can your people clear the stores?”

Mara answered from somewhere amid the Hall’s flooding galleries. “If the doors are not barred.”

“Pellan?”

“Give us six minutes.”

“You have four,” Jorren said.

“Then give us four.”

Ilyra heard machinery groan below the platform. The pressure graph climbed another mark.

“Sel,” she said, “what do you need to open?”

“Two mechanical confirmations and a district witness.”

“I am not the district witness.”

“No. We have a residents’ assembly forming at the irrigation station.”

“Then let them decide.”

Elian looked over her shoulder. “If they refuse, Sable collapses.”

“Yes.”

“And if they agree, Crown floods.”

“Yes.”

“You are willing to let them make the choice.”

“I am willing to stop pretending the choice belongs to me.”

The pressure graph flickered. A red lamp came on beside the Sable line.

Jorren’s voice sharpened. “Ilyra, we have water through the boiler-room vents. The four are alive. We can vent the north wall if the pressure drops, but we need the eastern trench open.”

“Can you reach Anja?”

“Rope route is holding.”

Maret came through, panting. “Rian and his grandmother are at the receiving shed. Live roll updated. I have two prisoners with me. We can take another group if the shed stays above the waterline.”

“Anja’s children are—”

“Still at Stair Four,” Senn said. “Leth, Ovan, Suri. I have them on the live roll. Their route is blocked by a collapsed furnace bridge.”

Ilyra’s eyes went to the Crown channel line. If it opened, the pressure would fall enough for Jorren to vent the boiler room and for Senn’s people to cross the lower service route. If it remained closed, the bridge would not matter. The entire foundry line would become a wall of water.

Above, the crowd in the galleries began to chant. The words were indistinct, but the rhythm was familiar. They had come to see the Ember Descent. They wanted a body to explain the flood.

“Sel,” Ilyra said, “tell the assembly exactly what I have told you. Tell them what happens if they refuse. Tell them what happens if they open. Include your own station. Include the names of the people you know are there.”

“Will you certify the figures?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because certification is what people use to turn predictions into permission.”

The line went quiet.

Then Sel said, “Understood.”

Elian’s broadcast carried the words outward. The map appeared in fragments on the surveillance lenses: blue channels, red pressure lines, black blocks where routes had collapsed. Across Veyr, people watched the protected gardens become what they had always been—a lid over a flood path.

The residents’ assembly argued for three minutes. Ilyra counted every second. At the second minute, someone reported the garden wall had split. At the third, a worker shouted that the upper gate was jammed. At the fourth, Sel returned.

“The assembly agrees,” she said. Her voice shook. “We open the Crown channel after the north arcade is cleared. The residents require the route confirmation first.”

“Who confirms?” Elian asked.

“Three residents, two workers, and Engineer Sel Vey.”

“Receiving capacity?”

“Crown Rise schoolhouse: one hundred and eighty, if the stores are removed. The dock district will take another two hundred, conditional on the eastern trench staying below the third marker.”

Mara’s voice arrived through the static. “Stores are out. Schoolhouse is open. I confirm receiving.”

A second voice followed, old and hard. “Crown Rise confirms.”

Senn said, “Hall relay confirms route to dock.”

Jorren: “Pressure at the eastern trench is falling by one mark. I confirm the boiler vent can open.”

Ilyra waited. “Sel?”

“Residents confirm.”

“Open.”

The command did not come from her. It passed through the channel, gathered by witnesses, and returned as an action shared among hands.

Somewhere beyond the chamber, a lock released.

The sound was not dramatic. No bell rang. No official declared victory. There was only a deep metallic shudder, followed by the rush of water finding a path.

The graph bent.

The Sable line dropped by one mark, then another. The Crown line flared white. Reports erupted through the relay.

“Water in the lower terraces!”

“North arcade clear!”

“Move the children!”

“Warehouse court collapsing—”

“Not the upper court. The lower court only.”

“Glasshouse Three breached.”

“Rian’s shed still standing.”

“Anja’s rope route open!”

“Boiler room venting!”

Ilyra gripped the table as the whole building lurched. The private garden basin gave way. Stone terraces folded into the water, ornamental pumps spinning once before vanishing. The flood tore through Crown’s lower streets, into warehouses stacked with grain, cloth, and imported luxuries. Barrels broke loose and struck the walls. Trees floated past the surveillance lenses, roots exposed, their leaves bright against the brown water.

Sable Ward did not escape. The foundry blocks filled to the windows. Homes collapsed where old brick had been left unrepaired. Machines, benches, tools, and family tables were carried into the channels together. But the pressure no longer rose as one solid front. It divided through the opened channel, the emergency basins, the industrial trench, and the routes workers had cleared by hand.

“Four in the boiler room coming out,” Jorren reported. “Alive.”

Senn’s voice broke with relief and exhaustion. “Anja and the children crossed. Leth, Ovan, Suri all present.”

Maret came next. “Rian and his grandmother are at Crown Rise. Alive. The receiving shed is lost.”

Ilyra let the words enter her without trying to own them.

Elian read the latest pressure marks. “The Crown reservoirs are exposed. The private lines are visible through the breach.”

“Broadcast it,” Ilyra said.

“It is already broadcasting.”

On the wall, the city’s water network glowed in broken colors. The Council’s protected infrastructure had not been a hidden miracle or a necessary defense. It had been a set of gates, gardens, warehouses, and sealed stairs built to make one district’s safety appear natural.

The flood had not chosen justice. It had taken homes from Sable and Crown alike. It had destroyed factories where people worked and gardens where officials entertained themselves. It had spared some families and drowned others according to elevations, walls, timing, and the luck of a rope holding another minute.

No calculation could turn that into balance.

But the channels had opened because people had heard the numbers and refused to let anyone else call their dead acceptable.

Ilyra looked once more at the master override. Water streamed around its base. The handle remained untouched.

“Next confirmation,” Elian said.

Ilyra nodded. “Next confirmation.”

set.name: Ilyra Voss
set.description: Location: in the damaged control chamber beneath the Ember Descent platform, beside the activated but unused master override while divided floodwater and heated water move around the machinery. Goal: continue coordinating shared gate responses, preserve lives, and keep no single person sovereign over the water. Relationships: tense practical ally of Elian, Senn, Maret, Jorren, Mara Quill, Pellan, relay workers, Sel Vey, and survivors; opposed by Pell and the Council; accountable to the dead and publicly exposed. Knowledge: Crown residents and workers opened the eastern channel after hearing projected deaths on both sides; the private garden basin has collapsed, Crown reservoirs and protected infrastructure are exposed, Sable Ward and Crown have both suffered major damage, Jorren’s boiler-room survivors are alive, Anja and her children crossed safely, and Rian and his grandmother reached Crown Rise.
